p.h: Was China's Tartar conqueror Tamerlane?
p.g: Ricci writes that China had never been wholly conquered by foreigners until a Tartar leader invaded; his line ruled until 1368, when the Chinese threw off the yoke and the Ming founder Hongwu expelled the Tartars. Some Jesuits guessed this conqueror was Tamerlane, because the Chinese called him 'Tiemor'. Ricci gives up and simply calls him 'the Tartar'. The Chinese name was almost certainly Tiemuzhen, that is Temüjin (Chinggis Khan), not Timur, who lived a century later and never reached China.
p.q: nunquam tamen prius ab externis populis legitur universim esse subactum, quam anno nostrae salutis … e Tartaria Dux nescio quis, regnorum domitor, in hoc regnum sese cum exercitu victore immisisset. Eum Ducem nonnulli e nostris, nec levibus, meo iudicio, coniecturis Tamerlanem, vel e successoribus eius aliquem fuisse arbitrantur. Eum enim Sinae Tiemor appellant … Quisquis is fuerit, Tartarum appellabo.
p.s: Matteo Ricci, edited and translated into Latin by Nicolas Trigault (1615)
p.t: yet we do not read that it was ever wholly conquered by foreign peoples until, in the year of our salvation …, some leader from Tartary, a conqueror of kingdoms, invaded this kingdom with his victorious army. Some of our men, on conjectures that in my judgement are not slight, think this leader was Tamerlane or one of his successors, for the Chinese call him Tiemor … Whoever he was, I shall call him the Tartar.
p.c: The year is illegible in both scans and is omitted. The Tamerlane identification is wrong.

p.h: The Tatar Hazaras, said to descend from Genghis's army
p.g: Burnes notes a Hazara tribe of about a thousand families called Tatar Hazaras, whom tradition made descendants of Genghis Khan's army. He points out that the only other people who called themselves Tatar were the Nogais on the Russian frontier. Earlier (vol. I, p.178) he says the Hazaras looked like Chinese and were 'Tartars by descent'.
p.q: Tradition states these people to be descendants of Jengis Khan's army, but their name of Tatar deserves remark, since the only other tribe so denominated by the people themselves is the Nogai on the frontiers of Russia.
p.s: Alexander Burnes (1834)
p.pl: Hazarajat (between the Hindu Kush and Bamiyan)
p.c: The descent from Genghis's army is tradition, which Burnes reports without proving.

p.h: Mongol and Tatar: twin sons, and a name that swallowed the rest
p.g: Katib Celebi tells the Islamic-Persian genealogy: the children of Turk son of Japheth spread over Turkestan, most of them nomads living in tents. Later Alinja Khan had twin sons, Mongol and Tatar, who divided the kingdom, so two clans arose. Eight Tatar rulers reigned before their line died out, and the Mongol line followed. Then comes a clear statement of the naming problem: 'Mongol' became a generic name for many tribes, so that by extension people say 'Turk', 'Tatar' and 'Mongol' for all of them, although the Mongols were really one kind of Turk.
p.q: مزبورك بطن واحددن ایکی اوغلی اولدی بری مغول و بری تاتار تسمیه اولنوب جمله مملکتنی بو ایکی اوغلی بیننده تقسیم ایلدی ... نیجه قبایل واقوامه لفظ مزبور اسم جنس اولمشدر انلردن اولمینه دخی مجاز طریقیله اطلاق وتعمیم ایدوب ترك وتاتار مغول دیرلر لکن حقیقتده مغول ترکدن برصنف ایدی
p.s: Katib Celebi, Cihannuma (Muteferrika print, Istanbul 1732)
p.t: From one womb he had two sons, one named Mongol and the other Tatar, and he divided his whole kingdom between these two sons … The said word became a generic name for many tribes and peoples, and it is applied by extension even to those who are not of them, so they say Turk and Tatar and Mongol; but in truth the Mongols were one kind of Turk.
p.c: A legendary genealogy from the Persian historical tradition (Rashid al-Din and later histories; Abu'l-Ghazi tells a version after Katib Celebi's time). The observation about names is Katib Celebi's own.

p.h: 'Unknown peoples': nobody knew who the Tatars were
p.g: The chronicler's first notice of the Tatars is an admission of ignorance. Nobody knew who they were, where they came from, what language they spoke or what faith they held. People called them Tatars, Taurmens or Pechenegs, and learned men linked them to the prophecy of Pseudo-Methodius about peoples locked away in the desert who would come out at the end of time.
p.q: придоша языци незнаеми, ихъ же добрѣ никто же не вѣсть, кто суть и отколѣ изъидоша, и что языкъ ихъ, и котораго племене суть, и что вѣра ихъ; а зовуть я Татары, а иніи глаголють Таурмены, а друзіи Печенѣзи, иніи же глаголють, яко се суть, о нихъ же Меѳодій Паторомьскыи епископъ съвѣдѣтельствуеть: яко си суть изъшли изъ пустыня Етріевьскыя
p.s: Novgorod First Chronicle (Synodal copy; PSRL vol. 3, 1841)
p.pe: Tatars (the Mongol army of Jebe and Subutai)
p.t: there came unknown peoples, whom no one clearly knows: who they are and whence they came, and what their language is, and of what tribe they are, and what their faith is; and they call them Tatars, and others say Taurmens, and others Pechenegs, and others say that these are the ones of whom Methodius, bishop of Patara, bears witness: that they came out of the Etrian desert
p.c: The Methodius reference is to the apocalyptic Revelation of Pseudo-Methodius, a book legend, not an origin the Mongols gave.

p.h: How Mongol conquerors became the Turkic 'Tatars' of Kazan and Crimea
p.g: Bichurin explains how the name moved: the Mongol lords on the Volga were few among Turkic subjects, married into them, took their language, customs and Islam, and so disappeared, reappearing under the Russian name 'Tatars' as a seemingly new people ruling Kazan, Astrakhan and Crimea. A footnote adds that the Tatars do not call themselves by that name but Uzbeks, Nogais and so on.
p.q: Побѣдители, перенявъ отъ Туркистанцевъ съ браками ихъ нравы и обыкновенія, ихъ языкъ и религію, мало по малу совершенно потерялись, такъ что наконецъ самое имя Татаньцевъ исчезло, и они подъ Россійскимъ названіемъ Татаръ содѣлались какъ бы новымъ народомъ, который въ послѣдствіи господствовалъ въ царствахъ: Казанскомъ, Астраханскомъ и Крымскомъ.
p.s: Iakinf (N. Ya. Bichurin), 1828
p.pe: Golden Horde Mongols and Turkic peoples
p.t: The conquerors, taking from the Turkestanis through marriage their manners and customs, their language and religion, little by little were completely lost, so that at last the very name of the Tatans disappeared, and under the Russian name of Tatars they became as it were a new people, which afterwards ruled in the tsardoms of Kazan, Astrakhan and Crimea.
p.c: Bichurin himself calls this a conjecture with probability on its side.

p.h: 'Sibir' was not the Tatars' name for their capital
p.g: Müller corrects a common belief that 'Sibir' is the Tatar word for the capital. When he asked the Tobolsk Tatars, they did not know the word at all; they called the place Isker. He thinks the name Sibir arose in Russia, taken from the Permians or Zyrians who first brought news of the land, and was only later attached to the Tatar capital.
p.q: Man glaubt insgemein, Sibir sey die Tatarische Benennung des Orts, welche soviel, als eine Hauptstadt, oder Residenz, bedeute. Fraget man aber die Tobolskischen Tataren nach diesem Umstande, so ist ihnen solcher ganz unbekannt. Sie nennen vielmehr den Ort Isker
p.s: Gerhard Friedrich Müller (Sammlung Russischer Geschichte, vol. 6, 1761-1762)
p.t: It is commonly believed that Sibir is the Tatar name of the place, meaning a capital or residence. But if one asks the Tobolsk Tatars about this, it is quite unknown to them. They call the place Isker instead

p.h: Poured forth from Tartarus, so rightly called Tartars
p.g: Rockhill's introduction quotes the English chronicler Matthew Paris, writing from St Albans, who never met a Mongol. He plays on the name: the Tartars burst out like devils from Tartarus, the classical underworld, so the name fits. The same passage goes on to call them monsters who drink blood and eat the flesh of dogs and men, a good example of wartime rumour.
p.q: a detestable nation of Satan, to wit, the countless army of the Tartars, broke loose from its mountain-environed home, and piercing the solid rocks (of the Caucasus), poured forth like devils from the Tartarus, so that they are rightly called Tartari or Tartarians.
p.s: Matthew Paris, Chronica Majora, quoted in W. W. Rockhill's introduction (1900)
p.c: Hearsay and propaganda from a monk in England; the pun on Tartarus is why Europeans wrote 'Tartar' with an extra r.

p.h: 'Most incorrectly' called Tartars
p.g: Muraviev says the scattered Turkmen tribes share a common origin but have been 'most incorrectly' called a Tartar race by European writers. He suggests the word came from Tatar, the founder of a tribe of that name still living in the far steppes.
p.q: This people has been most incorrectly denominated the Tartar race by several European authors. The term was probably borrowed from Tatar, the Chief who founded the tribe of that name, existing in the remoter steppes to the present day.
p.s: Nikolai Muraviev (translated by W. S. A. Lockhart, 1871)
p.c: The eponymous chief 'Tatar' is a traditional explanation, not established history.

p.h: 'Those Tatars smell bad': how Chinese turned Mongols into Tatars
p.g: The Naiman ruler Tayang plans to attack the upstart people to his east, and his mother Gurbesu sneers that they stink and wear dirty dark clothes, so only their good-looking women are worth fetching to milk the Naiman herds. In the Mongolian original these people are the Mongols; the Ming Chinese summary calls them Dada, the Chinese word for Tatars, while it keeps a different spelling for the actual Tatar tribe. The same summary has To'oril ask 'how can you Dada be without an emperor?' of Chinggis's people.
p.q: 塔陽說這東邊有些逹逹…如今咱去将那逹逹取了其母古児别速說那逹逹百姓歹氣息衣服黒暗取将来要做甚麽教逺有者
p.s: Ming Chinese summary translation of the Secret History (Sibu congkan text, Kanseki Repository transcription)
p.pe: Mongols, called Dada (Tatars) by the Ming translators; Naiman
p.t: Tayang said: 'Over here in the east there are some Dada (Tatars)... Let us go now and take those Dada.' His mother Gurbesu said: 'Those Dada people have a bad smell and their clothes are dark and grimy. What would we do bringing them here? Let them stay far away.'
p.c: The Mongolian text (de Rachewiltz p.105) says 'the Mongol people have always smelt bad'; 'Dada' is the Ming translators' word, not the Mongol author's.

p.h: Wiped out by the Tatars: the Mongols' escape from Ergenekun
p.g: Hammer retells the Mongol origin legend: long before Chinggis Khan the Mongols were exterminated by their enemies the Tatars, all but two men, Tegus and Kijan, who fled into a valley walled by steep rocks. Over centuries their descendants multiplied and, tired of their mountain prison and their mining, broke out by driving the flames of great wood piles with seventy bellows against the ore wall until it melted (p. 14). All true Mongols claimed descent from these two. Hammer suspects the story hides the real subjugation of the Xiongnu, who mined for their conquerors in the Altai, and notes that Persian poets placed this mountain prison behind the dam of Gog and Magog.
p.q: Ein Paar tausend Jahre vor Tschengischan, so erzählt die Volkssage, waren die Mongolen von ihren Feinden, den Tataren, bis auf zwei Männer ausgerottet worden, deren einer Tegus, der andere Kijan, d. i. Strom, hiess; sie flüchteten in ein rundum von steilen Felsen umschlossenes Thal, wo sie im Verlaufe von Jahrhunderten sich vermehrend, ihres Bergkerkers und Bergbaues endlich müde
p.s: Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall (1842), retelling a Mongol folk legend from his Persian sources
p.pl: Mongolia and the Altai (legendary valley of Ergenekun)
p.w: Legend set some two thousand years before Chinggis Khan
p.t: A couple of thousand years before Chinggis Khan, so the folk legend tells, the Mongols had been exterminated by their enemies, the Tatars, all but two men, one called Tegus, the other Kijan, that is, 'stream'; they fled into a valley enclosed all round by steep rocks, where, multiplying over the course of centuries, and at last weary of their mountain prison and their mining
p.c: An origin legend, not history; the Xiongnu interpretation is Hammer's own guess.

p.h: Tatars wanted to be Turks, Turks wanted to be Tatars
p.g: Hammer notes that the Black Tatars near Baikal and the Water Tatars on the Kerulen appeared at the end of the 12th century under the name Mongols. When Chinggis Khan raised this small people to world rule, Turkic and Tatar peoples claimed the name for themselves, just as earlier, while Turks and Tatars ruled, each had wanted the other's name. Only later, once that power had faded, did Mongols and Kalmyks refuse to be called Tatars and Ottomans refuse to be called Turks; his note cites Rubruck's remark that the Mongols did not want to be called Tartars. On p. 22 he adds that the Turkic peoples of Russia are called Tatars, 'though the name is incorrect'.
p.q: Als das kleine Volk, welches südöstlich vom Baikalsee … wohnte, durch Tschengis-Chan zum Herrscherstamme welterobernder Heere erhoben ward, nahmen türkische und tatarische Völker diesen Nahmen in Anspruch, wie, als die Türken und Tataren die Herrschaft inne hatten, Türken Tataren und Tataren Türken heissen wollten. Erst in neueren Zeiten … wollen die Mongolen und Kalmücken nicht mehr Tataren, und die Osmanen nicht mehr Türken heissen.
p.s: Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall (1840), drawing on Rashid al-Din, Abulghazi and Rubruck
p.t: When the small people living south-east of Lake Baikal … was raised by Chinggis Khan to be the ruling tribe of world-conquering armies, Turkic and Tatar peoples laid claim to this name, just as, when the Turks and Tatars held power, Turks wanted to be called Tatars and Tatars Turks. Only in more recent times … do the Mongols and Kalmyks no longer want to be called Tatars, nor the Ottomans Turks.
p.c: Hammer's own theory of name-borrowing, with a dismissive remark about the 'vanity of barbarous peoples'.
p.tg: names mongol tatar turk kalmyks ethnonym

p.h: How the Tartar borderlands split into three kingdoms
p.g: Semedo's origin story for the new enemy: after expelling the Tartars, Hongwu made the Tartar borderlands tributary and divided them into states with titles. These grew until they split into three kingdoms, East, West and North. The western and northern ones broke away at once; the eastern one stayed loyal until the Chinese, for no reason, decided to crush it, and it turned on them. The eastern kingdom is the Jurchen (Manchu) state.
p.q: Quando el Hum Vu, Trõco de la Familia q̃ oy tiene el cetro Chino, sacudiò de su Imperio al Tartaro, … dexando avassallados los cõfines de la Tartaria, los reduxo a tributarios, dividiẽdolos en Estados de titulos i dignidades diferẽtes. Crecierõ ellos despues tãto, q̃ se separarõ en tres Reynos: uno al Oriente, otro al Ocaso, i al Norte otro.
p.s: Álvaro Semedo, S.J. (Spanish edition by Manuel de Faria e Sousa, Madrid 1642)
p.pe: Tartars north of China (Mongols and the eastern Jurchen, later Manchus)
p.t: When Hum Vu, the founder of the family that today holds the Chinese sceptre, shook off from his empire the Tartar [who had ruled it for ninety years], … leaving the borders of Tartary as vassals, he reduced them to tributaries, dividing them into states with different titles and dignities. These afterwards grew so much that they separated into three kingdoms: one to the East, another to the West, and another to the North.
p.c: A simplified Chinese-court version of frontier history.

p.h: 'Do not call our lord a Christian, nor us Tartars'
p.g: As Rubruck left Sartaq's camp, the secretary Coiac and other court scribes warned him not to say their lord was a Christian: he was a Moal. Rubruck explains that the Mongols treat 'Christian' as the name of a nation and are so proud that they want their own name, Moal, above every other, and will not be called Tartars either, because the Tartars had been a different people.
p.q: « Nolite dicere quod dominus noster sit christianus. Non est christianus, sed Moal »; quia enim nomen christianitatis videtur eis nomen cujusdam gentis. In tantam superbiam sunt erecti, quod quamvis forte aliquid credant de Christo, tamen nolunt dici christiani, volentes nomen suum, hoc est Moal, exaltare super omne nomen, nec volunt vocari Tartari. Tartari enim fuerunt alia gens de quibus sic didici.
p.s: William of Rubruck (Latin text ed. Michel and Wright, 1839)
p.pe: Mongols (Moal) of Sartaq's court, Golden Horde
p.t: 'Do not say that our lord is a Christian. He is not a Christian but a Moal'; for the name of Christianity seems to them the name of some nation. They are raised to such pride that, though they may perhaps believe something about Christ, they will not be called Christians, wishing to exalt their own name, that is Moal, above every name; nor will they be called Tartars. For the Tartars were another people, about whom I learned as follows.

p.h: Call it 'Central Asia', not 'Tartary'
p.g: Meyendorff objects that the usual map label 'Tartary' covers lands never settled by Tartars while leaving out places where Tartar (Turkic) was actually spoken. A country, he argues, should only be named after a people who live there, so he proposes 'Central Asia' instead.
p.q: If in geography we give to a country the name of a people, it should be conditional on such people inhabiting that country. It appears to me then, that Central Asia would be a more appropriate name to introduce in lieu of Tartary, since I have found it more correct, and more geographical.
p.s: Georg von Meyendorff (translated by William Monteith, 1840)
p.c: The translator notes that this chapter was obscure even in French.

p.h: Tartary as the first land after the Flood
p.g: Touching on the 'Atlantis' debate of his day, de Tott argues that the high plateau of Tartary must have been the first land inhabited in Asia, the source of the swarms that later poured into Europe as Goths, Ostrogoths and Visigoths. He says a Tartar tradition told him by Khan Krim Giray supports this, and on the next page traces the Crimean dynasty back to Genghis Khan.
p.q: this country, possessed at present by the Tartars, must have been the first discovered land in Asia, and the earliest inhabited; the source of that population which first sent forth those swarms which, constantly driven back by the wall of China, and the defiles of Thibet and of Caucasus, fell upon the northern parts of Asia, and overflowed our Europe, under the name of Goths, Ostrogoths, and Visigoths.
p.s: Baron de Tott (English translation, 1785)
p.c: A speculative 18th-century theory based on geography and one conversation, not on evidence; de Tott himself calls it a 'hypothesis'.

p.h: My Tatar servant understood the Yakuts
p.g: Sarychev argues that the Yakuts descend from 'an ancient race of Tartars' who never became Muslim. His proof is practical: one of his own attendants was a Tatar, and he understood most of what the Yakuts said without difficulty. Modern linguists agree that Sakha is a Turkic language, related to Tatar.
p.q: The Jakuts are probably derived from an ancient race of Tartars not yet converted to Mahometanism. This appears evident from a similarity of their features, their mode of life, and still more their language, which approaches so nearly to the Tartar dialect, that one of my attendants, who was a Tartar, understood most of what they said without any difficulty.
p.s: Gavriil Sarychev (English translation, 1806)

p.h: Grand Cham of the Tartars, named after the river Tata
p.g: At Genghis Khan's proclamation, Pétis says, the new emperor praised the 'Soumoguls', called Tartars after the river Tata that ran through their land, and added 'Grand Cham of the Tartars' to his title to honour them. A footnote explains that this is how all the Scythian nations under Genghis came to be called Tartars, and that the Chinese, lacking an r, said 'Tata'.
p.q: And having much cause to praise the Soumoguls (who are particularly called Tartars, by reason of the River Tata that waters their Country) he declared in the Mogul Language, that he would add to his Title of Emperor of the Moguls that of Grand Cham of the Tartars, both to do that Nation Honour
p.s: François Pétis de la Croix (English translation, 1722)
p.c: A compiler's explanation drawn from Carpini (who first spoke of 'Su-Mongals' named after a river Tatar) and Oriental histories; the river origin of the name is not accepted today.
p.tg: tartar name etymology tatars genghis khan title

p.h: Chinggis's men were Mongols, not Tatars
p.g: Writing about Russian fortune-telling customs, Erman says the tribes of Chinggis Khan who overran Russia were really a branch of the Mongols from the Irkutsk region, who later joined with the 'Tatar hordes'. Over time, he says, Russian historians wrongly gave the Tatars the whole glory of the conquest.
p.q: In point of fact, we know that the tribes under Chingis Khan, who overran that country, were really a branch of the Mongol nation from the government of Irkutsk, who subsequently formed a union with the Tatar hordes; and to the latter the Russian historians, in process of time, incorrectly attributed the whole glory of the conquest.
p.s: Adolph Erman (translated by W. D. Cooley, 1848)
p.c: Erman's placing of the Mongol homeland 'from the government of Irkutsk' is his own view; the Mongol heartland lay farther south, in today's Mongolia.

p.h: "Held not by Tartars but in Tartarus"
p.g: In his opening letter Roger plays on the old pun that made 'Tartars' out of 'Tatars': whoever falls into their hands will feel he is held not by Tartars but in Tartarus, the pit of the underworld. He stresses that he writes from experience, having lived among them 'for a time and half a time', a biblical phrase for a long ordeal. The pun shows how the name itself carried a hellish ring for Latin Christians.
p.q: Et sciant cuncti haec me temere non referre; quod quisquis ad manus ipsorum deuenerit Tartarorum, si natus non fuisset melius esset ei; et sentiet se non a Tartaris sed in tartaro detineri. Hoc refero ut expertus. Fui enim per tempus et dimidium temporis inter eos; in quo mori solatium exstitisset, sicut supplicium fuit vita.
p.s: Master Roger (Rogerius), Carmen miserabile, in the 1885 Budapest edition (Chronica minora)
p.t: And let everyone know that I do not report these things rashly: whoever comes into the hands of these Tartars, it would have been better for him not to have been born, and he will feel himself held not by Tartars but in Tartarus. I report this as one who went through it. For I was among them for a time and half a time, in which death would have been a comfort, just as life was a punishment.

p.h: From Yuan emperors back to 'Dada'
p.g: The history of the Mongol domains says the Yuan's ancestors, the Mongols, came from the far northwest, conquered the world and unified it. After 1368 the Yuan heir fled north and kept his dynastic title, but a later usurper, Guilichi, called himself khan, dropped the dynastic name and 'again called [them] Dada', Tatars. The Qing record thus treats Tatar as the name the Mongols fell back on after losing China.
p.q: 元之先曰蒙古居西北極邊奄有天下遂成一統明初阿裕實哩達喇遯歸朔漠復其故號…果勒齊篡位稱可汗去國號復稱韃靼
p.s: Qing history office, Comprehensive Gazetteer of the Great Qing (Jiaqing recension, completed 1842; Sibu congkan text, Kanseki Repository transcription)
p.t: The forebears of the Yuan were called Menggu (Mongols); they lived on the far northwestern frontier, took possession of all under heaven and so unified it. At the start of the Ming, Ayushiridara fled back to the northern desert and resumed his old title... Guolegi (Guilichi) usurped the throne, styled himself khan, abolished the dynastic name and again called [them] Dada (Tatars).
p.c: The second half is in a small-character note drawn from Ming sources.

p.h: Whom do you call Tatars? A question put to Turkestanis in Beijing
p.g: Bichurin notes that Europeans called the belt from the Caspian to the Pacific 'Great Tartary'. While living in Beijing he asked people from Eastern Turkestan whom they called Tatars. Their answer: a people of their own stock living in Tobolsk, Kazan and Astrakhan. The Tatars themselves, he adds, said the name was given them by neighbours, and no people or clan in Central Asia used it of itself.
p.q: Великую полосу земли, простирающуюся отъ Каспійскаго моря до Восточнаго Океана, Европейцы назвали Великою Татаріею. Во время пребыванія моего въ Пекинѣ, неоднократно имѣя случай разговаривать съ жителями Восточнаго Туркистана,
p.s: Iakinf (N. Ya. Bichurin), translator's preface, 1829
p.pe: Turkestani Muslims (Uighurs of the Tarim oases); Volga and Siberian Tatars
p.t: The great belt of land stretching from the Caspian Sea to the Eastern Ocean the Europeans named Great Tartary. During my stay in Beijing, having had more than one occasion to talk with inhabitants of Eastern Turkestan,
p.c: The answer itself is on the next page (n14): 'now we call Tatars a people of the same stock as us, living in Tobol, Kazan and Astrakhan'.

p.h: The Mongols do not call themselves Tartars
p.g: Strahlenberg insists that the Mongols and Kalmyks, whom Europeans call Tartars, do not use the name and dislike it. In his view the name belonged to the 'original Tartars' near China and was stretched to cover the Mongols because they allied with them long ago. He adds that the Chinese used 'Tata' much as the Romans used 'barbarian'.
p.q: But to return to the Mungal Nations: We must know, that these are the People whom the Chinese, with Respect to their Situation, call West Tartars, and others West Mungals: But they do not reckon themselves Tartars, neither would they, by any Means, be thought so by others.
p.s: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (English translation, 1738)
p.c: His explanation of how the name spread rests on his own reading of Abulghazi and Chinese sources, and on guesswork about Oghuz Khan.

p.h: A prisoner names Batu's generals, and Guyuk
p.g: During the siege of Kiev the defenders captured a Tatar named Tovrul, who told them who was in Batu's army. The list matches Batu's Chinggisid relatives and generals known from Persian and Mongol sources. The chronicler adds that Guyuk turned back on hearing of the Great Khan's death and became khan himself, though (he believed) not of the khan's family but his first general.
p.q: Яша же въ нихъ Татарина, именемъ Товрулъ, и тъ исповѣда имъ всю силу ихъ; се бяху братья его силный воеводы: Урдюй, Байдаръ, Бирюй, Кайданъ, Бечакъ и Меньгу и Кююкъ (иже вратися увѣдавъ смерть канову и бысть каномъ, не отъ роду же его, но бѣ воевода его перьвый), Себѣдяй Богатуръ и Бурунъдай Багатырь
p.s: Hypatian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 2 (1843)
p.pe: Batu's commanders: Urdiui (Orda), Baidar, Biriui, Kaidan, Bechak, Mengu (Mongke), Kiuiuk (Guyuk), Subutai, Burundai
p.t: They captured among them a Tatar named Tovrul, and he told them all their strength; these were his brothers, strong commanders: Urdiui, Baidar, Biriui, Kaidan, Bechak and Mengu and Kiuiuk (who returned on learning of the khan's death and became khan, though not of his family, but he was his first commander), Sebediai the Bogatur and Burundai the Bagatyr
p.c: Guyuk was in fact a grandson of Chinggis Khan; the chronicler's remark about his descent is mistaken.
p.tg: batu guyuk subutai mongke generals prisoner testimony

p.h: 'Tartarestan', says Lorenzo: from the river Tartar
p.g: Here Katib Celebi reports what the European geographer he calls 'Lorenzo' wrote: the second part of Asia, beyond the Imaus mountains, is Tatarestan (Tartary). Its people are Mongol Tatars who have spread over most of Asia. Their origin is a river named Tatar, from which they took their name, and they were formerly known as Mongols. He is translating a European atlas (Mercator-Hondius), so this is the European 'Tartary' coming back into an Ottoman book.
p.q: قسم ثانی که ایماوس طاغلرندن اوته اولان تاتارستاندر لورنسو تحریری اوزره انلر مغول تاتارلری اولوب آسیانك اکثرینه یایلدیلر ... بونلر تاتار اصلیدرکه تاتار نام ارماقدن اسم اخذ ایتدیلر ومونغال دیمکله معروف یرکه
p.s: Katib Celebi, Cihannuma (Muteferrika print, Istanbul 1732)
p.pl: Inner Asia beyond the Imaus mountains
p.t: The second part, which lies beyond the Imaus mountains, is Tatarestan. According to Lorenzo's account, they are Mongol Tatars who spread over most of Asia … These are the original Tatars, who took their name from a river called Tatar, and were known by the name Mongal.
p.c: Second-hand from European atlases; the 'river Tatar' etymology comes from medieval European writers, not steppe tradition. 'Lorenzo' may be a Latin atlas author as rendered by Katib Celebi's translator.

p.h: How Turks came to be called Tatars
p.g: Klaproth explains the mix-up. When Chinggis Khan's son was sent west, the steppes north of the Caspian and Black Sea were full of Turkic peoples (Cumans, Pechenegs, Bulgars), who became subjects of the Kipchak khanate. Its rulers were Tatars (Mongols) but its people mostly Turks. When the empire broke up into the khanates of Crimea, Kazan and Astrakhan, the khans were still descendants of Chinggis, so the states kept the name 'Tatar' even though their armies and people were Turkic. On the previous page he tells how Chinggis himself got his birth name from a captured chief of the 'White Tatars'.
p.q: Seine Herrscher waren Tataren, die Unterthanen aber grösstentheils Türken. Gegen das Ende des XV Jahrhunderts zerfiel dieses Reich in mehrere kleine, unter denen die von der Krym, Kasan und Astrachan die bedeutendsten waren. Die Fürsten derselben stammten von … ab und waren Mongolen oder Tataren, aber ihre Heere waren es nicht mehr … Dennoch behielten diese Chanate den Namen Tatarische bei, weil die Chane Tataren waren.
p.s: Julius von Klaproth
p.pe: Mongol (Tatar) khans ruling Turkic subjects in the Golden Horde and its successor khanates
p.t: Its rulers were Tatars, but its subjects mostly Turks. Towards the end of the fifteenth century this empire broke up into several small ones, of which those of Crimea, Kazan and Astrakhan were the most important. Their princes descended from [Chinggis Khan] and were Mongols or Tatars, but their armies no longer were … Nevertheless these khanates kept the name 'Tatar', because the khans were Tatars.
p.c: Klaproth's own synthesis, argued with some polemic against other scholars.
p.tg: golden horde kipchak khanate turks crimea kazan astrakhan

p.h: Genghis Khan the blacksmith
p.g: At Bukhara Ibn Battuta retells what was said of the Tartars' founder: that Genghis Khan began as a blacksmith in the country of 'Khota', a big, generous man who won followers by feasting them, then conquered Khota, China, Kashgar and Almaliq before turning on Khwarezm. The translator notes that other histories give his origins very differently.
p.q: It is said that Jengiz Khan, who came with the Tartars into the countries of Islamism and destroyed them, was in his outset a blacksmith in the country of Khota.
p.s: Ibn Battuta (translated by Samuel Lee, 1829)
p.c: A popular story ('it is said'); the blacksmith tale may have grown from Temujin's name, which resembles the Turkic word for iron. The rest of the story continues on the next page (n115).

p.h: Nogais: 'unmixed descendants' of Genghis Khan's army
p.g: Pallas divides the Crimean Tatars into three classes. The Nogais, as their faces show, are 'unmixed descendants' of the Mongol tribe that formed the bulk of Genghis Khan's invading army. The steppe Tatars keep some Mongol features and build with unbaked clay bricks; the nobles and the mountain people are mixed with Turks and other nations.
p.q: All these Nagays are, as their features evince, the unmixed descendants of the Mongolian tribe, who formed the bulk of the army of Tshingis-Khan, which invaded Russia and the Crimea.
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas (English translation, 1812 edition)
p.pe: Nogais, steppe Tatars and mountain Tatars of the Crimea
p.c: His judgement rests on facial features, a method no longer accepted.
p.tg: nogais mongols genghis khan ancestry crimean tatars

p.h: 'Ask a Kazan Tatar if he is a Tatar'
p.g: Klaproth says that if you asked a so-called Tatar of Kazan or Astrakhan whether he was a Tatar, he would say no, and that he called his language Türki or Turuk, not Tatar. Remembering that his forefathers had been conquered by the Mongols or Tatars, he took 'Tatar' as an insult meaning robber. Klaproth concludes that Tatars must not be confused with Turks, rebukes the historian Schlözer for doing so, and adds that Chinese historians never called the Manchus 'Ta-ta', so the missionaries' phrase 'Tartar-Manchu' came only from their habit of calling every Central Asian a Tartar.
p.q: Man frage indessen einen sogenannten Tataren, von Kasan oder Astrachan, ob er ein Tatar sei, so wird er mit nein antworten; wie er denn auch seine Sprache nicht Tatari sondern Türki oder Turuk nennt. Eingedenk dass seine Vorältern von den Mongolen oder Tataren unterjocht worden, hält er Tatar für ein Schimpfwort, welches ihm mit Räuber gleich bedeutend ist.
p.s: Julius von Klaproth
p.pe: Volga Tatars of Kazan and Astrakhan
p.t: Ask, however, a so-called Tatar of Kazan or Astrakhan whether he is a Tatar, and he will answer no; just as he calls his language not Tatari but Türki or Turuk. Remembering that his forefathers were subjugated by the Mongols or Tatars, he considers 'Tatar' a term of abuse, which to him means the same as 'robber'.
p.c: A general claim about self-naming in Klaproth's day; other sources show Volga Muslims using several names for themselves.
p.tg: self-name turki kazan tatars manchus misnomer

p.h: Old maps of Tartary drawn before even the Russians knew it
p.g: In his preface Gerritsz attacks a German doctor, Helisaeus Röslin, who claimed ships could sail round Nova Zembla to Cathay. Röslin's 'absurdities', he says, rest on maps of Tartary drawn in very old times, when the Russians themselves did not know the country. A sharp early warning that the big 'Tartary' of old maps was guesswork.
p.q: This was also done by a certain Heliseus Röslin, a doctor of Hanau … in which (after many absurdities which he grounds on the maps drawn of Tartary from very old times, when the Russians themselves were unacquainted with it) he says: that the nearer the pole the warmer it is in summer time
p.s: Hessel Gerritsz, preface to the 1612 Dutch tracts (English translation by F. J. Millard in the 1878 facsimile edition)

p.h: 'Tatar' should mean Kazan
p.g: At Torzhok, famous for embroidered Russia-leather boots, Erman notes that the Russians learned the craft from the Tatars and still call the boots 'Kasan boots'. For Russians, he says, Kazan was the land of the Tatars, and he complains that Western European scholars too often call peoples 'Tatars' who had nothing to do with Kazan.
p.q: The Russians learned this art from the Tatars, whom they soon surpassed, and the name "Kasan boots," now usually given to the boots and shoes made in Torjok, points to a Tatar origin; for among the Russians, Kasan was originally the land of the Tatars; and the learned men of Western Europe too often give the name of Tatars erroneously to tribes who had no connexion with Kasan.
p.s: Adolph Erman (translated by W. D. Cooley, 1848)

p.h: 'In their own language they are called Mangoli'
p.g: Thomas opens his chapter 'On the nature of the Tartars' by saying he will report what he could hear from people who had looked into the matter closely. Their land lies where the East meets the North, and in their own language they are called 'Mangoli', that is, Mongols. He adds that their country is said to border on 'further India' and names their king in a garbled form. So a Dalmatian writer of the 1260s already knew that 'Tartar' was not what these people called themselves.
p.q: Nunc vero de natura, & habitu gentis illius prout ab his audire potui, qui rem curiosius indagarunt, pauca narrabo: Est enim regio illorum in ea parte orbis sita ubi Oriens conjungitur Aquiloni, gentesque illae secundum proprietatem linguae suae Mangoli appellantur. Ferunt tamen quod terra illorum confinis sit ulterioris Indiae
p.s: Thomas, archdeacon of Split, Historia Salonitana, in the first edition by Ivan Lučić (Lucius), Amsterdam 1666
p.t: Now I will tell a few things about the nature and dress of that people, as far as I could hear from those who investigated the matter more carefully. Their region lies in that part of the world where the East joins the North, and those peoples, in the proper usage of their own language, are called Mangoli. They say, however, that their land borders on further India
p.c: Thomas says plainly that this chapter is hearsay from informants.

p.h: 'Tartar' is a European blanket name borrowed from one tribe
p.g: Rémusat opens by defining his subject. The peoples between India, China and Persia, the Sea of Japan, the Caspian and the Arctic are known by the 'vulgar and collective' name of Tartars, a word unknown to many of the peoples it is applied to. It seems to be a corruption of Tatar, the name of one tribe so powerful and famous that it was stretched to cover the others when all of Tartary united under Chinggis Khan's house.
p.q: sont connus sous le nom vulgaire et collectif de Tartares. Cette dénomination, entièrement inconnue à plusieurs des nations auxquelles les Européens l'appliquent, paroît être une altération de Tatar, nom particulier d'une tribu qui, par sa puissance et sa célébrité, a mérité qu'on l'étendît aux autres.
p.s: Jean-Pierre Abel-Rémusat
p.pe: the peoples of high Asia called 'Tartares' by Europeans; the Tatar tribe
p.t: are known by the vulgar and collective name of Tartars. This name, entirely unknown to several of the nations to which Europeans apply it, seems to be an alteration of Tatar, the particular name of a tribe which, by its power and fame, earned the extension of its name to the others.

p.h: 'Manchu' from Manjushri, the bodhisattva of wisdom
p.g: The editors argue that the name Manchu (滿洲) was originally Manju, both syllables level in tone, and link it to the Tibetans' custom of addressing the Qing emperor each year as 'Great Emperor Manjushri'. Manju, they say, means 'wonderful auspiciousness'; the Chinese character zhou (continent) was borrowed because it looked like a place name, but Manchu is the name of a people, not a place.
p.q: 國書考之滿洲本作滿珠二字皆平讀我朝光啟東土每嵗西藏獻丹書皆稱曼珠師利大皇帝翻譯名義曰曼珠華言妙吉祥也
p.s: Agui, Yu Minzhong and the Qianlong commission, Researches on Manchu Origins (Siku quanshu Wenyuange copy, Kanseki Repository transcription)
p.t: [Examined in] our national (Manchu) script, Manzhou was originally written Manzhu, both syllables read in the level tone. Since our dynasty arose in the eastern land, every year Tibet presents red-ink letters all addressing 'the Great Emperor Manjushri'. The Fanyi mingyi (a Buddhist glossary) says: Manju in Chinese means 'wonderful auspiciousness'.
p.c: The Manjushri etymology is the court's own proposal and is disputed by modern scholars.

p.h: Tartary: the Chinese name for everything beyond the Wall
p.g: Discussing a Siberian Tatar story that Chinese once lived in Siberia, Müller suggests that at most the Chinese may have built some towns on the Daurian and Mongol frontiers and toward Liaodong, because in China all lands beyond the Wall are called Tartary. The name, in his view, is a broad outsiders' label, not the name of one country.
p.q: По всѣмъ обстоятельствамъ разсуждать можно, что развѣ о построенныхъ нѣкоторыхъ городахъ на границахъ Даурскихъ и Мунгальскихъ и къ Леотонгу, о чемъ и въ древнихъ временахъ примѣры имѣются, упоминать хотѣли, по тому что въ Китаѣ всѣ за стѣною находящіяся земли общимъ именемъ Татарія называются.
p.s: Gerhard Friedrich Müller (Russian edition, 1787 issue)
p.pe: Mongols and other peoples north of the Great Wall
p.t: By all the circumstances one may judge that they perhaps meant certain towns built on the Daurian and Mongol borders and toward Liaotung, of which there are examples in ancient times, because in China all the lands lying beyond the Wall are called by the general name Tartary.
p.c: Müller cites Martini's Chinese atlas and Witsen for this; it reflects European usage of his day.

p.h: Why 'Tartar' and not 'Tatar'?
p.g: In a long note, the editor explains why he writes 'Tatar' rather than the manuscript's 'Tartar': Russians, Armenians and the peoples themselves say Tatar, and the extra 'r' came in Western Europe by association with Tartarus (he cites the story about St Louis). He also records the theory that the name goes back to a Chinese name for the Mongols.
p.q: The Russian word Tatarui, or Tatars, says Ralston … modified in Western Europe by a reference to Tartarus into Tartars, is now generally applied by Russian writers to what used to be the Turkish subjects of the Mongol Empire.
p.s: Editor's note (J. Buchan Telfer, 1879), citing W. R. S. Ralston
p.c: This is a 19th-century editor's discussion, not Schiltberger's own words.

p.h: 'The Dada are the Mongols'
p.g: The chapter on the Tatars opens with a flat definition: the Dada are the Mongols, the descendants of the former Yuan dynasty. It then tells how the last Yuan emperor fled Beijing beyond the passes in 1368. For Ming and Qing officials, 'Tatar' was simply the name for the Mongols of the steppe.
p.q: 韃靼即䝉古故元後也太祖洪武元年大將軍徐逹率師取元元主自北平遁出塞居開平
p.s: Zhang Tingyu and the Qing history office, History of the Ming (Siku quanshu Wenyuange copy, Kanseki Repository transcription)
p.t: The Dada (Tatars) are the Mongols, the descendants of the former Yuan. In the first year of Hongwu (1368), under Taizu, the grand general Xu Da led an army to take the Yuan; the Yuan ruler fled from Beiping (Beijing) out beyond the frontier and stayed at Kaiping (Shangdu).

p.h: The Tartars were one of seven Mongol nations
p.g: Hayton says the Tartars first lived beyond the great mountain of Belgian, 'like beasts' without faith or law, serving other nations, until several tribes 'called Mogols' banded together. He then lists seven nations, and the first is named Tartars. So for Hayton 'Tartar' is both the name of one tribe and the name for the whole confederation, a distinction that matters for anyone asking where the word came from.
p.q: La primiere de [ces] VII nacions est nomée Tartars, la secunde Tangot, la tierce Eurach, la quarte Jalair, la quinte Sonit, la sime Mengli, la setime Tebet.
p.s: Hayton of Corycus, La Flor des estoires de la terre d'Orient (French text, 1307), ed. Ch. Kohler (1906)
p.pe: Tartars and the other Mongol tribes
p.t: The first of these seven nations is named Tartars, the second Tangot, the third Eurach, the fourth Jalair, the fifth Sonit, the sixth Mengli, the seventh Tebet.
p.c: The editor notes that 'Mengli' should read Merkit; the list mixes real tribes (Tatar, Jalayir, Sunit, Merkit) with Tangut and Tibet.

p.h: A Tartar named Sachalar, forefather of the Yakuts
p.g: Wrangel writes that the Yakuts' faces and language confirm their tradition of descent from the Tartars. In a footnote he gives the tradition itself: their ancestor was a Tartar called Sachalar, who crossed the mountains to Kirenga on the Lena, settled and married a Tungus woman. That, he explains, is why the Yakuts still call themselves Sachalary (Sakha).
p.q: Their countenance and language fully confirm the tradition of their descent from the Tartars. … According to this tradition, their ancestor was a Tartar, named Sachalar, who came from his own country on the other side of the mountains, to Kirenga on the Lena, where he settled and married a Tungusian woman; the Jakuti still call themselves Sachalary.
p.s: Ferdinand von Wrangel (English translation by Mrs Sabine, 1840), text and footnote
p.c: An origin tradition as reported to Wrangel. It differs from the Omogai legend recorded by Sauer (W008).

p.h: Kazakh, Kirghiz or Cossack?
p.g: Abbott explains a naming tangle: the steppe people between Khiva and Orenburg call themselves Kazakhs (Kuzzauks), but the Russians call them Kirghiz to tell them apart from Russia's own Christian Cossacks. The people themselves, he says, do not know the name Kirghiz.
p.q: The kingdom of Khaurism is separated from the Russian district of Orenburgh by a considerable belt of steppe, held by Kuzzauks, whose chief, or Sooltaun, is nominally tributary to Russia. The Russians call this people Kirgheez, to distinguish them from their own Kuzzauks, or Cossacks, who are Christians, but the name is unknown to the people themselves.
p.s: James Abbott

p.h: 'The Tatar peoples' in the 1774 treaty: free, and ruled by Genghis's line
p.g: The 1911 editor prints Article 3 of the Kucuk Kaynarca treaty between Russia and the Ottomans. It lists the 'Tatar peoples' by name, the Crimeans and the Nogay hordes of Budjak, Kuban, Yedisan, Jamboyluk and Yedichkul, and declares them independent, governed by khans of 'the line of Genghis' chosen by the Tatars themselves. Here 'Tatar' is a legal and diplomatic name for real, named peoples north of the Black Sea, and their rulers claim descent from the Mongol conqueror.
p.q: قریم وبوجاق وقوبان ویدیسان وجانبویلق ویدیچقول قبائل وبالجمله طوائف تاتار بلا استثنا دولتین طرفندن سربستیت وبغیر تعلق مستقل وجوهله اجنبی بر دولته تابع اولمامق اوزره اعتراف وقبول اولنه لر . طوائف تاتار بالجمله رأی واتفاقلریله آل جنکیز صویندن انتخاب و نصب اولنان کندی خانلری …
p.s: Editorial footnote in the Istanbul 1911 print of Halim Giray's Gulbun-i Hanan, giving the Ottoman text of Article 3 of the Kucuk Kaynarca treaty (1774)
p.pe: Crimean Tatars and Nogays (Budjak, Kuban, Yedisan, Jamboyluk, Yedichkul)
p.t: The tribes of Crimea, Budjak, Kuban, Yedisan, Jamboyluk and Yedichkul, and all the Tatar peoples without exception, shall be recognised and accepted by the two states as free and entirely independent, subject to no foreign state. Their own khans, elected and installed from the line of Genghis by the common vote and agreement of all the Tatar peoples …
p.c: An official treaty text reproduced by the 1911 editor; the 'independence' it granted was the first step to Russian annexation in 1783, as the main text goes on to say.

p.h: The people of Kazan, rank by rank
p.g: When Kazan surrendered its boy khan Utemish-Girey and his mother Siuiumbike in 1551, the author lists everyone who submitted: mullahs, seyyids, sheikhs, hafizes and other Muslim clergy; ulans, princes, murzas, ichki (court nobles) and 'rear-court' Cossacks; and the subject peoples, Chuvash, Cheremis, Votiaks, Mordva, tarkhans and Mozhars. It shows Kazan as a Muslim state of many peoples, not a single 'Tatar' mass.
p.q: Казанцы же молны, и сеиты, и шихъ … и афызы, и уланы, и князи, и мурзы и ички, и задворные казаки, и Чюваша и Черемиса, и Отяки, и Мордва, и тарханы, и Можары, и вся земля Казанская
p.s: Anonymous author of the History of the Kazan Tsardom, PSRL vol. 19 (1903)
p.pe: Kazan clergy, nobility and subject peoples
p.t: And the Kazan people, the mullahs, and seyyids, and sheikhs … and hafizes, and ulans, and princes, and murzas and ichki, and the rear-court Cossacks, and the Chuvash and Cheremis, and Votiaks, and Mordva, and tarkhans, and Mozhars, and all the Kazan land
p.c: Some Tatar titles are garbled in the manuscripts; the omitted words are variously spelled.

p.h: 'Rightly called Tartars, as if from Tartarus'
p.g: Under the year 1240 Matthew describes the Tartars bursting out of a homeland walled in by mountains 'like demons loosed from Tartarus', and adds that this is why they are rightly called Tartars, as if 'Tartareans'. This pun on Tartarus, the classical underworld, is why Latin writers turned the steppe name Tatar into 'Tartar'. The same paragraph compares them to locusts covering the earth.
p.q: eodem anno plebs Sathanae detestanda, Tartarorum scilicet exercitus infinitus, a regione sua montibus circumvallata prorupit; et saxorum immeabilium soliditate penetrata, exeuntes ad instar daemonum solutorum a tartaro, ut bene Tartari, quasi tartarei, nuncupentur, scatebant, et quasi locustae terrae superficiem cooperientes
p.s: Matthew Paris, Chronica majora, ed. H. R. Luard (Rolls Series, vol. 4, 1877)
p.t: in that same year a detestable people of Satan, namely a boundless army of Tartars, burst out from its region walled in by mountains; and, having broken through the solid mass of impassable rocks, they came swarming out like demons loosed from Tartarus (so that they are well called Tartars, as if 'Tartareans'), and like locusts covering the face of the earth
p.c: A preacher's wordplay, not an etymology; on p. 78 Matthew also offers a river 'Tartar' as the source of the name.

p.h: A Tibetan prince at the sacred mountain: where the Mongol khans came from
p.g: Jigme Namkha begins the Mongol royal line not with the wolf and doe of the Secret History but with a son of the Tibetan king Drigum Tsenpo, called Borte Chino in Mongolian, who went into Mongolia with his wife and came to the mountain Burkhan Khaldun. The local people, learning of his noble descent, made him their ruler. It is a Buddhist retelling that ties the Mongol khans to Tibet's royal house.
p.q: Jener jüngste Sohn des Königs K'ri gum btsan-po, mit Namen Na k'ri oder mongolisch Porta Zeba, nahm sich aus dem Lande rKoii-po eine Gattin G-n-ö Maral mit Namen, ging mit ihr in die Mongolei und kam an den Berg Porhan Galtona am Ufer des Päigal -Seees.
p.s: Jigme Namkha (translated from the Tibetan into German by Georg Huth, 1896)
p.pl: Burkhan Khaldun and Lake Baikal region
p.t: That youngest son of King Khri gum btsan po, named Nya khri, or in Mongolian Borte Chino, took a wife named Go(a) Maral from the land of Kongpo, went with her into Mongolia and came to the mountain Burkhan Khaldun on the shore of Lake Baikal.
p.c: Huth's transliteration of Mongol names is idiosyncratic ('Porta Zeba' for Borte Chino, 'Porhan Galtona' for Burkhan Khaldun), and the OCR garbles some letters; the placing of Burkhan Khaldun by Baikal is the author's.

p.h: Once they had writing, and knew lions and tigers
p.g: Near Sredne Kolymsk Wrangel befriended an 82-year-old Yakut who read and wrote Russian. The old man said his people had been more civilised before they split from 'the other Tartar races', and had once had their own writing, since lost. As proof that they once lived far to the south, he quoted old sayings that mention gold, gems, lions and tigers, things Yakuts no longer knew.
p.q: He complained of the ignorance of his countrymen, who he said, had been formerly more civilized; and that before they separated from the other Tartar races, to whom they are allied, they had possessed written characters, and consequently means of intellectual cultivation, which they have since lost. He maintained, that his race had once inhabited far distant southern regions
p.s: Ferdinand von Wrangel (English translation by Mrs Sabine, 1840), reporting a Yakut elder
p.c: One elder's memory of lost traditions, which he himself says were fading. Old Turkic peoples of the south did use runic writing, but the elder gives no specifics.

p.h: 'Tata', because the Chinese cannot say R
p.g: The appended East Indies volume includes a history of the Tartar conquests of China. It explains that the Chinese called the Tartars 'Tata' because they could not pronounce R, and then tells how the Mongols ruled China until 1368 and how a new Tartar kingdom, the Manchus of 'Niuche', overran it in the 1640s. The same word covers both conquests.
p.q: For in the year 1206, the Tartars, whom the Chineses call'd Tata, because they do not pronounce the Letter R, entred China with a powerful Army, and after a War of seventy two years became Masters of it
p.s: Appended section of Mandelslo's travels in this edition (compiled history, source not named)
p.pe: Mongols (1206) and Manchus (1600s), both called Tartars
p.w: compiled 1650s to 1660s, about events of 1206 to 1640s
p.c: Not Olearius or Mandelslo as eyewitnesses: a compiled history added to Mandelslo's travels in this edition. Mandelslo never went to China.

p.h: Where the word 'Tartary' came from
p.g: Wood suggests the peoples of Central Asia descend from the ancient Huns and that most of their names came from a person: Tartar, Nogai, Uzbek, Moghul. 'Tartar', he says, had been turned into 'Tartary', a catch-all word for what the Romans called Scythia, yet he never heard the Uzbeks of Kunduz use it, and he blames the habit for much confusion.
p.q: Most of their names have had a personal origin, such as Tartar, Noghai, Uzbek, and Moghul. The first, corrupted to Tartary, has now become a generic term for the Scythia of the Roman historians, though I do not remember to have heard it used by the Uzbeks of Kunduz. From this custom much ambiguity has resulted.
p.s: John Wood
p.pe: Peoples of Central Asia: Kalmyks, Kirghiz, Uzbeks, Turkmens
p.c: The Hun ancestry and the 'personal origin' of the names are Wood's own theories from reading, not local testimony.

p.h: How the map of Tartary was put together
p.g: The atlas foreword, summarising du Halde, says the Jesuits' manuscript maps passed through d'Anville's hands before engraving. For the general map of Tartary he used the travel memoirs of Father Gerbillon checked against the sheet maps, and for the lands between Tibet, Tartary and the Caspian, where the missionaries had only imperfect information, he combined their notes with whatever else he could learn.
p.q: elles ont passé par celles de Mr. d'Anville … qui en a formé ensuite les Cartes générales. Il s'est servi pour celle de la Tartarie des Mémoires du Pere Gerbillon, en les comparant avec les Cartes particulières … comme les Missionaires avaient eu quelques connoissances, quoi qu'imparfaites des Pays situez entre le Thibet, la Tartarie & la Mer Caspienne, Mr. d'Anville en a fait usage
p.s: Foreword (Avertissement) of the 1737 atlas, summarising du Halde's preface
p.t: they passed through the hands of Mr d'Anville … who then made the general maps from them. For that of Tartary he used the memoirs of Father Gerbillon, comparing them with the particular maps … as the missionaries had some knowledge, though imperfect, of the countries lying between Tibet, Tartary and the Caspian Sea, Mr d'Anville made use of it
p.c: The foreword separates surveyed provinces from compiled areas; the far west of 'Tartary' on these maps rests on report and inference, not measurement.

p.h: Tartary: a European label for everything east of the Ob
p.g: Introducing Siberia, Witsen explains his own usage: in Europe the name Tartary is commonly given to all lands east of the Ob and the Caspian Sea, and he uses it that way too, though strictly speaking Siberia does not lie in Tartary. A clear statement that 'Tartary' on his maps was a convention, not the name of a state.
p.q: gelijk met de naem Tartarye, meest doorgaens in Europa, alle Landen beoosten de Oby, en het Kaspische Meir, zoo als ik dezelve onder die benaming mede betrekke, bekent zijn; hoe wel dan eigentlijk genomen, dit Siberia in Tartarye niet en legt
p.s: Nicolaes Witsen
p.t: just as, under the name Tartary, most commonly in Europe, all lands east of the Ob and the Caspian Sea are known, as I too include them under that name; although, properly speaking, this Siberia does not lie in Tartary

p.h: 'When a European speaks of Tatars, no one knows who is meant'
p.g: Fischer complains that Europeans mispronounce the name as 'Tartar', perhaps imagining it comes from Tartarus, an allusion he says is common in old and new histories. Worse, they give it to every Asian people beyond Persia and India up to the Pacific, however different in looks, way of life, religion and language. He even doubts whether any single people ever properly bore the name, noting that Batu's army that invaded Hungary were Mongols, not Tatars.
p.q: Vielleicht haben sie sich eingebildet, daß der name von Tartarus herkomt. … Solcher gestalt geschiehet es, daß wenn ein Europäer von Tataren redet, man nicht weiß von wem die rede ist. Weil dieser name so gar allgemein ist, so habe ofters bei mir angestanden, ob auch jemals ein besonder volk auf dem erdboden gewesen sei, das den eigentümlichen namen Tatar geführet.
p.s: Johann Eberhard Fischer (Sibirische Geschichte, introduction, 1768)
p.pe: 'Tatars' as a European catch-all; Mongols of Batu
p.t: Perhaps they imagined that the name comes from Tartarus. … So it happens that when a European speaks of Tatars, one does not know whom he means. Because this name is so very general, I have often hesitated whether there was ever a particular people on earth that bore the proper name Tatar.

p.h: Three Tatar nations, one language
p.g: In his closing description of the Caucasus, Güldenstädt sorts the Tatars of the eastern Caucasus into three peoples: Kumyks (settled farmers, rice and cotton growers and fishermen), Terekeme or Turkmen Tatars (whose dialect is almost Ottoman Turkish), and Nogais (tent-dwelling nomads). All speak Tatar, one of the main languages of the Caucasus, in dialects that are mutually intelligible at a pinch. For him ‘Tatar’ is a label for Turkic speakers, and he compares their dialects with Turkish as Italian, Spanish and Portuguese compare with each other.
p.q: Im ostlichen Kaukasus trift man dreyerley tatarische Völker an, 1 Die Kumükischen. 2. Terekemenischen oder Truchmenischen und 3. Die Nogaischen Tataren. … Mir scheint die Aehnlichkeit des türkischen, des terekemenischen, kumükischen und nogayisch-tatarischen Dialekts mit der Aehnlichkeit zwischen der italienischen, spanischen und portugisischen Sprache vergleichbar.
p.s: Johann Anton Güldenstädt (ed. P. S. Pallas, 1787)
p.pl: Dagestan and the western Caspian coast
p.t: In the eastern Caucasus one finds three kinds of Tatar peoples: 1. the Kumyk, 2. the Terekeme or Turkmen, and 3. the Nogai Tatars. … The similarity of the Turkish, Terekeme, Kumyk and Nogai-Tatar dialects seems to me comparable to the similarity between the Italian, Spanish and Portuguese languages.

p.h: The Tartars are the old Scythian shepherds
p.g: After a harsh description of Tartar looks and singing, Fletcher identifies the Tartars with the 'Scythian nomads' of Greek and Latin writers. Following the Byzantine historian Laonicus Chalcocondylas, he adds that the Turks may have sprung from the Crimean Tartars, since 'Turk' was said to mean shepherd.
p.q: They are the very same that sometimes were called Scythae Nomades, or the Scythian shepheards, by the Greekes and Latines. Some thinke that the Turkes tooke their beginning from the nation of the Chrim Tartars.
p.s: Giles Fletcher (1591; ed. E. A. Bond, 1856)
p.c: A bookish identification drawn from classical and Byzantine writers.

p.h: Mountain Tartars who remember a lost capital
p.g: Klaproth reports the origin tradition of the Turkic mountain peoples the Georgians called Bassiani: their elders say they once lived on the steppe of the Kuma up to the Don, with a magnificent capital, Ckirck Madshar ('forty stone buildings'), which they identify with the ruins at Madzhar, before being driven into the high mountains.
p.q: Their elders report that they were long ago settled in the steppe of the Kuma as far as the Don… Their capital, which is said to have been very magnificent, was named Ckirck Madshar, which in their language signifies the forty stone buildings, or the forty four-wheeled waggons… They assert that the ruins of Madshar, which yet subsist, are the remains of this city.
p.s: Julius Klaproth (English translation, 1814), reporting the elders' tradition
p.c: An oral tradition; the dates are uncertain even to the tellers.

p.h: How Bahcesaray was founded, 'as the Tatar historians say'
p.g: Evliya reports the Crimean Tatars' own story of their origins: the first conquerors of Crimea settled at Eski Yurt near Salachik, coming from Mahan, Ahlat, Kerman and Yesu, and from Kazan, Astrakhan and Sarai. As the Tatars multiplied and the old site grew too small, they settled at Bahcesaray and spread over the whole peninsula, while the 'Genoese infidels' stayed in their seaside fortresses. He names Jochi Khan and 'Artogmuz Khan' as the conquerors behind its first building.
p.q: قوم تاتارك مورخلری قوللری اوزره ابتدا فاتح قریم اسکی صلاجق یوردنده ساکن اولوب ماهان واخلاط وکرمان ویسو شهرلرندن وقازان واژدرخان وسرای اولکه‌لرندن قریمه تاتارلر کله‌رك تناسل بوله‌راق اسکی یورده صغمیوب بوباغچه سرای یوردنده توطن ایدوب
p.s: Evliya Celebi (Ottoman text, Istanbul 1928, vol. 7)
p.t: According to the Tatar historians, the first conqueror of Crimea settled at the Eski Salachik yurt; Tatars came to Crimea from the cities of Mahan, Ahlat, Kerman and Yesu and from the lands of Kazan, Astrakhan and Sarai, and as they multiplied they no longer fitted into the old yurt, and settled at this Bahcesaray site.
p.c: A local origin tradition, retold with Evliya's own additions; it links Crimea to Kazan, Astrakhan and the Golden Horde capital Sarai.

p.h: What the Kalmyks call Tatars, Russians and themselves
p.g: Pallas ends his notes on Mongol learning with a list of Kalmyk names for peoples and places. The Kalmyks call the Tatars 'Manggot', a word meaning a goblin, which the Buryats and Mongols apply to the Russians instead; the Kalmyks call Russians 'Orross' and themselves 'Oelöt' or 'Chalmik'. The list also gives Tobolsk as 'Toboltora' and Bukhara as 'Chotton', 'the towns'.
p.q: Manggot, die Tataren, welchen Namen aber, der einen Kobolt bedeutet, die Buraten und Mongolen den Russen beylegen; Orroß werden leztere hingegen von den Kalmücken … genannt … sich selbst endlich Oelöt oder Chalmik
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas (Sammlungen historischer Nachrichten über die mongolischen Völkerschaften, part 2, 1801)
p.t: Manggot, the Tatars, a name which, however, means a goblin, and which the Buryats and Mongols give to the Russians; the latter, on the other hand, are called Orross by the Kalmyks … and themselves, finally, Oelöt or Chalmik

p.h: 'We are no other than a Colony of Tatars'
p.g: The anonymous English translator argues that Europeans should despise the Tatars less because Europeans descend from them: the Cimbrians, Celts, Gauls, Goths, Huns, Vandals and Franks were all 'swarms from the same hive' out of Tatary. On the next page he even toys with the idea that the Saxons were akin to the Uzbeks. This is 18th-century speculation about 'Scythian' origins, using 'Tatar' for any northern Asian people.
p.q: Our Contempt for the Tatars would still lessen perhaps, did we consider how nearly we stand related to them: that our Ancestors came originally from the North of Asia, and that our Customs, Laws, and way of Living were formerly the same with theirs: In short, that we are no other than a Colony of Tatars.
p.s: The anonymous English translator's preface (1730), not Abu'l Ghazi
p.pe: Europeans and 'Tatars' in the translator's broad sense
p.c: The translator's own theory, offered without evidence; nothing in Abu'l Ghazi's text says this.

p.h: 'Mogoli' from 'Magogoli': the Tartars and Gog and Magog
p.g: Riccoldo weighs the theory that the Tartars were the Lost Ten Tribes of Israel shut behind the Caspian mountains by Alexander, notes that they hate Alexander's name and that their script looks like Chaldean, then argues against it. He reports that they themselves claim descent from Gog and Magog, which is why they are called Mogoli, as if a corruption of 'Magogoli'. It is a textbook example of how Europeans fitted the Mongols into biblical and Alexander legends.
p.q: Ipsi vero dicunt se descendisse de Gog et Magog. Vnde ipsi dicuntur Mogoli, quasi corrupto vocabulo Magogoli.
p.s: Riccoldo of Monte Croce, Liber peregrinationis, ed. J. C. M. Laurent (Leipzig, 1864)
p.t: They themselves say they are descended from Gog and Magog. Hence they are called Mogoli, as if from a corruption of the word Magogoli.
p.c: A folk etymology. 'Mongol' has nothing to do with Magog; the claim that Mongols themselves said this is Riccoldo's report and is doubtful.
