p.h: The Manchus called 'Kin', lords of the golden mountains
p.g: The Dutch general description says the people of Niuche, 'properly East Tartary', are known to the Chinese and their neighbours as Kin, meaning gold, and are called lords of the golden mountains because the Chinese believe their land is rich in gold mines. Kin is the Jin, the dynastic name used by the Jurchen and again by the Manchus before 1636.
p.q: D'Inwoonders zijn by de Sinezen en Grens-buren met den naam van Kin bekent; dat Gout op Neêrduitsch te zeggen is. Gemeenlijk wordenze ook de Heeren en Meesters van de goude Bergen genoemt, dewijl het een gemeen gevoelen onder de Sinezen is, dat hun landschap, datze bezitten, zeer gout-rijke Mijnen in zich besloten houd
p.s: Johan Nieuhof, general description of China (Dutch, 1665); this part is compiled, largely from Martino Martini
p.t: The inhabitants are known among the Chinese and their neighbours by the name of Kin, which in Dutch means Gold. They are also commonly called the Lords and Masters of the golden Mountains, because it is a common belief among the Chinese that the land they possess holds very gold-rich mines

p.h: The 'Water Tatars' re-spelled out of existence
p.g: Quoting the History of the Yuan on the Hailan and 'Water Tatar' circuits of Manchuria, the editors change 水達達 (Shui Dada, 'Water Tatars') to 碩達勒達, explained as Manchu for 'a hidden place', and note that the old form has been 'now corrected'. The Qing court thus removed the Tatar name from the history of its own homeland.
p.q: 海蘭府碩達勒達等路元史海蘭(詳前金上京條)府碩達勒達(滿洲語隠避處也舊作水達達)(今改正)等路土地廣濶人民散居
p.s: Agui, Yu Minzhong and the Qianlong commission, Researches on Manchu Origins (Siku quanshu Wenyuange copy, Kanseki Repository transcription)
p.t: Hailan prefecture, Shuo Dalda and other circuits. The History of the Yuan: Hailan (see the Jin Upper Capital entry above) prefecture, Shuo Dalda (Manchu for 'a hidden, sheltered place'; formerly written Shui Dada, 'Water Tatars'; now corrected) and other circuits: the land is broad and the people live scattered.
p.c: The Manchu etymology is a Qianlong-era reinterpretation; Yuan sources clearly meant 'Water Tatars'.
p.tg: water tatars shui dada re-spelling ethnonym censorship

p.h: Twin brothers named Mogul and Tatar
p.g: In a Tabriz prison Wolff met a captive chieftain who wrote out his family tree for him. It calls him a 'Tatar of the family of Genghis Khan' and gives a traditional origin story: an ancestor had twin sons, Mogul Khan and Tatar Khan, from whom the Moguls and the Tatars descend.
p.q: Muhammed, son of Izhak Khan Kerahe, Tatar of the family of Ghengis Khan. The ancestors of Ghengis Khan were Oolinjah Khan and Olamgoo, a Mogul, who had twins : the name of the one was Mogul Khan, and the other Tatar Khan, from whom all the Tatars descend, as the Moguls do from Mogul Khan.
p.s: Muhammad Khan Qarai (in Wolff's translation of his autograph)
p.pe: Muhammad Khan Qarai, a Khorasani chief claiming descent from Genghis Khan
p.c: A traditional genealogy (a version of the Mongol origin story found in Persian and Turkic histories), not history.
p.tg: genealogy mogul tatar genghis khan origin story

p.h: Tartar and Tartarus: why the name stuck in Europe
p.g: Erskine reports that the Mongols (Kalmyks) regarded 'Tatar' as an insult meaning something like 'robber', and asks why a name its bearers rejected became so widespread. His answer is the old pun: 'Tartar' sounded like Tartarus, the classical underworld, and fitted the terror the invaders caused in Europe.
p.q: It is singular that a name thus rejected among the nations to whom it is applied, should have had so much currency. The resemblance between Tartar and the infernal Tartarus, joined with the dread and horror in which the Tartar invaders were held, while they scattered dismay over Europe, probably, as has been well conjectured, preserved the name in the west.
p.s: William Erskine, editor's introduction (1826)
p.pe: Mongols and Turks (as named by Europeans)
p.c: Editorial conjecture; Erskine says it 'has been well conjectured' by others.

p.h: Bulgars and Mongols merged into Tatars
p.g: Haxthausen explains who the Kazan Tatars are: a mixed people in whom the old Volga Bulgar population and the Mongol conquerors have blended. He quotes Herberstein calling them 'half Mongols', but his own description (oval faces, curved noses, light complexions) mostly contradicts a Mongol look, apart from the eyes.
p.q: The Kazan Tatars belong, both mentally and physically, to the nobler races of mankind ; they are a mixed people, and possess high mental qualities, but Mohammedanism only permits their development in a limited degree. The ancient Bulgarian and Mongol population has been completely merged in the Tatar. The aspect of the Tatars clearly indicates their consanguinity with the Mongols : Herberstein describes them as half Mongols.
p.s: August von Haxthausen (translated by Robert Farie, 1856)
p.c: Uses the racial ranking language of the 1840s; his origins theory is his own opinion.

p.h: Tatar and Moghul, twin sons of a Turkish king
p.g: Timur asks his father for the family history, and hears the Turkic origin legend: the Turks descend from Yafet Aghlan, son of the biblical Japhet, and a later king had twin sons named Tatar and Moghul who split Turkestan between them. Tatar's eight sons and Moghul's nine founded the tribes, who then fought each other on the plains. The same story is told by the Khivan khan and historian Abu'l-Ghazi in the seventeenth century.
p.q: when his fifth son Aljeh Khan ascended the throne, the all gracious God bestowed on him twin sons, one of which was called Tatar, the other Moghul ; when they were grown up, Aljeh Khan divided the kingdom of Turkestan between them during his life-time
p.s: Attributed to Timur (Persian text of Abu Talib al-Husayni, translated by Charles Stewart, 1830)
p.pe: Turks, Tatars and Mongols (as legendary ancestors)
p.w: Legendary antiquity (told as by Timur, c.1350s)
p.c: A genealogical legend, retold in a work whose authorship is disputed.
p.tg: origin legend tatar moghul japhet turks

p.h: The 'river Tartar' is imaginary
p.g: Rémusat reviews earlier guesses about the name Tatar and dismisses them. Bergeron's river Tartar (taken from Matthew Paris) is 'entirely imaginary' in the light of better geography; his Syriac 'abandoned' and lost-tribes theory is 'more untenable still'; Fischer's claim that the Chinese called all neighbours Ta-ta is false; and Muslim writers' ancestor 'Tatar, brother of Mongol' is a genealogical invention modelled on the Bible.
p.q: Bergeron propose, d'après Matt. Paris, le nom d'une rivière Tartar ou Tatar, sur les bords de laquelle habitoit la tribu en question; mais des notions plus exactes acquises sur la géographie de ces contrées, permettent de regarder la rivière Tartar comme entièrement imaginaire.
p.s: Jean-Pierre Abel-Rémusat
p.t: Bergeron proposes, after Matthew Paris, the name of a river Tartar or Tatar, on whose banks the tribe in question lived; but more exact knowledge of the geography of these regions allows us to regard the river Tartar as entirely imaginary.

p.h: The Yakuts' own story: fleeing from Lake Baikal
p.g: The Yakuts told Sauer they call themselves Sakha and came from the south. Their chief Omogai Bey led his tribe and cattle from the plains west of Lake Baikal to escape a stronger horde, fought the Buryats, and followed the Lena north to the meadows around today's Yakutsk. A related people near Krasnoyarsk, which Sauer calls Mongols, also called themselves Sakha and spoke the same language.
p.q: The nation known among the Russians by the name of Yakuti call themselves Socha, and say that they came originally from the south. … The Toyon (i.e. Chief) Omogai Bey, with all his tribe and cattle, left the fertile plains situated to the west of the lake Baical, or Baighal, to make way for a more powerful horde
p.s: Martin Sauer (1802), relating Yakut tradition
p.c: Oral tradition recorded through interpreters. The Sakha language is Turkic, so calling the Krasnoyarsk kin 'Mongals' is Sauer's loose label.

p.h: 'Kirghiz-Kaisak' is a foreign name: they call themselves Kazak
p.g: Levshin opens his history by saying that Europe gives the Kazakhs a name neither they nor their neighbours use. They call themselves Kazak, and Persians, Bukharans and Khivans know them by that name; the Chinese say Hasak. Russia too called them the Kazakh horde until the 18th century, when the prefix 'Kirghiz' was added, partly to tell them apart from Russia's own Cossacks.
p.q: и что онѣ себя до нынѣ иначе не называютъ, какъ Казаками (Казакъ). Подъ симъ же именемъ извѣстны они Персіянамъ, Бухарцамъ, Хивинцамъ и прочимъ народамъ Азіи. Китайцы, смягчая начальную букву К, говорятъ Хасаки. До XVIII столѣтія и въ Россіи не знали Киргизъ-Кайсаковъ, но именовали ихъ Казаками, Казачьею ордою.
p.s: Aleksei Levshin (1832)
p.t: and that to this day they call themselves nothing but Kazakhs (Kazak). Under this same name they are known to the Persians, Bukharans, Khivans and other peoples of Asia. The Chinese, softening the initial K, say Hasak. Until the 18th century Russia too did not know 'Kirghiz-Kaisaks', but called them Kazakhs, the Kazakh horde.

p.h: Tartars as runaway 'Indian lords' who came in 1212
p.g: Before describing Astrakhan, Olearius turns to the Polish scholar Matthias of Miechow. Miechow said the Tartars must not be confused with the ancient Scythians and Sarmatians, since they were only known from the thirteenth century; a comet of 1211 foretold their coming, and they were 'Indian lords' who had killed their king David and fled west. Olearius then says he will stick to what he saw himself.
p.q: a Physician, and Canon of Cracow, who liv'd at the beginning of the last age, says that those, who confound the Tartars with those Nations, which the Antients called Getae, Scythae and Sarmatae, are much mistaken, in as much as the Tartars have not been known, but since the thirteenth Age. … They were certain Indian Lords, who having kill'd their King, David, got away
p.s: Adam Olearius (English translation by John Davies, 1669)
p.c: Book learning passed on second-hand; the 'King David' story echoes medieval Prester John legends.

p.h: Eight banners each of Manchu, Mongol and 'Tartarized Chinese'
p.g: A footnote to Parrenin's letters on the persecuted Christian princes of the Sunu family explains the Qing banner system: eight banners of Manchu Tartars, eight of Mongol Tartars and eight of 'Tartarized Chinese', each with its own coloured flag, its own quarter in the Tartar city of Peking and its own courts, apart from those of the ordinary people. 'Tartar' here is a legal status as much as an ancestry.
p.q: Il y a huit bannières de Tartares Mantcheoux, huit autres de Tartares Mongous, & huit de Chinois tartarisés. … Chaque bannière a son quartier dans la ville Tartare, & sa justice particulière indépendante de celle du peuple.
p.s: Footnote in Parrenin's letter to Du Halde (Peking, 22 October, mid-1730s; probably added by the editors)
p.t: There are eight banners of Manchu Tartars, eight more of Mongol Tartars, and eight of Tartarized Chinese. … Each banner has its own quarter in the Tartar city, and its own justice, independent of that of the common people.
p.tg: eight banners bannermen tartar city identity

p.h: The 'Thirty Tatars' mourn the first Turk khans
p.g: The Kul Tegin stone opens with the Turks' own origin story and then says that when the first khans, Bumin and Istemi, died, peoples came 'weeping and lamenting' from the east: the Chinese, the Tibetans, the Kirghiz, the Three Qurıqan, the Thirty Tatars, the Kitay (Khitan) and the Tatabi. This is one of the oldest written uses of the name Tatar anywhere, carved in stone by the Turks themselves, and here the Tatars are one steppe people among many.
p.q: Pleurant et se lamentant arrivèrent de l'avant, du côté du soleil levant, les puissants peuples du désert (c'est-à-dire étrangers?), les Chinois, les Thibétains, les Apar et Apourim, les Kirghiz, les Trois-Kourikans, les Trente-Tatars, les Kitaï, les Tatabi, … tous ces peuples vinrent se lamenter et pleurer: si vaillants avaient été ces kagans.
p.s: Bilge Qaghan (inscription composed by Yollugh Tegin), Kul Tegin inscription, 732, in Vilhelm Thomsen's French translation (1896)
p.pe: Otuz Tatar (the Thirty Tatars), a Mongolic people east of the Turks
p.t: Weeping and lamenting there came from the front, from the side of the rising sun, the mighty peoples of the desert (that is, foreign peoples?): the Chinese, the Tibetans, the Apar and Apurim, the Kirghiz, the Three Qurıqan, the Thirty Tatars, the Kitay, the Tatabi … all these peoples came to lament and weep, so valiant had these khagans been.
p.c: Thomsen marks several words as uncertain; the list of mourners is a royal boast carved some 180 years after the funeral it describes.
p.n: Checked against the page image.
p.tg: otuz tatar thirty tatars ethnonym orkhon earliest

p.h: Ask a Kazan Tatar if he is a Tatar
p.g: In a long footnote Klaproth explains that the khanates of Kazan, Astrakhan and Crimea were called Tatar because their rulers descended from Chinggis Khan, even though their subjects were Turks. He adds that a so-called Tatar of Kazan or Astrakhan will deny being a Tatar, calls his language 'Turki', and hears 'Tatar' as an insult meaning brigand.
p.q: Qu'on demande, cependant, à un soi-disant Tatar de Kazan ou d'Astrakhan, s'il est un Tatar; il répondra négativement ; il appellera l'idiome qu'il parle turki, et jamais tatari. N'ayant pas oublié que ses ancêtres ont été subjugués par les Mongols ou Tatars, il regarde ce dernier nom comme une injure équivalente au mot brigand.
p.s: Julius Klaproth (footnote)
p.t: Yet ask a so-called Tatar of Kazan or Astrakhan whether he is a Tatar: he will say no; he will call the language he speaks Turki, and never Tatari. Not having forgotten that his ancestors were subjugated by the Mongols or Tatars, he regards that name as an insult equal to the word brigand.
p.c: Klaproth gives this as general experience, not a dated conversation. Later, many Volga Muslims did come to use 'Tatar' as their own name.
p.tg: kazan astrakhan ethnonym turki golden horde

p.h: 'Tartar' as a convenient catch-all
p.g: In a footnote Matthew Guthrie admits that scholars like Georgi and Tooke had tried to separate Mongols from Tartars, but says the steppe peoples are so alike that everyone will go on using one generic name, 'Scythians' for ancient times and 'Tartars' for modern ones, simply to save trouble.
p.q: Notwithstanding all the trouble taken by Professor Georgi, Mr. Tooke, &c. to distinguish the Monguls, &c. from the Tartars, there is so much similitude… that a generic name for the whole will always be employed by every one who is not minutely treating of their subdivisions, let professed historians do what they please to prevent it
p.s: Matthew Guthrie (editor's footnote in the Appendix, 1802)

p.h: Samarkand, 'the head of Tartary' on the maps
p.g: Describing the Mogores (Mughals), who he says now rule Sind and have made many wars on Cambay, Cruz says the head of their kingdom is 'the great Samarkand', which the maps of his day label 'the head of Tartary'. He then uses Josephus to make these people Scythians descended from Japheth, son of Noah, through Magog. This is book learning, not observation: it shows 'Tartary' working as a map label in the 1560s.
p.q: Ha cabeça de seu reyno se chama ho grã Samarcam, q̃ nos Mappas se chama cabeça de Tartaria: estes sam cõtados antre os Scythas, como testefica Josepho no liuro primeiro das antiguidades, os quaes segũdo elle descendem de Japha filho de Noe por Magog.
p.s: Gaspar da Cruz, O.P. (Tractado, Évora 1569)
p.pe: Mogores (Mughals), counted by Cruz among the Scythians
p.t: The head of their kingdom is called the great Samarkand, which on the maps is called the head of Tartary. These are counted among the Scythians, as Josephus testifies in the first book of the Antiquities, who according to him descend from Japheth son of Noah through Magog.
p.c: Cruz is repeating maps and Josephus; he never went near Samarkand.

p.h: 'Now we call Tatars our kin in Tobolsk, Kazan and Astrakhan'
p.g: The answer Bichurin got from Turkestanis in Beijing, and his conclusion. It shows 'Tatar' as a name used by outsiders for particular Turkic communities under Russian rule, not the name of a vast state.
p.q: я спрашивалъ ихъ, кого они называютъ Татарами? Вотъ ихъ отвѣтъ: „нынѣ мы называемъ Татарами единоплеменный съ нами народъ, обитающій въ Тоболѣ, Казани и Астрахани.“ Напротивъ, сами Татары утверждаютъ, что сіе названіе дано имъ отъ сосѣднихъ народовъ. … но только нынѣ нѣтъ ни одного не токмо народа, но и поколѣнія въ Средней Азіи, которое бы называлось симъ именемъ.
p.s: Iakinf (N. Ya. Bichurin), translator's preface, 1829
p.pe: Volga and Siberian Tatars, as seen by Turkestani Muslims
p.t: I asked them whom they call Tatars. Here is their answer: 'Now we call Tatars a people of the same stock as us, living in Tobol, Kazan and Astrakhan.' The Tatars themselves, on the contrary, assert that this name was given them by neighbouring peoples. … but now there is not a single people, nor even a clan, in Central Asia that calls itself by this name.
p.n: The scan's machine-read text is too damaged to confirm this quote automatically. Check it against the page.

p.h: Are the Kirghiz Tatars or Mongols?
p.g: Meyer thinks a Tatar origin for the 'Kirghiz' (the Kazakhs) far likelier than a Mongol one, judging by faces and language. He then gives the three hordes and adds that the Great Horde is often called the 'golden horde', a striking reuse of the old name. A few lines on he notes that the Russians call some of its tribes the wild, stone or black Kirghiz.
p.q: Doch ist die Annahme eines tatarischen Ursprungs wohl viel wahrscheinlicher, und sie wird durch die Gesichtszüge und Sprache besser unterstützt, als die Meinung, daß sie von den Mongolen herstammen. Man theilt die Kirgisen in drei Haupthorden, die große, mittlere und kleine Horde. Die große Horde wird auch oft die goldne Horde genannt
p.s: Carl Anton Meyer (diary printed in Ledebour's Reise, part 2, 1830)
p.pe: Kirghiz (Kazakhs of the Great, Middle and Little Hordes)
p.t: Yet the assumption of a Tatar origin is much more probable, and it is better supported by their facial features and language than the opinion that they descend from the Mongols. The Kirghiz are divided into three main hordes, the great, middle and little horde. The great horde is also often called the golden horde
p.c: 'Kirghiz' here means the Kazakhs; the 'black Kirghiz' are the true Kyrgyz. Meyer says he adds nothing new on origins and relies on informants and a Russian journal article.
p.tg: kirghiz kazakhs hordes golden horde origins

p.h: Thomsen: the Tatars of the stones were Mongols, not Turks
p.g: In his notes Thomsen comments on 'Otuz Tatar' (Thirty Tatars) and 'Toquz Tatar' (Nine Tatars): the name meets us here 'for the first time in history', appears in Chinese books only in the ninth century, and belongs to the Mongols or one of their tribes, not to a Turkic people. He places them between the Oghuz (Uighurs) to the west and the Khitan to the east, near the Kerulen river. So the original Tatars were a real Mongolic group on the edge of the Turk empire.
p.q: nom bien connu que nous rencontrons ici pour la première fois dans l'histoire Dans la littérature chinoise, Ta-ta se présente au commencement du IXe siècle. C'est aux Mongols ou plutôt à une de leurs tribus que revient cette dénomination, et non à aucun peuple de race turque
p.s: Vilhelm Thomsen, commentary in Inscriptions de l'Orkhon dechiffrees (1896)
p.pl: Eastern Mongolia (east and southeast of Lake Baikal)
p.t: a well-known name that we meet here for the first time in history. In Chinese literature, Ta-ta appears at the beginning of the ninth century. This name belongs to the Mongols, or rather to one of their tribes, and not to any people of Turkic race.
p.c: Thomsen's 1896 identification; later scholars still debate how Mongolic the eighth-century Tatars were.
p.n: Checked against the page image.

p.h: 'Eastern Tartars': a Manchu dynasty from a small horde chief
p.g: Careri opens his chapter on the 'Eastern Tartars' by saying their princes' origin is so obscure that everyone who writes of it tells fables. They began only in this century from 'a small Horde chief, or captain of outlaws or wandering Tartars' called Tien-mim (Nurhaci). He goes on to divide Tartary into Eastern (Manchu lands, poor, with only two or three small towns) and a far more powerful Western Tartary, both mostly living in tents.
p.q: E' così oscura di questi Principi l'origine, che chiunque ha voluto parlarne ha dato nelle favole. Eglino hanno avuto principio in questo secolo da un picciol Capo d'Horda, o Capitano di fuorusciti, o Tartari erranti, che si chiamava Tien-mim
p.s: Giovanni Francesco Gemelli Careri (Giro del Mondo, part IV, Naples 1700), compiling Martini and other Jesuit histories
p.pe: Manchus ('Eastern Tartars'), as against 'Western Tartars' (Mongols, Oirats)
p.t: The origin of these princes is so obscure that whoever has tried to speak of it has fallen into fables. They had their beginning in this century from a small chief of a Horde, or captain of outlaws or wandering Tartars, who was called Tien-mim
p.c: Compiled from printed Jesuit histories; 'Tien-mim' is Tianming, Nurhaci's reign name, not his personal name.

p.h: Europeans kept calling the Muslim Turks 'Tatars'
p.g: The authors argue that after the Mongol conquests Europeans went on calling all the Muslim, Turkic-speaking peoples of Kazan, Astrakhan, the Crimea and Turkestan 'Tatars', which caused endless confusion. On the same page they conclude that the name lost all meaning in Asia and survives 'only in the European vocabulary', and that the Tatars of southern Russia are really Turks, Cumans or Pechenegs once ruled by the Mongols.
p.q: After the Mongol torrent had subsided, Europeans persisted in giving the appellation of Tatars to all those Mussulman nations originally of Turkish origin, that to this day occupy the territory of Kasan and Astrakhan, the Crimea and the region called Turcomania
p.s: Xavier Hommaire de Hell (English translation, 1847)
p.pe: Turkic Muslims of Russia and Central Asia
p.tg: tatars turks kazan crimea european label

p.h: 'Tartar' from a river, or from a word for 'multitude'
p.g: Thomas insists that 'Tartar' is not the people's own name. He offers two explanations he had heard: that they were named after a river flowing past their country, or that 'Tatar' means 'multitude'. The river story also appears in Matthew Paris; neither explanation is how historians now explain the name, which came from the Tatar tribe that the Mongols had defeated.
p.q: Hoc autem nomen Tartari non nomen est gentis proprium, sed a quadam aqua, quae illorum praeterfluit regionem sic appellati sunt, vel secundum quosdam Tatar idem sonat, quod multitudo
p.s: Thomas, archdeacon of Split, Historia Salonitana, in the first edition by Ivan Lučić (Lucius), Amsterdam 1666
p.t: This name Tartars is not the people's own name, but they were so called from a certain river that flows past their region; or, according to some, Tatar means the same as 'multitude'
p.c: Both explanations are reports Thomas heard; he does not choose between them.

p.h: Manchus are 'Eastern Tartars', Mongols 'Western Tartars'
p.g: Parrenin, sending the Académie des Sciences his Manchu translation of a French anatomy commissioned by the Kangxi emperor, stops to explain what 'Tartar language' means: the language of the Manchus, who have reigned in China for eighty years and are called Eastern Tartars, not that of the Mongols, called Western Tartars and almost all tributaries of the emperor. The two languages, he says, are very different.
p.q: je parle de la langue des Mantcheoux qui régnent à la Chine depuis quatre-vingts ans, & qui s'appellent Tartares Orientaux. Je ne parle nullement de la langue des Mongols, qu'on nomme Tartares Occidentaux, & qui sont presque tous tributaires de l'Empereur. Ces deux langues sont très-différentes entr'elles.
p.s: Dominique Parrenin, letter to the Académie des Sciences (Peking, 1 May 1723)
p.t: I mean the language of the Manchus, who have reigned in China for eighty years and are called Eastern Tartars. I do not at all mean the language of the Mongols, who are called Western Tartars and are almost all tributaries of the Emperor. These two languages are very different from each other.

p.h: The Tartars of Tobolsk, once subjects of Kuchum Khan
p.g: At Tobolsk the envoys asked about a people the Russians called Tartars (Ta-ta-la), who lived from the Irtysh to Kazan. Russians told them these people had once been subjects of Kuchum Khan (Ku-tching Khan), the last khan of Sibir, and had spread out after Tobolsk became Russian. Tulishen noted that those who had not become Orthodox Christians looked like Chinese Muslims (Hui): short hair, small caps, no pork.
p.q: the Russians said: "This people was formerly subject to the Ku-tching Khan, otherwise called Ho-tung. … Some among them have conformed to our religion, but others have not." Such of this people as have not conformed to the religion of the Russians, have the appearance of being (Hoei-tse) Mahometans. They wear small caps, and their hair cut short. They eat no pork
p.s: Tulishen (translated from the Chinese by George Thomas Staunton, 1821)
p.c: The origin story is what Russians told the envoys. The last clause of this passage in the Chinese text (T1072, juan 1, 46a: 别供佛像) differs from Staunton's 'offer no sacrifices to their Divinities', so that detail is uncertain.

p.h: In the Cumans' own language, 'Tatar' simply meant 'Turkic'
p.g: Kuun's index of the Cuman words in the Codex gives the entry 'Tatar' as meaning 'a Turk' or 'Turkish', and the phrase 'tatar til' ('Tatar tongue') as meaning plain, sincere speech. So the merchants and friars who compiled the book heard the steppe people use 'Tatar' for their own Turkic language, not for a lost empire. The phrase occurs on page 229 of the Codex.
p.q: Tatar «Turca», «turcicus», tatar til «sermo sincerus» pag. 229.
p.s: Geza Kuun, Cuman word index to the Codex Cumanicus (1880)
p.t: Tatar: 'a Turk', 'Turkish'; tatar til: 'honest (plain) speech', page 229.
p.c: Kuun's gloss of 'tatar til' as 'sermo sincerus' is his reading of a phrase in the German part of the Codex; later editors (Bang, Gronbech) revised many of his readings.
p.n: Checked against the page image.

p.h: A people made famous by those who destroyed it
p.g: Drawing on the historian D'Ohsson, the authors explain that 'Tatar' was first the name of a real Mongolian tribe, whom Genghis Khan wiped out. Yet the name spread from nation to nation and stuck to Genghis's own armies. By a strange accident, they say, a destroyed people became famous through the conquests of its destroyers.
p.q: It is a fact established by the statements of many writers, and by D'Ohson himself, that Genghis Khan annihilated the white Tatars, and thus it has come to pass by a most curious freak of accident, that this extinguished people became celebrated all over the East by the conquests of its very destroyers.
p.s: Xavier Hommaire de Hell (English translation, 1847)
p.pe: the Tatar tribe and the Mongols of Genghis Khan
p.c: A summary of 19th-century scholarship, not the authors' own research.
p.tg: tatar tribe genghis khan mongols origins

p.h: How the name Tatar lived on and spread to the Turkic peoples
p.g: In a note on a feud in the chronicle, Schmidt argues that the Taichiud and the Tatar formed one people with the other Mongol tribes. After Chinggis Khan's time the name Taichiud vanishes from history, but the name Tatar lived on, grew better known and wider in meaning, passing to the Turkic peoples the Mongols conquered in western Asia. A compact statement of how 'Tatar' became a catch-all label.
p.q: Ausgemacht ist es übrigens, dass die Taidschigod und Tatar mit den andern mongolischen Stämmen nur ein Hauptvolk bildeten, dass ferner der Name Taidschigod nach Tschinggis Chaghan's Zeit in der Geschichte nicht mehr gefunden wird, der Name Tatar aber fortdauerte, und sogar bekannter wurde und eine ausgedehntere Bedeutung erhielt, indem derselbe auch auf die, im Westen Asiens unterjochten, türkischen Völkerschaften überging.
p.s: I. J. Schmidt (editor's note 35, 1829)
p.pe: Tatar and Taichiud tribes; Turkic peoples later called Tatars
p.t: It is settled, moreover, that the Taichiud and Tatar formed only one main people with the other Mongol tribes; further, that the name Taichiud is no longer found in history after Chinggis Khan's time, but the name Tatar lived on, and even became better known and acquired a wider meaning, since it passed also to the Turkic peoples subjugated in the west of Asia.
p.c: Schmidt's own scholarly judgement; modern scholars debate whether the medieval Tatars spoke Mongolic or Turkic.

p.h: The Giray khans: a dynasty 'planted' by Lithuania
p.g: Michalo claims the Crimean Christians, weak and luxurious, invited a band of Tartars from the Volga horde to defend them, and that this Tatar power grew until it took the peninsula. He adds that the Crimean khans came from Lithuania: the last, 'Aczkirei' (Haci Giray), born near Trakai and sent by Grand Duke Vytautas to rule, whose descendants all bear the name Giray. He calls the dynasty a stock 'planted there by the brave right hand of Your Majesty's ancestors' that now repays Lithuania with endless trouble.
p.q: Ultimus vero ex Lituania Caesarum Aczkirei, hic apud Troki natus, & hinc a divo Withowdo ad imperium illud missus, genuit imperans ibi in Taurica filium Menglikirei. … Haec igitur est Kireorum stirps, dextra forti progenitorum S. Mtis Vestrae ibi plantata
p.s: Michalo the Lithuanian, De moribus Tartarorum, Lituanorum et Moschorum, fragment 1 (c. 1550; Basel, 1615)
p.t: The last of the khans from Lithuania, Aczkirei, was born near Trakai and sent from here by the late Vytautas to that throne; ruling there in Taurica he fathered a son, Mengli Giray. … This, then, is the stock of the Girays, planted there by the strong right hand of Your Majesty's ancestors
p.c: Partly true: Haci Giray, founder of the khanate, did spend time in Lithuania and had Lithuanian backing, but the claim of Lithuanian birth and appointment is a Lithuanian patriotic version.

p.h: Why the Chinese say 'Tata'
p.g: Martini defines his subject: the Tartars are simply the people living north of the Great Wall, which for 300 German leagues has served as a rampart against them. He adds that the Chinese, lacking the letter R, have always called them 'Tata', and that the name covers both the Eastern Tartars, unknown in Europe, and the Western ones stretching from Kashgar to the sea above Japan.
p.q: I call that Nation Tartars, which inhabiting the Northern parts, behind that famous Wall which stretching out above 300. German Leagues from East to West, hath ever served for a Rampart to hinder their irruptions into the said Empire. This Country the Chineses having a defect of the letter R. antiently called Tata:
p.s: Martino Martini (English translation, London 1654)
p.pe: Tartars in general: Eastern (Manchu/Jurchen) and Western (Mongol)
p.c: Chinese 'Dada' (韃靼) is a real name for the Tatars; the 'missing R' explanation is Martini's.
p.tg: name origin tata great wall manchus mongols

p.h: Why say 'Tartar' when they say 'Totar'?
p.g: Avril reports that the Chinese call the Tartars 'Totai' because of a missing letter in their language, and then wonders why Western Europeans say 'Tartar' at all, when Poles, Russians and the Tartars themselves say 'Totar'. It is a rare early admission that the extra 'r' of 'Tartar' is a Western habit.
p.q: This Relation adds, that the Chineses call the Tartars Totai, because they have not the Letter K in their Language. Nor do I know why we call 'em Tartars, seeing that in Poland, Muscovy and even in Tartary it self, they abridge the Name, and call 'em only Totar.
p.s: Philippe Avril (English translation, 1693)
p.c: The scan reads 'Letter K'; the sense (Chinese has no r sound) suggests the original printed 'R'.

p.h: 'We are Kazakhs, not Kirghiz'
p.g: Meyendorff noticed that the steppe people the Russians called Kirghiz never used that name themselves. They called themselves Kazakh, which some said meant 'horseman' and others 'warrior', and they believed the Bashkirs had given them the name Kirghiz.
p.q: they never make use of this name among themselves ; they invariably style themselves Kasak ; which, according to some, signifies horseman, and to others warrior. They say the Bachkirs call them Kirghiz, but are ignorant from whence the name is derived
p.s: Georg von Meyendorff (translated by William Monteith, 1840)

p.h: Mukden, capital of Eastern Tartary, where Chinese count as Tartars
p.g: Noël reports a plan to open a mission at Chin-yam (Shenyang, the Manchu Mukden), capital of Liaodong and all Eastern Tartary, where the emperor had set four supreme tribunals for the Tartars' affairs. He adds that Liaodong now counts as part of Tartary and its people are regarded 'not as Chinese, but as true Tartars'. The label followed political allegiance, not ancestry.
p.q: Chin-yam capitale de Leaoton, & de toute la Tartarie orientale. Cette ville est considérable, & l'Empereur y a établi quatre Tribunaux souverains pour y juger en dernier ressort toutes les affaires des Tartares; car le Leaoton passe aujourd'hui pour être de la Tartarie, & on n'en regarde plus les habitans comme Chinois, mais comme de véritables Tartares.
p.s: François Noël, Mémoire on the state of the China missions
p.pe: Manchus and the people of Liaodong
p.t: Chin-yam, capital of Liaodong and of all Eastern Tartary. This city is considerable, and the Emperor has set up four supreme tribunals there to judge in the last resort all the affairs of the Tartars; for Liaodong now passes for part of Tartary, and its inhabitants are no longer regarded as Chinese, but as true Tartars.

p.h: The Tatars: a separate nation that Chinggis crushed in 1202
p.g: D'Ohsson, following Rashid al-Din and the Chinese annals, treats the Tatars as a distinct people: seventy thousand households around Lake Buir by the Jurchen frontier, split into six feuding tribes and bitter enemies of the Mongols. In spring 1202 Temüjin attacked and defeated them.
p.q: Cette nation, qui habitait le pays environnant le lac Bouyour, près de la frontière des Tchourtchés, comptait alors soixante-dix mille huttes, ou familles, et se divisait en six tribus … Il régnait une grande animosité entre eux et les Mongols.
p.s: Constantin d'Ohsson (from Rashid al-Din and the Chinese annals)
p.pe: the Tatar tribe; Mongols under Temüjin
p.t: This nation, which lived in the country around Lake Buir, near the frontier of the Jurchen, then numbered seventy thousand huts, or families, and was divided into six tribes … There was great hostility between them and the Mongols.

p.h: 'Unknown peoples': who are these Tatars?
p.g: The first Suzdal notice of the Tatars admits that nobody knows who they are, where they came from, what language they speak or what faith they hold. People called them Tatars, Taumens or Pechenegs, while bookish men tied them to a prophecy of Methodius of Patara. The chronicler adds that he writes them down only 'for the memory of the disaster of the Rus princes' at the Kalka.
p.q: явишася языци, ихже никтоже добрѣ ясно не вѣсть, кто суть и отколѣ изидоша, и что языкъ ихъ, и которого племени суть, и что вѣра ихъ; и зовуть я Татары, а инии глаголють Таумены, а друзіи Печенѣзи, ини глаголють, яко се суть, о нихъ же Меѳодій Патомьскый епископъ свѣдѣтельствуеть
p.s: Laurentian Chronicle (Suzdal annal), PSRL vol. 1 (1846)
p.pe: Tatars (the Mongol army of Jebe and Subutai)
p.t: there appeared peoples whom no one clearly knows: who they are and whence they came out, and what their language is, and of what tribe they are, and what their faith is; and they call them Tatars, and others say Taumens, and others Pechenegs, and others say that these are the ones of whom Methodius, bishop of Patara, bears witness
p.c: The editors note that other chronicles read 'Taurmens' (Turkmens). The Methodius link is a book legend, not anything the Mongols said of themselves.

p.h: How 'Tatar' became 'Tartar': the pun of St Louis
p.g: Humboldt's note continues: the r in 'Tartar' was added in Western Europe by 'false erudition', linking the Mongols to Tartarus, the classical underworld. He quotes King Louis IX of France telling his mother in 1241 that the 'Tartars' would either be driven back to their Tartarean home or send the French to heaven. On the same page he compares it to the Spanish turning 'Carib' into 'cannibal' and warns against using 'Tartar' as a catch-all name.
p.q: Tatar wurde dazu durch falsche Erudition in West-Europa zu Tartaren umgewandelt, Ein Wortspiel des heiligen Ludwig drückt diese Erudition lebhaft aus, … sagte Ludwig der Heilige zu seiner Mutter: „Erigat nos, mater, coeleste solatium, quia si perveniant ipsi, vel nos ipsos, quos vocamus Tartaros, ad suas tartareas sedes, unde exierunt retrudemus, vel ipsi nos omnes ad coelum advehent.”
p.s: Alexander von Humboldt (footnote in Rose's Reise, vol. 1, 1837), quoting Louis IX of France
p.pe: Mongols (Tatars) of the 1241 invasion; Western Europeans
p.t: Tatar was moreover changed into Tartar in Western Europe by false erudition. A pun of St Louis vividly expresses this erudition … St Louis said to his mother: 'Let heavenly comfort lift us up, mother, for if they come, either we shall push them, whom we call Tartars, back to their Tartarean seats whence they came out, or they will carry us all to heaven.'
p.c: Humboldt gives no source for the saying; it comes from the English chronicler Matthew Paris.
p.tg: tartarus tartar pun louis ix etymology

p.h: 'Their name by no means indicates their origin'
p.g: In a footnote Clarke quotes Thomas Thornton's book on Turkey (1809) to explain the couriers: 'Tartar' was the name of the job, not of a nation. The men came from every province and were marked out by the Tartar calpac (fur cap) they wore instead of a turban. A good reminder that 'Tartar' could mean a role or a costume.
p.q: The Tartars are public couriers, much respected for their good conduct and fidelity. Their name by no means indicates their origin, as they are taken indifferently from all the provinces in the empire, and are distinguished by the Tartar calpac, which they wear instead of the turban.
p.s: Thomas Thornton, The Present State of Turkey (1809), quoted in a footnote by Clarke

p.h: Seven Tartar nations, and the 'water Mongols' named after a river
p.g: Sanudo lists seven Tartar nations 'of greater excellence': Tartar, Tangoth, Eurath, Ialayr, Sonit, Mengli and Theboth (roughly Tatar, Tangut, Oirat, Jalayir, Sunit, and others). Then, from another source, he says the land of Mongal had four peoples, the second being the Su Mongol or 'water Mongols', who 'call themselves Tartars, from a river of theirs called Tartar'. Chinggis rose from the first people and conquered the rest.
p.q: quarum prima vocatur Tartar, secunda, Tangoth, tertia Eurath, quarta Ialayr, quinta Sonit, sexta Mengli, septima Theboth. Præfata quoque terra Mongal, quatuor olim habebat populos: quorum primus Iechamongla, id est, magni Mongali vocabatur: Secundus, Summongal, id est, aquatici Mongali: hii se ipsos Tartaros appellant, à quodam suo fluuio qui Tartar dicitur
p.s: Marino Sanudo Torsello (Liber secretorum fidelium crucis, c. 1321; ed. Bongars, Hanau 1611)
p.t: of which the first is called Tartar, the second Tangoth, the third Eurath, the fourth Ialayr, the fifth Sonit, the sixth Mengli, the seventh Theboth. The said land of Mongal also once had four peoples: the first of which was called Iechamongla, that is, great Mongols; the second, Summongal, that is, water Mongols: these call themselves Tartars, from a certain river of theirs which is called Tartar
p.c: Stitched from Hayton (the seven nations) and Carpini (the four peoples); the river Tartar is a folk etymology.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image; long s normalized.
p.tg: seven nations tatar su mongol origin name

p.h: How Witsen gathered his Tartary
p.g: Witsen answers that the map grew out of a visit almost 28 years earlier to the country of the Tsar, where he talked with local people and 'Tartars of all sorts'. Since then he had kept up letters with Moscow, Astrakhan, Georgia, Isfahan, Poland, Constantinople and Peking, and collected journals and drawings made to his order. He then admits his biggest doubts are about the sea coasts, which he drew in pale colour to show the uncertainty.
p.q: I not only Conversed with the Inhabitants of those Countreys, but with Tartars of all sorts … I have maintain'd a constant Correspondence in Mosco, Astracan, Georgia, Ispahan, Polonia, and Constantinople, I have had Letters every year from Peking the chief City of China, I have gathered Volumes of Journals and Registers
p.s: Nicolaas Witsen (letter printed in Philosophical Transactions, 1686)
p.pe: 'Tartars of all sorts' met in Muscovy
p.c: The country Witsen visited is garbled in the scan; his known journey of 1664 to 1665 was to Muscovy.

p.h: Kazakh horde, Great and Lesser Nogais: the peoples on the old map
p.g: The preface lists what the old Great Map showed in the south and east: the 'nomad Kazakh horde', the camps of the Great Nogais, the towns of Bukhara and Urgench, the Volga to Astrakhan and the Don to Azov, and the fields between Azov and Astrakhan 'where the Lesser Nogais roam'. The steppe is named by its nomad peoples, not by a single 'Tartary'.
p.q: и кочевую Казацкую орду, и большихъ Нагаевъ кочевье, и Бухарскіе и Юргенскіе города, и рѣку Волгу до Астарахани, и рѣку Донъ до Азова, и межъ Азова и Астарахани до Хвалинскаго, и до Азовскаго, и до Чернаго моря, поля и рѣки, что кочують малые Нагаи.
p.s: Razriad clerks, preface to the Book of the Great Map (1627), ed. Yazykov (1838)
p.pe: Kazakhs ('Kazatskaia orda'), Great Nogai, Lesser Nogai; Bukhara and Urgench
p.t: and the nomad Kazakh horde, and the nomad camps of the Great Nogais, and the Bukharan and Urgench towns, and the river Volga to Astrakhan, and the river Don to Azov, and between Azov and Astrakhan to the Khvalyn [Caspian] and to the Azov and Black Seas, the fields and rivers where the Lesser Nogais roam.
p.n: The scan's machine-read text is too damaged to confirm this quote automatically. Check it against the page.

p.h: 'Tartars of Kin', lords of the golden mountains, now masters of China
p.g: Introducing the Dutch embassy to Peking, Thévenot explains in a margin note who these new 'Tartars' are. Eastern Tartary is called Kin, 'gold', by the Chinese; its people are known as lords of the golden mountains; the country is bounded by another Tartar kingdom, Niulhan, to the north, by the Korean peninsula to the south and by a great river, the 'Linohang', to the west, and 'these Tartars are the ones who are now masters of China'.
p.q: La Tartarie Orientale est appellée Kin par les Chinois, c'est à dire l'or, on appelle communément ces Tartares les seigneurs des montagnes d'or, parce que leurs païs en sont fort riches.
p.s: Melchisédech Thévenot (editor's margin note)
p.t: Eastern Tartary is called Kin by the Chinese, that is to say gold; these Tartars are commonly called the lords of the golden mountains, because their countries are very rich in it.
p.c: Editor's gloss built on Martini and other Jesuit writers; 'Kin' is the Jin dynasty name the Manchus first used (Later Jin).

p.h: 'Tatars' who seized China thirty years ago
p.g: In a dispatch to Tsar Aleksei from Yeniseisk, Spafarii passes on what Russian traders just back from Peking (Kambalyk) told him. The 'Nikan kingdom' the Chinese were fighting, he explains, is simply the old Chinese kingdom: about thirty years before, 'Tatars' had taken the Chinese realm, the old royal line fled to distant coastal provinces, and 'the Bogdykhan's Tatars' now call it Nikan. Russian deserters in Peking whispered that two thousand soldiers could win all Dauria for the tsar.
p.q: И то Никанское царство нѣтъ иного, опричь стараго Китайскаго царства, потому что нынѣ есть лѣтъ съ тридцать завладѣли Китайскимъ царствомъ Татары, а поколѣніе царское бѣжало въ дальніе приморскія китайскія страны, и то нынѣ называютъ Богдыхановы Татары Никанскимъ царствомъ.
p.s: Nikolai Spafarii, dispatch from Yeniseisk to Tsar Aleksei, July 1675, reporting traders' news (ed. Yu. V. Arsenyev, 1882)
p.pe: Manchus (called Tatars) and the Han Chinese 'Nikan' kingdom
p.t: And that Nikan kingdom is nothing other than the old Chinese kingdom, because it is now some thirty years since the Tatars took possession of the Chinese kingdom, and the royal line fled into the distant coastal Chinese lands, and the Bogdykhan's Tatars now call that the Nikan kingdom.
p.c: Second-hand from traders. The editor's footnote explains that the war was the revolt of the southern provinces led by Wu Sangui, not a restored Ming kingdom; 'Nikan' was the Manchu word for the Han Chinese.

p.h: Bergeron's guesses: a river Tartar, or Syriac for 'abandoned'
p.g: In his Traicté, Bergeron lists Hayton's seven Mongol nations and offers two origins for the name: a river called Tartar, or a Syriac word meaning 'the abandoned', favoured by those who made the Tartars descendants of the ten lost tribes of Israel. He reports claims that some northern hordes bore the tribal names Dan, Zabulon and Naphtali, but on the next page calls the theory weak, resting on an apocryphal book.
p.q: Le nom de Tartar, Tatar, ou Totar, vient du fleuue Tartar; ou du mot Totar, ou Tatar, qui en langage Syrien veut dire delaissez, ou abandonnez, suiuant l'opinion de ceux qui les veulent faire descendre des dix lignées Israëlites releguées en Medie, & depuis venuës au pays d'Arsareth.
p.s: Pierre Bergeron (Traicté des Tartares, 1634)
p.t: The name Tartar, Tatar or Totar comes from the river Tartar, or from the word Totar or Tatar, which in the Syrian language means 'forsaken' or 'abandoned', according to the opinion of those who would make them descend from the ten tribes of Israel exiled in Media and afterwards come to the land of Arsareth.
p.c: Compiled speculation; Abel-Rémusat (W261) later dismissed both etymologies and the river Tartar as imaginary.

p.h: White, wild and black Tatars
p.g: Klaproth summarises a Song Chinese general's account of the northern tribes before Chinggis Khan's rise. The 'White Tatars' cut their cheeks and were probably Turks, the 'Wild Tatars' were slaves to them, and the 'Black Tatars' were the tribe into which Temujin, the future Chinggis Khan, was born.
p.q: Tatars blancs, ceux-ci n'avaient rien de rebutant dans leur extérieur; cependant ils se faisaient des incisions dans les joues (se tatouaient, comme cela se pratique encore aujourd'hui parmi les Toungouses). … La seconde tribu mentionnée par Meng koung est celle des Tatars sauvages. Ceux-ci étaient stupides et servaient d'esclaves aux premiers. La troisième était celle des Tatars noirs, parmi laquelle Tchinghiz khan naquit
p.s: Julius Klaproth, summarising the Chinese account he credits to the general Meng Hong (d. 1246)
p.pe: Tatar tribes of the early 13th century (Mongols and Onggut)
p.t: White Tatars: these had nothing repulsive in their appearance; yet they made cuts in their cheeks (tattooed themselves, as the Tungus still do today). … The second tribe mentioned by Meng Hong is that of the Wild Tatars. These were stupid and served as slaves to the first. The third was that of the Black Tatars, among whom Chinggis Khan was born
p.c: The Chinese report (the Mengda beilu of 1221) is now usually credited to the envoy Zhao Gong rather than Meng Hong; its labels reflect a Chinese outsider's view.
p.tg: black tatars white tatars chinggis khan chinese sources

p.h: The Khazars' Jewish king and Turk-like people
p.g: Ibn Rusta says the Khazars had a king called Isha who ran the army, while the supreme king, the Khazar Khaqan, had only the name. The supreme ruler was of the Jewish religion, as were Isha and the commanders and nobles who followed him; the rest followed a religion like that of the Turks.
p.q: ولهم ملك يقال له ايشا والملك الاعظم انما هو خزر خاقان وليس له من طاعة الخزر الا الاسم … ورئيسهم الاعظم على دين اليهود وكذلك ايشا ومن يميل ميله من القواد والعظماء والبقية منهم على دين شبيه دين الاتراك
p.s: Ibn Rusta (Arabic text ed. M. J. de Goeje, 1892)
p.t: They have a king called Isha; the supreme king is the Khazar Khaqan, but he has nothing of the Khazars' obedience except the name … Their supreme chief follows the religion of the Jews, and so do Isha and those commanders and great men who lean his way; the rest of them follow a religion like the religion of the Turks.
p.c: Copied from an earlier report; the Khazar state was destroyed c.965, long before the word Tartar came into use.

p.h: 'The Mongols are the true Tatars'
p.g: Klaproth opens his essay on the Tatars by calling it a common error to mix up Tatars and Turks. In the age of Mongol power, he says, only the Mongols bore the name; only in the last few centuries has it spread to all the eastern Turks and even to unrelated peoples. He asks scholars to drop the habit.
p.q: C'est une erreur généralement adoptée que de confondre les Tatars et les Turcs … car dans le tems de la puissance des Mongols, qui sont les véritables Tatars, ce nom ne fut donné qu'à eux. … Je veux tâcher d'éclaircir cette confusion, et j'invite tous les savans à abolir un abus qui occasionera toujours des méprises dans les recherches ethnographiques.
p.s: Julius Klaproth
p.pe: Mongols; Turkic peoples wrongly called Tatars
p.t: It is a generally accepted error to confuse the Tatars with the Turks … for in the time of the power of the Mongols, who are the true Tatars, that name was given to them alone. … I wish to try to clear up this confusion, and I invite all scholars to abolish an abuse that will always cause mistakes in ethnographic research.
p.c: Modern historians treat the medieval Tatars as a separate steppe confederation that Chinggis Khan destroyed, so Klaproth's simple equation of Mongols and Tatars goes too far.

p.h: The Tatars: one of the oldest Turkic tribes
p.g: In his chapter on the tribes, Abu'l Ghazi describes the Tatars as a specific tribe, once 70,000 families under one powerful khan, that split into branches and declined. The main branch lived on the frontier of 'Kitay' (northern China) and was subject to its emperor, rebelling often. This is the historical Tatar confederation that Chinggis Khan later crushed, not the later Volga or Crimean Tatars.
p.q: The Tribe of the Tatars is one of the most antient and famous of the Turkish Nations; it was heretofore above 70000 Families strong, and had only one Chan who was very potent: But being afterwards divided into several Branches, its Power by degrees began to decline.
p.s: Abu'l Ghazi Bahadur Khan (English translation, 1730)
p.pl: Mongolia and the borders of northern China
p.pe: Tatar tribe (a Turkic people in Abu'l Ghazi's scheme)
p.n: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR for this volume is unreadable); long s normalized.
p.tg: tatar tribe turkic kitay china origins

p.h: Why 'Tartar' is a pun, not a name
p.g: In a footnote to their chapter on the origin of the Tatars, the authors refuse to use the spelling 'Tartar' at all. They say it comes only from a play on words by St Louis, King of France, who in the 1240s punned on Tatar and Tartarus, the classical underworld. This is the famous Tartarus pun, stated plainly by a 19th-century writer.
p.q: We have entirely rejected from our discussion the word Tartar, which owes its origin only to a jeu de mots, of which St. Louis was the author.
p.s: Xavier Hommaire de Hell (footnote, English translation, 1847)
p.c: The St Louis story is traditional (it is told in Matthew Paris's chronicle of the 1240s). The pun was widespread, and the story does not prove where the spelling began.
p.tg: tartarus pun st louis spelling names

p.h: Batu's 'Mongol' army had very few Mongols
p.g: In footnotes to his account of Batu's conquest of Russia and sack of Kiev in 1240, Klaproth points out that Batu's army contained very few Mongols and that he ruled as prince of the Kipchak Tartars. The khans of Kipchak called themselves Tartar sultans and lived at Sarai on the Akhtuba; after their empire split, the khans of Kazan, Astrakhan and Crimea kept the title.
p.q: Batu-chan had very few Mongols in his army, and had become prince of the Kipdschak Tartars… The chans of Kipdschak styled themselves Tartar sultans, and resided in the city of Sarai or Saratschik on the river Achtuba; an arm of the Wolga, till the division of their extensive dominions.
p.s: Julius Klaproth (his own footnotes, English translation, 1814)

p.h: In Bhutan, Tartary is called 'Sopo'
p.g: In a Portuguese letter of 1627 from the kingdom he calls Cambirasi (Bhutan), Estevao Cacella reports that the local king says the people of Sopo are more valiant than the Chinese and usually beat them, which Cacella links to the well known wars of the Tartars with China. He then explains why nobody there has heard of 'Cathay': local people use quite different names, calling China 'Guena', Tartary 'Sopo' and Tibet 'Potente'.
p.q: porem que a do Sopo he mais esforçada, e assi commummente esta vence os Chinas, o que tudo diz com o que he tão sabido da guerra dos Tartaros com as Chinas … pois nem a China nem a Tartarea, nem o Tibet são conhecidos por estes nomes, dos quaes não tem noticia; e a China chamão Guena, a Tartarea Sopo e ao Tibet Potente
p.s: Estevao Cacella, S.J., Portuguese letter from Cambirasi (Bhutan), 4 October 1627, printed in Wessels's Appendix II
p.pe: Sopo (Mongols) as described to Jesuits in Bhutan
p.t: but that the [people] of Sopo are more valiant, and so this one commonly defeats the Chinese, all of which agrees with what is so well known of the war of the Tartars with the Chinese … for neither China nor Tartary nor Tibet is known by these names, of which they have no knowledge; and they call China Guena, Tartary Sopo and Tibet Potente
p.c: Cacella is reporting what the Bhutanese king told him and matching it to European ideas about Tartars and Cathay; the equations are his own guesses.

p.h: Only a descendant of Genghis may be khan
p.g: The memoir sets out what happens when a Crimean khan dies or the Tatar peoples agree to depose him. Because it is 'among impossible things' for anyone outside the line of Genghis to hold the rank of khan, they must elect and install another khan from Genghis's descendants, and then notify both Russia and the Ottoman sultan. Five centuries after the Mongol conquest, the Crimean Tatars' rulers still drew their legitimacy from Genghis Khan.
p.q: خانك وفاتنده ويا خود طوايف تاتاريه بالاتفاق عزلنی مراد ايدوب سلسله جنکيزيه‌دن غيری اشبو خانلق رتبه‌سنه نايل اولمق مواد ممتنعاتدن اولمغيله اعقاب جنکيزيه‌دن آخر بر خان انتخاب ونصب ايتدکلرنده
p.s: Ottoman chancery memoir on the Tatars and their khans (item IV in the library catalogue, put into Turkish by the reis ul-kuttab Abd al-Razzaq Efendi), undated copy c.1775 to 1780
p.pe: Crimean Tatars and Nogays ('the Tatar peoples')
p.t: On the khan's death, or if the Tatar peoples by common agreement wish to depose him, since it is among impossible things for anyone other than the line of Genghis to attain this rank of khan, when they elect and install another khan from the descendants of Genghis
p.c: A diplomatic text written for the post-1774 arrangements, not a description of daily life; the copyist is unknown.

p.h: Hungarian hymns called the Cumans 'Tartars'
p.g: Kuun shows how loosely the name was used in medieval Hungary. Hymns to St Ladislaus sometimes call the Cumans 'Tartars', and the chronicler Thuroczy says the chief of the Cumans whom King Stephen II took in (in 1129) was himself named Tatar. This is more than a century before the Mongol invasion of 1241, so 'Tatar' here is a personal name and a label for steppe Turks, not for the Mongols.
p.q: In antiquis hymnis latinis et hungaricis sancti Ladislai Cumani interdum Tartari nuncupantur … Thuroczy in suis Chronicis, Cumanorum a rege Stephano II in Hungariam receptorum summum ducem itidem Tatar nominat: «Rex autem Stephanus, diligebat Cumanos tunc temporis; quorum dux nomine Tatar, qui a cede imperatoris (Graecorum), cum paucis, ad regem fugerat»
p.s: Geza Kuun, Latin introduction to his edition of the Codex Cumanicus (Budapest 1880), quoting the Hungarian chronicler Janos Thuroczy (1488)
p.t: In the old Latin and Hungarian hymns of St Ladislaus the Cumans are sometimes called Tartars … Thuroczy, in his Chronicle, likewise names the supreme chief of the Cumans received into Hungary by King Stephen II 'Tatar': 'King Stephen loved the Cumans at that time; their chief, named Tatar, had fled with a few men to the king from the slaughter by the (Greek) emperor'.
p.c: Kuun is assembling medieval Hungarian testimony; Thuroczy wrote in the 1480s about events of 1129.
p.n: Checked against the page image.

p.h: 'Kalmyk': a Tatar word for those who stayed behind, or turned away
p.g: Bergmann spells the name 'Kalmük' after the pronunciation of the Russians and Tatars, because the name itself comes from Tatar. The Kalmyks once called themselves Oelöt (Oirats). He rejects Strahlenberg's idea that the name comes from kalpak, a cap, and follows the Khivan historian Abulghazi: the Tatar word means either 'those left behind' or 'apostates'. On the next page he guesses that Tatars and Mongols once shared one religion, and that when the Mongols turned to Lamaist Buddhism the Muslim Tatars called them apostates.
p.q: Weit wahrscheinlicher ist die Herleitung von … Worte Chalimäk. Abulhasi selbst scheint das dadurch zu bestätigen, daß er diesem Volke den Namen Khalmak beilegt. Dem eben angeführten tatarischen Ausdrucke nach, bezeichnet der Name Kalmük entweder Abtrünnige oder Nachgebliebene.
p.s: Benjamin Bergmann
p.pl: Kalmyk steppe west of the lower Volga (Kalmykia)
p.pe: Kalmyks (Oirats), named by their Tatar neighbours
p.t: Far more likely is the derivation from the word khalimak. Abulghazi himself seems to confirm this by giving this people the name Khalmak. According to this Tatar expression, the name Kalmyk means either apostates or those who remained behind.
p.c: An etymology argued from earlier writers; the religious explanation on the next page is Bergmann's own hypothesis.
p.tg: etymology kalmyk oirats abulghazi tatar language

p.h: Born in Beijing, but still Tartars
p.g: Staunton explains that the Qianlong emperor, though four generations removed from the conquest and born in Beijing, was seen by everyone, and saw himself, as a Tartar. His ministers, generals, wives and servants were mostly of the same race, and every male of Tartar descent drew a stipend from birth. Here 'Tartar' plainly means the Manchu conquerors.
p.q: Tho the Emperor Chen-Lung, be the fourth in descent from him who successfully invaded China in the last age, and tho the last three succeeding generations were all born at Pekin, yet they are universally regarded by their subjects, and they regarded indeed themselves, as Tartars. Their principal ministers, their confidential servants, the chiefs of their armies, most of their wives, concubines, domestics, and eunuchs, are of that race.
p.s: George Leonard Staunton

p.h: 'Were the name Moghul written in gold'
p.g: After his defeat by the Uzbek Shaybani Khan, Babur complains bitterly that the Mongol troops sent to help him did not fight but turned on his own men, unhorsing and stripping them, and he says this was their usual practice. He sums up with a couplet that shows how sharply a Timurid Turk could separate himself from the Mongols, though he was one by descent.
p.q: If the Moghul race were a race of angels, it is a bad race ; And were the name Moghul written in gold, it would be odious.
p.s: Babur (translated by John Leyden and William Erskine, 1826)
p.c: Written in anger after a defeat; a partisan judgement.

p.h: Rebels against Prester John's son
p.g: This origin story says that in 1202, 'according to some', the Tartars, living in Tartary 'which borders on India', rose against their lord King David, son of Prester John, emperor of India, killed him by treachery and went out to destroy peoples. The chapter goes on to have Chinggis Khan organise them by tens, hundreds and thousands. It is a crusader-era legend; the real event behind it is Chinggis Khan's overthrow of the Kereit ruler Ong Khan in 1203.
p.q: Anno Domini 1202. secundum quosdam, Tartari post occisionem Domini sui exierunt in populorum destructionem. Hi etenim post adhuc in terra sua videlicet Tartaria quæ affinis est Indiæ, residentes contra Regem Dauid Dominum suum videlicet presbyteri Ioannis quondam dominatoris & Imperatoris Indiæ filium conspirauerunt, eumque dolose machinando, interfecerunt.
p.s: Vincent of Beauvais, Speculum historiale (Douai 1624), from material he says he received from Simon of Saint-Quentin
p.t: In the year of the Lord 1202, according to some, the Tartars, after the killing of their lord, went out to destroy peoples. For while they were still living in their own land, namely Tartary, which borders on India, they conspired against King David their lord, son of Prester John, formerly ruler and emperor of India, and killed him by treacherous scheming.
p.c: Legend; the text itself flags it as what 'some' say.

p.h: Tsar On and a commoner called Chingis
p.g: Esipov's history of the Siberian rulers begins with a Muslim 'tsar named On' on the Ishim river, overthrown by a man 'from the simple people' named Chingis, who killed him 'like a robber' and took his realm. A servant saved On's son Taibuga, founder of the Taibugid princes. In this local legend the world conqueror Chinggis Khan has become a Siberian upstart, and the 'Ong Khan' of Mongol history has become a Muslim tsar.
p.q: на сей же рѣцѣ Ишимѣ бѣ царь Моаметова закону именемъ Онъ. И воста на него его же державы отъ простыхъ людей именемъ Чингисъ, и шедъ на него, яко разбойникъ, съ прочими, и уби царя Она, и царство самъ приемлетъ Чингисъ.
p.s: Savva Esipov, Siberian Chronicle (1636), in Sibirskie letopisi (1907)
p.pe: Early rulers of the Siberian Tatars: 'Tsar On', 'Chingis', Taibuga
p.t: on this river Ishim there was a tsar of Muhammad's law named On. And there rose against him, of his own realm, from the simple people, one named Chingis, and he went against him like a robber with others, and killed Tsar On, and Chingis himself took the realm.
p.c: A dynastic legend told among Siberian Tatars and retold by a Russian; it garbles Chinggis Khan and Ong Khan of the Kereit.
p.tg: origin legend chinggis taibuga ishim dynasty

p.h: The Russians named the Mongols 'Tatars', and Europe copied them
p.g: Bichurin says the invaders of 1237 to 1240 were Mongols of the 'Tatan' confederation, among whom the Tatar tribe near the Argun was only one conquered clan. In his view the Russians made the first mistake by calling the whole army 'Tatars', Carpini copied it through poor interpreters, and geographers without further inquiry called the whole belt from the Caspian to the Pacific 'Great Tartary'.
p.q: И такъ, по моему мнѣнію, Россіяне при первомъ нашествіи Татаньцевъ, назвавъ ихъ Татарами, первые погрѣшили и сообщили сію погрѣшность западнымъ народамъ. … а Географы, безъ дальняго изслѣдованія, всю полосу отъ Каспійскаго моря до Восточнаго назвали Великою Татаріею.
p.s: Iakinf (N. Ya. Bichurin), 1828
p.t: And so, in my opinion, the Russians, calling the Tatans 'Tatars' at their first invasion, were the first to err and passed this error on to the western peoples. … and geographers, without further investigation, called the whole belt from the Caspian Sea to the Eastern Sea Great Tartary.
p.c: Bichurin's own argument; he is disputing Klaproth, who held that the Mongols were rightly called Tatars. 'Tatan' is his rendering of Chinese Dada.

p.h: The Zagatays: Tartars who stayed and gave their name
p.g: Clavijo explains Timur's people. An 'emperor of Tartary' divided his lands among four sons, and Zagatay (Chagatai) received Samarkand; when the locals killed him, his followers who stayed were called Zagatays. Timur descends from these 'Zagatay Tartars', and many Samarkand people now call themselves Zagatays to share in the famous name. Markham's note corrects the details of the story.
p.q: Timour Beg, and the other Zagatays who follow him, are descended from these Zagatay Tartars; and many people of the land of Samarcand have now taken this name of Zagatay, that they may share in the great name which the Zagatays have now attained.
p.s: Ruy González de Clavijo (translated by Clements R. Markham, 1859)
p.pe: Zagatays (Chagatai Mongols and Turks of Timur's realm)
p.c: Local tradition as told to the envoys; Markham notes that Chagatai was not killed by his subjects.

p.h: 'Tartar or Tatar is unknown here, and so is Tibet'
p.g: Gerard lists what the people actually call themselves and their land: Bhoteeas or Zhads to the lowlanders, Bhot for the country, Keao for the people of Gnaree, and he notes that Zhad is an insult. Then he says flatly that neither 'Tartar' nor 'Tibet' was known there. 'Tartar' was the European name he was using for convenience.
p.q: The Tartars are called by the inhabitants of the lower parts, Zhads, Bhoteeas or Bootuntees, and their country is often named Bhot and Bootunt … Zhad is reckoned a term of reproach, and is applied by the Hindoos to those who eat bullock's flesh … Tartar or Tatar is unknown here, and so is Tibet.
p.s: Alexander Gerard (ed. George Lloyd, 1841)
p.pe: Tibetans of upper Kinnaur and western Tibet

p.h: One name for many nations
p.g: Herberstein warns his readers that 'Tartar' is not the name of one people. It is a label drawn from one group and stretched over many nations living far apart. It is a useful early statement that the word was an umbrella term.
p.q: He who attempts to describe the Tartars will have to describe many races ; for they derive this name from one sect alone, while they consist of various nations lying wide apart from each other.
p.s: Sigismund von Herberstein (translated by R. H. Major, 1851-52)

p.h: Tatar and Mogul: twin brothers
p.g: In Abu'l Ghazi's genealogy, a king named Alanza Khan, descended from Japheth son of Noah, had twin sons, Tatar and Mogul, and split his realm between them. So the Tatars and the Mongols begin as two rival brother nations. A footnote in the printed edition insists that the Tatars are named after this prince, not after a river 'Tata'.
p.q: Alanza Chan had two Twin-Sons, the one called Tatar, and the other Mogull … 'Tis from this Prince the Tatars take their Name, and not from the River Tata, as the Mogulls from Mogull.
p.s: Abu'l Ghazi Bahadur Khan (English translation, 1730); the second sentence is a footnote in the English edition
p.c: A genealogical legend; the twins are not historical people.

p.h: Friar Julian: the Tartars' first land was 'Gothia'
p.g: Friar Julian, a Hungarian Dominican who had travelled to the edge of Rus' looking for the pagan 'Greater Hungarians', tells the papal legate what he learned 'from many': that the Tartars once lived where the Cumans now live, are 'in truth' called Ishmaelites but wish to be called Tartars, and came out of a land called 'Gothia'. He then tells a tangled origin story of a duke named Gurgutha whose vengeance war launched their conquests.
p.q: Relatum est enim a pluribus, quod Tartari, qui prius inhabitabant terram quam Cumani nunc inhabitant, dicuntur in veritate illi Ysmahelite, volunt nunc Tartari appellari. Terra autem de qua prius sunt egressi Gothia vocatur
p.s: Friar Julian of Hungary, O.P., report to the bishop of Perugia (c. 1238), in the text printed by Hormayr (1842)
p.t: For it is reported by many that the Tartars, who formerly lived in the land the Cumans now inhabit, are in truth called Ishmaelites, but now wish to be called Tartars. The land from which they first came out is called Gothia
p.c: Hearsay gathered on the Russian frontier; the 'Ishmaelite' label is biblical classification, and the Gurgutha story has no basis in Mongol history. The OCR is badly garbled and the wording is reconstructed from it.

p.h: Proud of their Scythian descent and divided into hordes
p.g: The opening of the work: the Tartars, though Lithuanians think them barbarous and poor, pride themselves on their restraint and on the antiquity of their 'Scythian' race, which they claim never served anyone, and are divided into hordes ('Ordas, that is, nations'). Michalo lists the Perekop (Crimean) Tatars and their Budjak neighbours, the Nogai, the Volga horde (homeland of Batu, 'once ruler of the Muscovites and all Ruthenians'), Kazan, Kazakh, Bukhara and Samarkand hordes, and links their twelve rulers to the twelve princes promised to Ishmael.
p.q: Etsi Tartari, barbari & inopes habeantur a nobis, gloriantur tamen continentia vitae, & antiquitate gentis suae Scythicae, asseverantes eam semen esse … nemini servivisse unquam … & varias nunc divisam in Ordas, id est, nationes.
p.s: Michalo the Lithuanian, De moribus Tartarorum, Lituanorum et Moschorum, fragment 1 (c. 1550; Basel, 1615)
p.pe: Tatars (Crimean, Nogai, Volga and other hordes)
p.t: Although the Tartars are held by us to be barbarous and poor, they nevertheless glory in the restraint of their life and in the antiquity of their Scythian race, asserting that it is a seed … that has never served anyone … and that it is now divided into various Hordes, that is, nations.
p.c: The OCR is damaged at 'semen esse'; the omitted words are illegible.

p.h: Were the Tatars Herodotus's Scythians?
p.g: In an appendix Schlözer prints what the Athenian historian Laonikos Chalkokondyles, writing in the later 1400s, said about the north. Like other learned Byzantines he gave new peoples old classical names and called the Tatars Scythians. Schlözer points out the result: taking them for Herodotus's Scythians of Moldavia, Chalkokondyles had them migrate from Europe into Asia instead of the other way round. He adds that the Polish writer Miechowita mocked this error and distinguished four kinds of Tatars: Chagatai east of the Caspian, the Kipchak Horde between the Don and the Yaik, the Crimeans, and the Lithuanian Tatars.
p.q: Der gute Chalkokandyles scheint wirklich die Tataren seiner Zeit, die von der Donau an bis zum Altaj hin unter mehreren mogolischen Beherrschern lebten, für die Scythen des Herodots in der Moldau zu halten: folglich mußten sie freilich aus Europa nach Asien, nicht umgekehrt, gewandert seyn!
p.s: August Ludwig Schlözer (1785), footnote on Laonikos Chalkokondyles
p.pe: Tatars of the Golden Horde and its successors
p.t: The good Chalkokondyles really seems to take the Tatars of his time, who lived from the Danube to the Altai under several Mongol rulers, for the Scythians of Herodotus in Moldavia: consequently they must of course have migrated from Europe to Asia, not the other way round!

p.h: Descendants of Chinggis, come from the Volga
p.g: Broniewski says the Tatars moved gradually into the steppe between the Don and the Dnieper and reached Crimea about 160 years before his time. Their khans were anciently called the 'Cyngisson' line (descendants of Chinggis Khan), all tracing descent from one khan he calls Lochtonus, the first ruler of Crimea. On the previous page he says these Crimean or Perekop Tatars sprang from and were named after the Volga (Rha).
p.q: Porrò inter celebratissimos, altissimos & maximos Tanaim seu Donum & Boristhenẽ Septentrionis fluuios in campos paulatim progressos fuisse, ab annis verò centum sexaginta, vel paulo amplius in Tauricam seu peninsulam eos peruenisse manifestè apparet. … Chanorum vel Principum Tartarorum illorum Cyngissonum genus antiquitus nuncupatum fuit, ex quo Lochtonus quispiam Chanus, à quo vniuersi Chani ortum trahunt.
p.s: Marcin Broniewski (Martin Broniovius), Tartariae descriptio (written 1579), printed in the 1595 Cologne edition of Possevino's Moscovia
p.pe: Crimean Tatars and their Giray khans
p.t: Further, it is clear that they advanced gradually into the plains between the very famous, deep and great northern rivers Tanais or Don and Borysthenes, and reached Taurica or the peninsula a hundred and sixty years ago or a little more. ... The line of the khans or princes of those Tartars was anciently called the Cyngissons, from which came a certain khan Lochtonus, from whom all the khans take their origin.
p.c: 'Lochtonus' is a garbled name (probably Toqtamish); the dates are approximate lore.

p.h: Three tribes of the Great Tartars
p.g: Schiltberger names three tribes among the 'Great Tartars': Kayat, Inbu and Mugal. The editors identify these as the Kerait, the Uighurs and the Mongols, so he correctly grasped that the Horde was a mix of peoples with the Mongols as one part. He also notes that Russia paid tribute to the Tartar king.
p.q: Item, the kingdom of Rewschen, which is tributary to the Tartar king. It is to be noted, that there are three tribes amongst the Great Tartars. One is called Kayat, the other Inbu, the third Mugal.
p.s: Johann Schiltberger (translated by J. Buchan Telfer, 1879)
p.c: The tribe identifications (Kerait, Uighur) are the editor's footnotes.

p.h: A bird that cried 'Chinggis'
p.g: A learned Mongol lama gave Müller a story from Tibetan and Mongol books about the rise of Chinggis Khan. A khan's son and nine nobles fled rather than become monks; the peoples they met joined them and chose the son as khan. As the nine debated his new name, a small bird landed nearby and cried 'Chinggis, Chinggis', and so he was named. Müller calls the story very fabulous but prints it because nothing like it had been published.
p.q: Zu derselben Zeit sey ein kleiner Vogel angeflogen gekommen, welcher in der Nähe der Rathsversammlung sich niedergesetzet, und mit vernehmlicher Stimme Tschingis, Tschingis, geschrieen. Alsobald habe man einmüthig beschlossen, diesen von dem Vogel angestimmten Nahmen dem Chane beyzulegen.
p.s: Gerhard Friedrich Müller (Sammlung Russischer Geschichte, vol. 6, 1761-1762), reporting a Mongol lama's account
p.pe: Mongols (their own tradition of Chinggis Khan)
p.t: At that same time a little bird came flying up, settled near the council, and cried out in a clear voice, 'Chinggis, Chinggis'. At once they unanimously decided to give the khan this name that the bird had sung.
p.tg: chinggis khan origin story lamas birds

p.h: Humboldt: Tatars are Turks, but the name first meant Mongols
p.g: In a long footnote written for Rose, Humboldt explains that in the Russian Empire 'Tatars' always means a Turkic people (Crimean, Kazan and Tobolsk Tatars), not a Mongol-looking one. Among Asian writers, however, the name first belonged to the Mongols, and Ming-dynasty word lists in Peking translate 'Mongol' as Tata or Tataeul. He goes on to say the name passed to the Turks because Mongol conquerors ruled over them.
p.q: Im Russischen Reiche gilt die Benennung Tataren stets für einen türkischen Menschenstamm … die Tataren der Krimm, des Gouvernements Kasan und die von Tobolsk gehören zu dem sogenannten Caucasischen Menschenstamm, Tataren sind Türken, aber die Benennung Tataren gehörte ursprünglich bei asiatischen Schriftstellern den Mongolen an, Das Wort Mongol (Mogul) wird nach Vocabularien, die im funfzehnten Jahrhundert unter der Dynastie Ming in Peking angefertigt sind, durch Tata oder Tataeul … übersetzt
p.s: Alexander von Humboldt (note communicated to Rose and printed as a footnote in Rose's Reise, vol. 1, 1837)
p.pe: Tatars of Crimea, Kazan and Tobolsk; Mongols
p.t: In the Russian Empire the name Tatars always stands for a Turkic race … the Tatars of the Crimea, of the government of Kazan and those of Tobolsk belong to the so-called Caucasian race. Tatars are Turks, but among Asian writers the name Tatars originally belonged to the Mongols. According to vocabularies made in Peking in the fifteenth century under the Ming dynasty, the word Mongol (Mogul) is translated as Tata or Tataeul …
p.c: Uses the race categories of its day ('Caucasian race'); the point about names is the useful part.

p.h: A name Tatars called dishonourable
p.g: In the written instructions the Academy gave Klaproth, a scholar remarks that peoples sometimes adopt names their neighbours use: just as the Tartar nations in Russia call themselves 'Tartars' for outsiders, though at home they consider the name dishonourable.
p.q: They perhaps assume it for the purpose of accommodating their neighbours, as the Tartar nations in Russia give themselves the name of Tartars, which in their own countries they consider as dishonourable.
p.s: Instructions for Klaproth from the St Petersburg Academy of Sciences (section II, probably by A. C. Lehrberg or Ph. Krug), printed in Klaproth's Travels

p.h: Who lived in the Kazan land: Bulgars, Cheremis and runaway Rostovians
p.g: The author says the khan drove the Rus out of the district and brought in 'a fierce pagan people' from the Kama, the Bulgar commoners with their princes and elders, as savage, he adds, as the 'dog-headed Samoyeds'. He also claims the Cheremis, called Votiaks, were Rostov commoners who fled there to escape baptism. It shows a Russian view of Kazan as a mix of peoples under a Tatar ruler, with a dose of prejudice and folk etymology.
p.q: и наведе исъ Камы языкъ лютъ, поганъ, Болгарскую чернь, со князи ихъ и со старѣишинами ихъ, и много ему сущу убо подобну суровствомъ, обычаемъ злымъ, песьимъ главамъ Самоедомъ. Наполни такими людми землю ту, еже Черемиса, зовемая Отяки, тое жъ глаголють Ростовскую чернь, забежавши тамо отъ крещенія Русково
p.s: Anonymous author of the History of the Kazan Tsardom, PSRL vol. 19 (1903)
p.t: and he brought from the Kama a fierce, pagan people, the Bulgar commoners, with their princes and elders, much like in savagery and evil custom to the dog-headed Samoyeds. He filled that land with such people, that is the Cheremis, called Votiaks; these, they say, are the Rostov commoners who fled there from Russian baptism
