p.h: Tibet plus Mongolia make 'great Tartary'
p.g: Writing from Tsaparang in 1626, the Portuguese Jesuit Antonio de Andrade lists the kingdoms of Tibet and says that, together with the empire of the 'Sopo' (Mongols), they make up 'great Tartary'. He also demotes fabled Cathay to a single large town ruled by the Mongol king. It is a neat example of how elastic the European label 'Tartary' was: here it swallows Tibet as well as Mongolia.
p.q: Together with the great empire of the Sopò [Mongolia], which borders on China on the one side and on Moscovia on the other, they form great Tartary". … "The famous Cathayo is not a separate kingdom but a large town which is called Katay, the capital of a province situated much nearer to China and which is said to be ruled by the great king of the Sopôs"
p.s: Antonio de Andrade, letter of 15 August 1626, in C. Wessels's English translation (1924); bracketed word is Wessels's
p.c: Andrade had not been to Mongolia; his picture of 'great Tartary' and Cathay comes from what he was told in western Tibet and from European maps.

p.h: Tatar and Mongol, the two sons of one khan
p.g: Commenting on the new French edition of Abulghazi's 'Genealogical History of the Tatars' (Leiden 1726), Strahlenberg retells its origin story: a khan (Alenzie or Alinja Khan) had two sons, Tatar and Mungel, both of Turkish descent, whose followers split into two branches named after them. It is a Central Asian Muslim tradition, passed on through the Swedish prisoners' translation.
p.q: weil der Alenzie-Chan zwey Söhne gehabt, einen Tater den andern Mungel, so zwar beyde Türckischer descendence, wie der Autor recht zeiget, so haben sich solche doch von Stund an in diese beyde branches getheilet, indem jener mit seinem Türckischen Volck gegen Osten gegangen, welche hernach von ihm den Nahmen angenommen, der Mungel aber in Westen mit den Seinigen geblieben
p.s: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (Vorbericht, Stockholm 1726), paraphrasing Abulghazi Bahadur Khan
p.t: since Alenzie Khan had two sons, one Tater, the other Mungel, both indeed of Turkish descent, as the author rightly shows, these nevertheless divided at once into these two branches, the former going east with his Turkish people, who afterwards took their name from him, while Mungel stayed in the west with his own people

p.h: One northern nation, parent of Huns, Turks, Mongols and Tartars
p.g: Deguignes opens his history of the ancient Huns with his big claim: a famous nation north of China's frontier provinces gave rise to the peoples later known as Huns, Turks, Mongols, Hungarians and Tartars. He lists the names the Chinese gave it over the dynasties, ending with Hiong-nou, which he thinks produced the name Hun.
p.q: Au Nord des frontières Septentrionales des Provinces de Chensi, de Chansi & de Petcheli, habitoit autrefois une Nation célèbre, qui a donné naissance à celles que nous avons connues depuis sous le nom de Huns, de Turcs, de Mogols, de Hongrois & de Tartares
p.s: Joseph de Guignes
p.pl: Mongolia (north of Shaanxi, Shanxi and Beijing)
p.pe: Xiongnu (Hiong-nou), in Deguignes' view the ancestors of the Huns and later Tartars
p.t: North of the northern frontiers of the provinces of Shaanxi, Shanxi and Beizhili there once lived a famous nation, which gave birth to those we have since known under the names of Huns, Turks, Mongols, Hungarians and Tartars
p.c: A scholarly theory, not a report; the Xiongnu-Hun link is still debated and 'Hungarians' in this list is Deguignes' own speculation.

p.h: Moabites from the desert: a Russian origin legend
p.g: From the Russian chronicles Herberstein copies a story that the Tartars were 'Moabites' who came out of the north-eastern deserts, driven by a prophet named Gideon who preached the end of the world. The chronicle's date of AD 1025 for the Kalka battle is wrong (it was 1223), and the editor Major notes the attribution to Bishop Methodius is an anachronism.
p.q: They say that the Moabites, who were afterwards called Tartars, and who differed from the rest of mankind in language, manners, and dress, came to the river Calka ; but that no one knew whence they came, or what religious doctrine they held.
p.s: Sigismund von Herberstein, retelling the Russian annals (translated by R. H. Major, 1851-52)
p.c: A biblical-style legend from the chronicles; Herberstein reports it without endorsing it.

p.h: The Mongols would like to erase the Tartar name
p.g: Rubruck, told at the Mongol court, explains that the Tartars were a separate poor people living next to the Moal (Mongols). Chingis (Genghis) united both and sent the Tartars ahead in every war, so Europeans heard only 'The Tartars are coming!'. By Rubruck's time the Tartars had mostly been killed off and the Mongols disliked the name. Rockhill's note quotes Rashid al-Din saying the same.
p.q: Now this Chingis used to despatch the Tartars in every direction, and so their name spread abroad, for everywhere was heard the cry : "The Tartars are coming !" But through the many wars they have been nearly all killed off, and now these Moal would like to extinguish even the name and raise their own in its stead.
p.s: William of Rubruck (translated by W. W. Rockhill, 1900)
p.c: Rubruck's story of Genghis's rise (as a blacksmith, and Prester John's brother 'Unc chan') mixes real events with legend.

p.h: Descended from Kublai Khan? The Manchu origin story
p.g: Davis explains that the 'Eastern Tartars' now called their country Manchow, 'the full region'. Earlier, as the Kin or 'golden' race, they had ruled north China before the Mongols drove them out. He then repeats a story that the last Mongol emperors, expelled by the Ming, took refuge among these Eastern Tartars and intermarried, so that the Manchu emperors descend from Kublai Khan.
p.q: When the last of the Mongols, descendants of Koblai Khan, were expelled from China by the founder of the Ming, or Chinese race, they sought a refuge among the Eastern Tartars, and from their intermarriages with the natives sprung the Bogdoi Khans, or Manchow princes, who were destined to expel the Ming. It is in this manner that the Emperors of the present dynasty derive their descent from Koblai Khan.
p.s: John Francis Davis (The Chinese, 1836)
p.pe: Manchu Tartars (the Kin or Jin 'golden race')
p.c: This descent from Kublai is a European and dynastic legend, not established history; Davis presents it as fact.

p.h: Tartar prisoners in Canton, called 'Tatos'
p.g: Here Cruz speaks as an eyewitness: in Canton he saw many Tartar captives whose only 'captivity' was serving as soldiers far from home. They wore red caps as a badge but otherwise dressed like the Chinese, and received a fixed royal pay. The Chinese, he says, call them 'Tatos' because they cannot pronounce the letter R. Chinese Dada (Tatar) is real; the missing-R explanation is his.
p.q: Na cidade de Cantam vi eu muitos tartaros catiuos, os quaes nã tem mais catiueiro q̃ seruirẽ por homẽs darmas noutras partes longe de tartaria, e trazẽ por diuisa barretes bermelhos, no demais trazem ho trajo dos chinas com quẽ viuẽ … Chamam os chinas a estes Tatos, porque nam podem pronunciar esta letra. r.
p.s: Gaspar da Cruz, O.P. (Tractado, Évora 1569)
p.pe: Tartar (Mongol) captives serving the Ming as soldiers
p.t: In the city of Canton I saw many Tartar captives, whose only captivity is to serve as men-at-arms in other parts far from Tartary. They wear red caps as a badge; otherwise they wear the dress of the Chinese among whom they live … The Chinese call these people Tatos, because they cannot pronounce this letter r.
p.c: The explanation of the name is Cruz's own.

p.h: Five Tartaries on the map
p.g: Here 'Tartary' is a geographer's label for most of northern Asia, carved into five parts: Crim Tartary, the hordes under the Tsar (including Kazan and Astrakhan), Zagatay or the Uzbek country where Tamerlane reigned, Cathay or Great Tartary, and an unknown far north-east. It shows how loosely the name was spread over many peoples.
p.q: Tartary is devided into five parts, the first is the lesser Tartary, or Tartary of Precop, called also Crim Tartary. The second is Sarmatia Asiatica, which containeth many Hordes of the Tartars subject to the Great Duke of Moscovia, as the Czeremisses, the Nagais, Zauolhans, and those of Cazan and Astracan.
p.s: Pierre Chevalier (translated by Edward Brown, 1672)
p.pe: Crimean Tatars, Volga Tatars, Nogais, Uzbeks and the peoples of 'Great Tartary'
p.c: A textbook geographic scheme, not observation. The list continues on p.35 with Zagatay (where Tamerlane reigned), Cathay or Great Tartary, and an unknown north-east.

p.h: 'Tartary full of towns' and the meaning of 'horde'
p.g: Arriving at Caffa, Chardin explains the map names. Geographers call Crimea 'Crim Tartary', which he takes to mean 'Tartary full of towns', because Crimean Tatars mostly live in towns, at least in winter, unlike the Nogais outside the peninsula, who live in hordes. Horde, he adds, is a Turkish and Persian word for an army camp or a court's train. Together they make 'Lesser Tartary', as against the Asian Tartars beyond the Sea of Azov.
p.q: The Modern Geographers call it Crim Tartary and Precopensian Tartary. As much as to say Tartary full of Towns; to distinguish the Tartars of this Peninsula that live for the most part in Cities, especially all the Winter long, from those other European Tartars, which inhabit without the Peninsula, call'd Nogays … Hordes or Hordou, a word which signifies an Assembly
p.s: Jean Chardin (English translation, London, 1691)
p.c: This etymology is Chardin's own and is not the usual explanation of the name.

p.h: Hill people with 'Tartar' faces who say they came from the Moguls
p.g: Elphinstone is puzzled by the Aimaqs and Hazaras: they live in the heart of Afghanistan but look, speak and behave quite differently. They have no history of their own origin and speak a dialect of Persian, yet their features and a tradition point to Mongol ancestry. He goes on to cite the historian Abu'l-Fazl, who says they are remnants of a Mongol prince's army.
p.q: Their features, however, refer them at once to the Tartar stock, and a tradition declares them to be the offspring of the Moguls. They are, indeed, frequently called by the name of Moguls to this day, and they are often confounded with the Moguls and Chagatyes, who still reside in the neighbourhood of Heraut.
p.s: Mountstuart Elphinstone (1815)

p.h: Yedisan, the 'Seven Thousand' horde that made a khan
p.g: Correcting a Moldavian chronicler, Peyssonnel explains that the name Yedisan belongs only to the plains beyond the Dniester, taken from one of the four Nogai hordes under the Crimean khan. Yedi-san means 'seven thousand', the horde's original number of men. He adds that this horde alone, in revolt, deposed Khan Alim Girai and put Qirim Girai on the throne, events he witnessed and reported to the French court in 1759.
p.q: Cette Horde s'appelle Iedsan, ou Iedi-San, c'est-à-dire, sept mille, parce qu'elle étoit originairement composée de sept mille hommes … Cette seule Horde révoltée a dépossédé Alim Gueraï Khan, & placé sur le Trône Crim Gueraï Khan qui règne aujourd'hui. On voit les détails de cet événement dont j'ai été témoin, dans la Relation que j'en ai envoyée à la Cour en 1759.
p.s: Charles de Peyssonnel
p.pl: Yedisan (between the Dniester and the Southern Bug)
p.pe: Yedisan Nogais, subjects of the Crimean khan
p.t: This horde is called Yedsan or Yedi-San, that is, seven thousand, because it was originally made up of seven thousand men … This one horde, in revolt, deposed Alim Girai Khan and placed on the throne Qirim Girai Khan, who reigns today. The details of this event, which I witnessed, can be seen in the report I sent to the Court in 1759.

p.h: 'All the land was Tartary, and all the peoples Tartars'
p.g: In his preface Gmelin explains why Peter the Great sent the expedition. Before it, he says, European geographers knew nothing of the far north: every land there was simply 'Tartary' and every people 'Tartars'. On the next page he adds that in Russia itself people talk far less about 'Tartary' than elsewhere, the way real experts talk less about hidden qualities than those still in the dark.
p.q: In den Nordlichsten Ländern war bey den Erdbeschreibern nichts als Dunkelheit. Alles Land war Tatarey, und alle Völker selbiger Gegenden Tataren.
p.s: Johann Georg Gmelin, preface (German original, Göttingen, 1751)
p.pe: Everyone in northern Asia, as European maps saw them
p.t: In the northernmost lands the geographers had nothing but darkness. All the land was Tartary, and all the peoples of those regions Tartars.

p.h: Blame Marco Polo and the friars
p.g: Strahlenberg blames Marco Polo and the thirteenth-century friars (Carpini, Rubruck) for spreading the 'Chinese conceit' that every steppe people is a Tartar. It is an early and explicit statement that 'Tartary' was an outsiders' label, not a nation's own name.
p.q: And because Marcus Paulus Venetus, when he was in China, was not rightly inform'd of the State of Things, he, as well as the Monks sent into Tartary, viz. Plan, Carpin, Rubriquis, &c. have themselves taken up, and misled us Europeans, with the Chinese Conceit, that all those People, whether Kalmucks or Mungals, must go under the Denomination of Tartars:
p.s: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (English translation, 1738)

p.h: Russia's Tatars are 'Nogais' to the Kazakhs; 'Tatar' is a cursed name
p.g: In a footnote to his chapter on ruins Levshin notes that Kazakhs call the Tatars living in Russia only 'Nogais'. The word 'Tatar' itself they did not use; in their view it belonged to some base people cursed by a Muslim prophet. Bukharans and Khivans thought the same. The same story was reported by Rychkov seventy years earlier (W175).
p.q: Киргизъ-Казаки иначе не называютъ Татаръ въ Россіи живущихъ, какъ Ногаями. Само Татары совсѣмъ у нихъ не употребительно, и принадлежитъ по ихъ мнѣнію какому то подлому народу, проклятому однимъ Магометанскимъ пророкомъ. Бухарцы и Хивинцы тоже думаютъ, и также называютъ Татаръ Россійскихъ Ногаями.
p.s: Aleksei Levshin, footnote (1832)
p.pe: Tatars of Russia (as seen by Kazakhs, Bukharans and Khivans)
p.t: The Kirghiz-Kazakhs call the Tatars living in Russia nothing but Nogais. The (word) Tatar itself is not used by them at all, and in their opinion belongs to some base people cursed by a certain Muslim prophet. The Bukharans and Khivans think the same, and also call the Russian Tatars Nogais.

p.h: Nogais said to be Indians, and Astrakhan named after King Astra
p.g: In his 'short account of the Tartars', Bruce says the ancients knew them only as Scythians and Sarmatians, and that the Tartars were really several nations. He repeats a story that the Nogais and Kazan Tatars were Indians who rebelled around 1212 and migrated to the Sea of Azov, and that Astrakhan was named after its founder, a Tartar king called Astra.
p.q: The Nagayans, with the Tartars of Casan, and some others inhabiting between the Wolga and the Don, or Tanais, are said to have been Indians, who revolting from their sovereigns about the year 1212, emigrated … Astrachan, their principal city, they relate to have been built by a Tartar king, whose name being Astra, gave his city the name of Astra chan, or king.
p.s: Peter Henry Bruce (published 1782)
p.c: Both stories are origin legends reported as hearsay ('are said', 'they relate'); they appear in earlier writers such as Olearius.

p.h: The emperor of China as a 'Mongol or East Tartar'
p.g: Brand gives a close portrait of the Kangxi emperor seen at the audience, and labels him a 'Mongal or East Tartar'. Kangxi was in fact a Manchu. The confusion shows how Europeans of the 1690s used 'Tartar' as one label for the Manchu rulers of China and the Mongols.

Jahr, schön von Taille und hatte grosse schwartze Augen, eine gebogne Nase, einen über die Lippen herabhangenden schwartzen Knebel-Bahrt, hingegen wenig Bahrt an dem Kinn, dabey war die Haut seines Gesichts sehr pockengrübicht
p.s: Adam Brand (Neu-vermehrte Beschreibung, Lübeck 1734)

p.c: Kangxi was born in 1654, so he was about 39, not 45 to 50; Brand's 'Mongal' is a mislabel for Manchu.

p.h: 'Turali': the Tatars who lived in towns
p.g: Discussing the word 'tura' (town or fortress in Tatar and Bukharan), Müller reports that the Bashkirs call the Tyumen Tatars, and after them the Tobolsk Tatars, only 'Turali'. On the next page he gives the Bashkirs' explanation: these Tatars had lived since ancient times in towns and fortresses, or at least in fixed places, while the Bashkirs often moved their dwellings about the steppe.
p.q: Man kann hier leicht auf die Gedanken kommen, da Tura in der Tatarischen und Bucharischen Sprache eine Stadt, oder Festung, bedeutet, daß vielleicht der Fluß Tura von dieser alten Tatarischen Festung Tschimgi den Nahmen empfangen. Die Baschkiren haben für die Tümenischen Tataren, und nach selbigen auch für die Tobolskischen, keinen andern Nahmen, als daß sie solche Turali nennen
p.s: Gerhard Friedrich Müller (Sammlung Russischer Geschichte, vol. 6, 1761-1762)
p.pe: Tyumen and Tobolsk Tatars, as named by the Bashkirs
p.t: One may easily think here, since Tura in the Tatar and Bukharan language means a town or fortress, that perhaps the river Tura received its name from this old Tatar fortress of Chimgi. The Bashkirs have no other name for the Tyumen Tatars, and after them for the Tobolsk Tatars too, than to call them Turali

p.h: Tatars, Turks and a name some found insulting
p.g: Georgi opens his section on the 'Tatar nations' by noting that most of these peoples call themselves Turks or Turkomans rather than Tatars. Following the Khivan khan and historian Abulghazi, he traces both names to an ancestor Turk and his grandson Tatar. He adds that many Tatars found the name itself offensive because their rulers used it with contempt.
p.q: Die unter so verschiedenen Namen in und ausser Rußland befindlichen Tatarischen Stämme nennen sich bald Tataren, bald und meistens Turuken, Turken, auch Turkomanen. Beyde Benennungen leiten ihre Geschichtschreiber, besonders Abulgasi Bajadur Chan … von ihrem fruchtbaren Stammvater Turuk, oder Turk und einem seiner Enkel Tatar … so halten ihn viele Tataren für kränkend.
p.s: Johann Gottlieb Georgi (citing Abulghazi Bahadur Khan)
p.pe: Turkic 'Tatar' peoples of the Russian Empire
p.t: The Tatar tribes found under such varied names inside and outside Russia call themselves sometimes Tatars, but mostly Turuks, Turks, also Turkomans. Their historians, especially Abulghazi Bahadur Khan, derive both names from their fruitful ancestor Turuk or Turk and one of his grandsons, Tatar … so many Tatars regard it [the name Tatar] as insulting.
p.c: The Turk and Tatar ancestor story is Abulghazi's seventeenth-century genealogy, a tradition rather than documented history.

p.h: A misused name, kept for three related peoples
p.g: Schott opens by placing the homeland of his language family on the Altai and naming four peoples who spread out from it: Tunguses, Mongols, Turks and Chudes or Finns. In this footnote he admits that the name 'Tatars' has been misused in Asia and even more in Europe, but says it can be tolerated as long as it means only the Tungusic, Mongolian and Turkic peoples, whose common descent he thinks their languages prove. He refers readers to his separate essay on the oldest Chinese reports of Mongols and Tatars, which he dates to Berlin 1847.
p.q: Bekannt ist der Missbrauch, den man in Asien, und noch mehr in Europa, mit dem Namen Tataren getrieben hat; er verdient aber wenigstens Duldung, so lange wir dabei nur an die erwähnten drei Völker denken, über deren gemeinsame Abstammung tiefere Erforschung ihrer Sprachen keinen Zweifel lässt.
p.s: Wilhelm Schott (footnote to his introduction)
p.pe: Tungusic (including Manchu), Mongolian and Turkic peoples
p.t: The misuse that has been made of the name Tatars in Asia, and still more in Europe, is well known; but it deserves at least toleration so long as we mean by it only the three peoples mentioned, whose common descent a deeper study of their languages leaves in no doubt.
p.c: The 'common descent' of these peoples is Schott's linguistic theory, not an established fact.
p.tg: ethnonym altaic language family altai misnomer

p.h: 'Czar' is a Tartar word, not 'Caesar'
p.g: At the peace talks Possevino mediated, the Muscovite envoys begged that their master be styled 'Czar of Kazan and Astrakhan'. Possevino replied that Kazan and Astrakhan were not important enough to add a new imperial title, and that if the emperor allowed it, it should be understood that 'Czar' did not mean Caesar but a royal title 'used by the Tartars'. A few pages on (n166) the Polish side refuse to call a Christian prince by 'a Tartar or Turkish title, like that Tartar Czar'.
p.q: vt ille Czar Casani, & Astracani diceretur … non esse tantam rem Casanum, & Astracanum, vt nouus titulus quasi alterius Cæsaris, Imperatoris, vel Regis addatur. Si Cæsar id fecerit, sciri vocem istam Czar non Cæsarem, sed aliquid aliud à Tartaris vsurpatum, quasi Regium titulum designari.
p.s: Antonio Possevino, S.J. (Moscovia, Vilnius 1586) (minutes of the peace congress)
p.pe: Muscovite envoys; the Kazan and Astrakhan khanates as sources of the title
p.t: that he be called Czar of Kazan and Astrakhan ... Kazan and Astrakhan were not so great a matter that a new title, as of another Caesar, Emperor or King, should be added. If the Emperor did it, it should be known that the word Czar does not mean Caesar, but something else used by the Tartars, signifying a kind of royal title.
p.c: Possevino's etymology serves his argument; the Russian title tsar does derive ultimately from Caesar, though Muscovites also used it for the Tatar khans.

p.h: A Kalmyk khan asks if Manchus and Mongols were once one people
p.g: In his long interview Ayuki Khan asked the envoys a question about origins: Manchus and Mongols look so alike that they must spring from one source, so how did they become separate nations? He asked them to put it to the emperor. The envoys promised to do so. He went on to ask about Manchu writing and why there were 'old' and 'new' Manchus.
p.q: "The Mantchoos and the Mongals bear a great resemblance to each other: I imagine therefore that they sprang anciently from the same origin. But how has it happened that they have since formed separate states and nations? The causes of this, are no doubt well known to your Emperor.
p.s: Ayuki Khan, as reported by Tulishen (Staunton translation, 1821)

p.h: Tatars keep the law of Muhammad; the Kalmyks, 'I do not know'
p.g: Esipov opens with the peoples living along the Tobol, Irtysh and Ob: Tatars, Kalmyks, Mongols, the 'Piebald Horde' (Selkups), Ostyaks and Samoyeds. The Tatars, he says, keep Muhammad's law; as for the Kalmyks, he honestly does not know their faith, since he found nothing written and could not find out. The Ostyaks and Samoyeds, he adds, have no law and worship idols.
p.q: По сихъ же рѣкахъ жителствуютъ мнози языцы: Тотаровя, Колмыки, Мугалы, Пѣгая орда, Остяки, Самоядь и прочая языцы. Тотаровя законъ Моаметовъ держатъ; Колмыки же который законъ или отецъ своихъ преданіе держатъ, невѣмъ, понеже писменно о семъ не обретохъ ни испытати возмогохъ.
p.s: Savva Esipov, Siberian Chronicle (1636), in Sibirskie letopisi (1907)
p.pe: Tatars, Kalmyks, Mongols, the 'Piebald Horde', Ostyaks, Samoyeds
p.t: Along these rivers live many peoples: Tatars, Kalmyks, Mongols, the Piebald Horde, Ostyaks, Samoyeds and other peoples. The Tatars keep the law of Muhammad; which law or tradition of their fathers the Kalmyks keep, I do not know, since I found nothing written about it and could not find out.

p.h: Eastern Tartars and Western Tartars
p.g: Huc sets out how he uses the word: following the Tartars and Chinese themselves, he divides 'the Tartar people' into Eastern Tartars (Toung-Ta-Dze), the Manchus, and Western Tartars (Si-Ta-Dze), the Mongols. He dismisses European map labels such as 'Kalmoukia' and 'Great and Little Bukharia' as 'purely imaginary'.
p.q: we will divide the Tartar people into Eastern Tartars (Toung-Ta-Dze), or Mantchous, and Western Tartars (Si-Ta-Dze), or Mongols. … Great and Little Boukaria, Kalmoukia, Great and Little Thibet … all these denominations seem to us purely imaginary.
p.s: Évariste Huc (translated by William Hazlitt, 1852)

p.h: The Tatar horde revolts, and the Jin are 'Eastern Tartars'
p.g: In the story of young Temüjin, Gaubil writes that 'the horde of the Tatars' rebelled against the Jin emperor, keeping the Tatars as one tribe distinct from the Mongols. His footnote explains that the Jin were 'Eastern Tartars' who ruled the steppe north and north-east of Liaodong and much of northern China, and to whom the petty princes of both Tartaries paid tribute.
p.q: La Horde des Tatars se révolta contre l'Empereur des Kin. … L'Empereur des Kin dont il est ici parlé, est l'Empereur des Tartares orientaux qui étoient alors maîtres de la Tartarie qui est au Nord, & Nord-Est du Leaotong
p.s: Antoine Gaubil (text and his own footnote)
p.pe: the Tatar tribe; the Jin (Jurchen) emperors; Mongols
p.t: The horde of the Tatars revolted against the Emperor of the Kin. … The Emperor of the Kin spoken of here is the Emperor of the Eastern Tartars, who were then masters of the part of Tartary lying north and north-east of Liaodong
p.tg: tatars jin jurchen eastern tartars mongols

p.h: 'The stinking Tartars': what the Chinese called them
p.g: In his 'Observation' on d'Herbelot's article Tatar, Visdelou traces the Chinese names: first Tha-tche, then Tha-tha, commonly Tha-tçe, and in contempt Sao-tha-tçe, 'the stinking Tartars'. He says the Chinese added a character meaning raw hide to show how low they ranked these peoples, and that the Jurchen and Mongols, once they had conquered China, dropped the insulting character. The volume's index adds an older name, Kiuen, 'dog'.
p.q: Les Chinois les ont nommé au commencement Thatche, ensuite Tha-tha, & vulgairement Tha-tçe; enfin par mépris Sao-tha-tçe, c'est-à-dire les puants Tartares. … Aussi les Niou-tchin & les Moumgols, après avoir conquis la Chine, ont retranché cette lettre injurieuse
p.s: Claude de Visdelou (Observation on d'Herbelot)
p.pe: Tatars / Tartars as named in Chinese sources; later Jurchen and Mongol rulers
p.t: The Chinese first called them Thatche, then Tha-tha, and commonly Tha-tçe; finally, in contempt, Sao-tha-tçe, that is, the stinking Tartars. … So the Jurchen and the Mongols, after conquering China, removed this insulting character
p.c: The spellings Tha-tçe and Sao-tha-tçe are taken from the volume's own index; the OCR on this page garbles them.

p.h: Cathay: the Tartars' name for China
p.g: Ricci explains why Europe thought Cathay and China were two countries. Marco Polo came when the Tartars ruled China, perhaps with them, and so Europe learned the country under the names the Tartars used: Cathay, with its royal city Cambalu. The Portuguese later brought home the name China and the city name Peking, and mapmakers drew two kingdoms side by side. On the previous page he offers a folk etymology that splits Campalu into Tartar 'Cam' (great) and the Chinese words 'Pa' (north) and 'Lu' (Tartars); the name is really Turkic Khanbaliq, 'city of the khan'.
p.q: inde plane apparet, Marcum Paulum Venetum eo tempore in hoc regnum penetrasse, quo Tartari Sinis imperitabant, & fortasse cum illis ipsis eo penetrasse. Eius deinde commentariis Europae, Sinarum Regnum innotuit eo nomine, quo Tartari utebantur, Cataium videlicet & urbem Regiam Cambalu appellantes. … Hoc tamen tempore nulla extra muros Sinenses Regio reperitur, quae Cataium vocitetur.
p.s: Matteo Ricci, edited and translated into Latin by Nicolas Trigault (1615)
p.pe: Tartars (Mongols) who ruled China in Marco Polo's day
p.t: From this it is plain that Marco Polo the Venetian entered this kingdom at the time when the Tartars ruled the Chinese, and perhaps entered with them. Through his writings the kingdom of China became known to Europe by the name the Tartars used, calling it Cathay and its royal city Cambalu. … At present, however, no region outside the Chinese walls is found that is called Cathay.

p.h: The Tartars descend from Noah's son Cham
p.g: Mandeville explains the title 'Chan' by making the Tartars descendants of Noah's cursed son Cham (Ham). He says that only about 160 years earlier the Tartars were subject herdsmen, and that of their seven 'lineages' the noblest was called Tartar. He then tells how a poor old man, Changuys (Genghis), was chosen emperor after a vision of a white knight.
p.q: Natheles, the sooth is this ; that Tartars and they that dwell in the great Asia, they came of Cham ; but the Emperor of Cathay clepeth him not Cham, but Can, and I shall tell you how. It is but little more but eight score year that all Tartary was in subjection and in servage to other nations about.
p.s: 'Sir John Mandeville' (Cotton manuscript, modern spelling ed. A. W. Pollard, 1900)
p.c: The Cham genealogy is a Christian learned invention; the list of seven lineages and the Genghis story draw on Hayton and similar sources.
p.tg: origin cham noah genghis khan white knight

p.h: How Tatars and Mongols merged
p.g: Meyendorff offers his theory of the name: Genghis Khan's Mongols conquered the Tatars, who were more numerous, and took up their Turkic language. From that mixture, he says, came all the peoples called 'Mongol Tartars', and he sees no real difference in looks between a Kazakh, an Uzbek, a Turkmen and a Tatar of Kazan or Crimea.
p.q: The Asiatic people to whom the Russians give the name of Tartars, have the nose slightly flattened, the cheek bones prominent, little beard on the chin, and small eyes … Gengis Khan, at the head of the Mongols, subjugated the Tartars, who became incorporated with his army, and those of his successors. As they were the most numerous, the conquerors adopted the Turkish language, barbarous as it was
p.s: Georg von Meyendorff (translated by William Monteith, 1840)
p.pe: Tatars and Mongols; Kazakhs, Uzbeks, Turkmens, Kazan and Crimean Tatars
p.c: Meyendorff's own theory, mixed with racial typing of the period.
p.tg: tatars mongols genghis khan language names

p.h: The Mongols disliked the name; the Chinese called all outsiders 'Ta-ta'
p.g: Fischer notes that in Europe and western Asia 'Tatar' (or 'Tarter') is better known than 'Mongol', although Chinggis Khan was a Mongol and not a Tatar. The mix-up, he says, is as old as the Mongol empire, and the Mongols themselves did not like to be called Tatars. He suggests the usage may come from the Chinese, who called all peoples living beyond their Great Wall 'Tata'.
p.q: Wiewol die Mogolen selbst es nicht gerne höreten, wenn man sie mit dem namen Tatar belegete … Die ursache solcher benennung mag wol von den Schinesern herrüren, als welche allen ausserhalb ihrer großen mauer wonhaften und an Schina grenzenden völkern den namen Tata zu geben pflegen
p.s: Johann Eberhard Fischer (Sibirische Geschichte, introduction, 1768)
p.pe: Mongols; peoples beyond the Great Wall
p.t: Although the Mongols themselves did not like to hear it when they were given the name Tatar … The cause of such naming may well come from the Chinese, who are accustomed to give the name Tata to all peoples living outside their great wall and bordering on China

p.h: Tibet: 'the kingdom of dwellers in houses'
p.g: The Capuchin della Penna, who lived in Lhasa for many years, explains the name Tibet as a Tatar (Mongol) word: Tangat katzar, which he says means the kingdom of people who live in houses, because the Tatars lived in tents of felt or yak-hair cloth while Tibetans lived in houses. Whatever the real etymology, it shows how people at the time drew the line between the two peoples by their dwellings.
p.q: The word Tibet is a Tatar corruption, the proper term being Thobot, or Tangat katzar. Tangat means dwellers in houses, and katzar country or kingdom; so the whole expression signifies "the kingdom of dwellers in houses," the Tatars dwelling in tents of felt, or of a coarse material woven from the hair of the yak or hairy ox, and the Tibetans in houses.
p.s: Francesco Orazio della Penna, Capuchin missionary (English version in Markham's appendix, from Klaproth's edition)
p.c: The etymology is della Penna's and is doubtful; the contrast in ways of living is the useful part.

p.h: The Emperor of China is not the Great Khan, only a small Manchu prince
p.g: Dapper corrects a long European belief: the Tartar ruler in Peking is not the Great Cham of all Tartary but one of the smallest Tartar princes, whose grandfather was raised to kingship by the people of a small province of East Tartary called Muncheu (Manchu). The same page names the present emperor Konchi (Kangxi), a youth of about sixteen, son of the Shunzhi emperor.
p.q: Men zeid de Tartersche Vorst, die heden het gewest van Sina bezit, en sijn verblijf in de Hooft-stadt Peking heeft, de groote Cham en Heer van geheel Tartarije niet is, gelijk tot dus lang gelooft is; maer een van de kleinste Vorsten der Tarters: waer van sijn groot-vader d'eerste Koning van zijnen stam was, verheven tot die waerdigheid door d'inwoonders van zijn land
p.s: Olfert Dapper, compiled general description of China
p.t: It is said that the Tartar prince who today possesses the land of China and resides in the capital Peking is not the Great Cham and lord of all Tartary, as has been believed until now, but one of the smallest princes of the Tartars, whose grandfather was the first king of his line, raised to that dignity by the inhabitants of his land

p.h: Call a Kazan Tatar a 'Tatar' and he hears 'robber'
p.g: Ritter, summarising the orientalist Julius Klaproth, explains that the khanates of Kazan, Astrakhan and Crimea were called 'Tartar' because their khans descended from Chinggis Khan, although their people were Turks. The people themselves, he says, reject the name, call their speech Turki, and treat 'Tatar' as an insult meaning robber, because their ancestors had been conquered by the Mongols and Tatars. He adds that the same mix-up runs deep into Siberia past Tobolsk, Tomsk and Yeniseisk, and settles on the scholars' compromise term 'Turk-Tatar'.
p.q: Aber, fragt man einen sogenannten Tartar von Kasan oder Astrachan, ob er denn ein Tartar sey: so wird er es verneinen, wie er selbst auch seinen Dialect Turki oder Turuk, niemals aber Tartari, nennt. Eingedenk, daß seine Vorfahren von den Mongol und Tatar einst unterjocht wurden, hält er Tatar für ein Schimpfwort, welches ihm mit Räuber gleichbedeutend ist.
p.s: Carl Ritter (summarising the argument of Julius Klaproth)
p.pe: Turkic-speaking Tatars of Kazan and Astrakhan, and the 'Tatars' of Siberia
p.t: But if you ask a so-called Tartar of Kazan or Astrakhan whether he is a Tartar, he will deny it, just as he himself calls his dialect Turki or Turuk, but never Tartari. Remembering that his ancestors were once subjugated by the Mongol and Tatar, he takes Tatar for a term of abuse, which to him means the same as robber.
p.c: Ritter did not interview anyone; this is Klaproth's claim about Tatar self-naming, passed on second-hand.

p.h: Hordes that hate being called Turks
p.g: Herberstein explains that 'horde' means a multitude, that the Tartars are split into hordes (Savolha, Precop, Nogai and others), all Muslim, and that they take offence at being called Turks, preferring 'Besermani' (Muslims). He then describes their looks: broad faces, shaved heads, and black hair kept only by the great men.
p.q: The word " horde" among them signifies a concourse or multitude. But although each horde has its peculiar name, such as the horde of Savolha, Precop, Nahaisa, and many others, and all are of the Mahometan religion, yet they are highly offended if they are called Turks, and consider it a reproach, but delight in being called Besermani
p.s: Sigismund von Herberstein (translated by R. H. Major, 1851-52)

p.h: 'Mayst thou never know happiness': where the Nogais got their name
p.g: European books said the Nogai horde was named after a Tatar general called Nogai. Xavier collected the Nogais' own traditions, which say nothing of such a general and derive the name from 'neogai', a curse on their hard wandering life. He prefers the Nogai version, arguing that a people so proud of their ancestry would have remembered a founder.
p.q: their chronicles allege that the name of the nation is derived from neogai (which may be translated by the phrase, mayst thou never know happiness), and that it was bestowed on them in their old country, on account of their precarious and vagabond life.
p.s: Xavier Hommaire de Hell (English translation, 1847)
p.c: A folk etymology; modern historians generally connect the name with the 13th-century Mongol commander Nogai, the view Xavier rejects.

p.h: In Bukhara and Khiva, 'Tatar' was an insult
p.g: Rychkov questioned Muslim scholars and Russian envoys sent from Orenburg to Khiva and Bukhara about the names 'Scythians' and 'Tatars'. He concludes that no people there called itself Tatar. The word meant a lawless, inhuman people supposed to live somewhere in far Siberia, and calling someone a Tatar was like calling him a barbarian or a worthless peasant.
p.q: ибо я совершенно увѣренъ, что во всѣхъ тамошнихъ сторонахъ ни одного народа нѣтъ, которой бы Татарами имяновался. Подъ именемъ Татаръ разумѣютъ они народъ весьма беззаконной и безчеловѣчной, признавая, якобы жительствуетъ онъ въ Россійскихъ, а паче въ самыхъ отдаленныхъ Сибирскихъ мѣстахъ … И имя Татаръ почитаютъ они за весьма безчестное и поносное, такъ какъ бы сказать, Варваръ, Смердъ, и ни къ чему годной человѣкъ.
p.s: Pyotr Rychkov (1762)
p.pe: Peoples of Central Asia; Tatars as a label
p.t: for I am fully certain that in all those parts there is not one people that calls itself Tatars. By the name Tatars they understand a very lawless and inhuman people, which they suppose lives in the Russian, and above all in the most remote Siberian, places … And they regard the name Tatar as very dishonourable and abusive, as if to say barbarian, serf, and good-for-nothing.
p.c: Based on Rychkov's interviews with Muslim scholars and returning envoys, not on travel of his own to Khiva or Bukhara.
p.n: The scan's machine-read text is too damaged to confirm this quote automatically. Check it against the page.

p.h: 'Destroyed by the Manchu Tartars, not the Chinese'
p.g: Amiot corrects the French traveller Chappe d'Auteroche, who had written that the Kalmyk nation was destroyed 'by the Chinese' after a ten-year war. It would be more exact, Amiot says, to say it was destroyed by the Manchu Tartars, since no Chinese took part, and the war lasted only about three and a half years. The distinction matters for anyone reading 'Tartar' in these sources.
p.q: Il eût été plus exact de dire: elle a été détruite par les Tartares Mantchoux; car aucun Chinois n'y a eu part: & la guerre qui a exterminé les Eleuths n'a duré qu'environ trois ans & demi, & non pas dix ans.
p.s: Joseph-Marie Amiot (remarks on Chappe d'Auteroche's Voyage en Sibérie)
p.t: It would have been more exact to say: it was destroyed by the Manchu Tartars, for no Chinese had any part in it; and the war that exterminated the Eleuths lasted only about three and a half years, not ten.

p.h: The other two Tartar empires
p.g: Besides the Great Tartar of Cathay and the Tartar emperor of Persia, Jordanus has heard of two more Tartar empires: one 'now of Osbet' called Gatzaria, and one of 'Dua and Cayda', now of 'Elchigaday'. Yule's note identifies Osbet as Uzbek, khan of the Golden Horde (1313 to 1340), and Elchigaday as the Chagatai khanate, and explains that Chinggis Khan's conquests had split among his heirs. An early sketch of the divided Mongol world.
p.q: But other two empires of the Tartars, as I have heard, to wit, that which was formerly of Cathay, but now is of Osbet, which is called Gatzaria, and the empire of Dua and Cayda, formerly of Capac and now of Elchigaday, extend over more than CC days' journey.
p.s: Jordanus Catalani, translated by Henry Yule (Mirabilia descripta, Hakluyt Society, London 1863)
p.pe: Golden Horde (Uzbek Khan) and Chagatai khanate
p.c: Hearsay; several names are garbled, and the identifications are Yule's.
p.tg: golden horde uzbek chagatai gatzaria mongol empires

p.h: Why they are called Tartars: the horde that gave its name
p.g: Johannes Melman, a Dutch East India Company interpreter in China from 1656, wrote down for Witsen what 'the most sensible Tartars' in Peking told him about their origins. The Scythians beyond Mount Imaus lived in seven hordes, one of them called Tartar; because the khan they elected came from that horde, all his subjects took the name Tartar and kept it.
p.q: Daerenboven bestonden de Scyten, ten tijde dezer verdeelinge, die achter de Berg Imaus zich onthielden, in zeven Horden, welke genoemt wierden, Tartar, Tangur, Cunat, Tateyr, Sonic, Mongli, en Tebeta … en om dat dezen gekoren Keizer uit de Horde der Tartaren was voort gekomen, zoo hebben alle zijne onderdanen dien naem van Tartar … aengenomen, en tot noch toe behouden.
p.s: Johannes Melman (Dutch East India Company interpreter), report printed by Nicolaes Witsen
p.pe: Tartars (Mongols, as told to a Dutch interpreter in Qing China)
p.w: report written after 1656; story set c. 1187
p.t: Moreover, at the time of this division, the Scythians who lived beyond Mount Imaus consisted of seven hordes, which were called Tartar, Tangur, Cunat, Tateyr, Sonic, Mongli and Tebeta … and because this elected emperor had come from the horde of the Tartars, all his subjects took that name of Tartar … and have kept it to this day.
p.c: The seven names closely match the list of Tartar nations in Hayton's Flower of the Histories of the East (1307), so book learning seems to be mixed into this 'Tartar' testimony.
p.tg: name origin hordes scythians chinggis khan

p.h: 'Saracenized Tartars' in Persia
p.g: Jordanus, who lived in Tabriz, lists Persia's peoples: Saracens (Muslims), 'Saracenized Tartars', and Christians of many sects, plus a few Jews. The phrase captures the Mongol rulers of Persia after their conversion to Islam around 1295. He calls their ruler simply 'the emperor of Persia'.
p.q: Ista Persida habitatur per Saracenos et per Tartaros saracenatos, atque per Christianos schismaticos diversarum sectarum, seu per Nestorianos, Jacobitas, Græcos, Georgianos, Armenos, et per paucos Judæos.
p.s: Jordanus Catalani of Séverac, O.P. (Latin text, ed. Coquebert de Montbret, Recueil de voyages IV, Paris 1839)
p.pe: Tartars of the Ilkhanate (Mongols in Persia converted to Islam)
p.t: This Persia is inhabited by Saracens and by Saracenized Tartars, and by schismatic Christians of various sects, that is Nestorians, Jacobites, Greeks, Georgians and Armenians, and by a few Jews.
p.n: OCR normalized against the page image.

p.h: 'Barbarian nations that call themselves Tartars', like locusts
p.g: King Bela IV of Hungary, writing to the German king Conrad IV after the disaster at Mohi, describes the invaders as barbarian nations 'which call themselves Tartars', coming out of the East like locusts from the desert. He lists Greater Hungary, Bulgaria, Cumania, Rus', Poland and Moravia as ravaged, with only some castles and strongholds still holding out, and his own kingdom beyond the Danube occupied.
p.q: barbare nationes, que se Tartaros appellant, de plaga orientali velut locuste ex heremo prodeuntes majore Ungaria, Bulgaria, Cumania, Ruscia nec non Polonia et Moravia, castris et munitionibus quibusdam exceptis, que usque hodie se ipsos defendunt, depopulatis
p.s: King Bela IV of Hungary, letter to Conrad IV, Vienna, June 1241 (printed by Hormayr, 1842)
p.t: barbarian nations which call themselves Tartars, coming out of the eastern region like locusts from the desert, having laid waste Greater Hungary, Bulgaria, Cumania, Rus' and also Poland and Moravia, except for certain castles and fortifications which still defend themselves to this day

p.h: Cathay is China: Goes reaches the Wall
p.g: Semedo retells how the Jesuit brother Bento de Goes, travelling from India to find Cathay, learned from a caravan that Cathay and China were the same land under different names. He then passed Turfan and Hami to 'Quiaicion' (Jiayuguan), where one sees the wall dividing the Chinese from the Tartars, and on to Suzhou. This settled that 'Cathay' was simply northern China.
p.q: i otra que la China era lo mismo que el Catayo: no aviendo diferencia en las tierras, si no en los nombres. … passò por estas poblaciones, Puchan, Turfan, Aramuth, Camul, Quiaicion (de donde se vè aquella repetida muralla, que divide a los Chinos de los Tartaros) Sucheu
p.s: Álvaro Semedo, S.J. (Spanish edition by Manuel de Faria e Sousa, Madrid 1642)
p.pe: Tartars beyond the Wall; Muslim merchants of the caravan road
p.t: and the other, that China was the same as Cathay, there being no difference in the lands, but only in the names. … he passed through these towns: Puchan, Turfan, Aramuth, Camul, Quiaicion (from where one sees that much-repeated wall that divides the Chinese from the Tartars), Suzhou
p.c: Semedo retells Goes's journey from Jesuit papers; he did not travel it.

p.h: A name the conquerors themselves rejected
p.g: In his introduction Erskine explains that 'Tartar' was first used by thirteenth-century European travellers and that Genghis Khan's family disliked it. He cites Rubruck, who was warned at the court of Sartaq (actually Batu's son, not Genghis's grandson) to call him Moal, a Mongol, because the Tatars were a different, conquered tribe. The European name for the whole empire was thus the name of one of its subject peoples.
p.q: This name of Tartar, however, by which we are accustomed to designate Chengiz Khan and his successors as well as their empire, these princes themselves rejected with disdain. Rubriquis, who visited the court of Sartakh, Chengiz Khan's grandson, about the year 1254, was cautioned, therefore, to call him Moal (that is Moghul), and not Tartar
p.s: William Erskine, editor's introduction (1826), citing William of Rubruck
p.c: Editorial synthesis, not Babur. Sartaq was Batu's son, a great-grandson of Genghis Khan, and in Rubruck's own account the warning was not to call Sartaq a Christian; the remark that the Mongols disliked being called Tartars is Rubruck's general comment.

p.h: Nogais, Cheremis, Mordvins and 'Chircasses': other 'Tartars'
p.g: Fletcher files several quite different peoples under 'Tartar': the Nogais (the best warriors, but the most savage), the Cheremis (actually the Finnic-speaking Mari), the Mordvins (also Finnic) and the 'Chircasses'. He says they differ more in name than in way of life, except the Chircasses, who border south-west towards Lithuania, follow Polish fashions, are far more 'civil', and are partly subject to the king of Poland and Christian. That description fits the Dnieper Cossacks, whom Russians called Cherkasy, better than the Circassians of the Caucasus.
p.q: There are divers other Tartars that border upon Russia, as the Nagais [Nogais], the Cheremissens, the Mordwites, the Chircasses, and the Shalcans, which all differ in name more then in regiment or other condition from the Chrim Tartar, except the Chircasses
p.s: Giles Fletcher (1591; ed. E. A. Bond, 1856; bracketed words are Bond's)
p.pl: Middle Volga, Nogai steppe and the Polish-Lithuanian borderlands
p.pe: Nogai, Cheremis (Mari), Mordvins, 'Chircasses' (probably the Dnieper Cossacks, Russian Cherkasy)
p.c: A good example of 'Tartar' as a catch-all: the Mari and Mordvins are not Turkic peoples at all, and the Christian 'Chircasses' near Lithuania were probably Cossacks.

p.h: The White Mountain, old home of 'our Tartars'
p.g: At Jilin on the Sungari, Verbiest describes the mountain the Manchus revered as the cradle of their people. He translates its name, Cham-pe (Changbai), as 'the white mountain', and says that when the Kangxi emperor 'saw it' he got off his horse, knelt by the river and bowed three times to the ground towards it. Verbiest calls the Manchus 'our Tartars', the people he served at court.
p.q: This Mountain so famous in the East for having been the Antient Seat of our Tartars, is alwayes covered with Snow, from whence it had its name, because Cham-pe signifyes the white Mountaine. So soon as the Emperour saw it, he alighted from his Horse and fell on his knees on the bank of the River, and bowed himself three times to the ground to Salute it
p.s: Ferdinand Verbiest (English translation, 1686)
p.c: Verbiest also says the mountain lay 400 miles away, so the emperor was most likely saluting it from afar, as in the Qing rite of worshipping Changbai at a distance.
p.tg: changbai manchu origins kangxi sacred mountain

p.h: Scythians, then Turks, then Tatars
p.g: In his introduction Reinaud explains that the same northern peoples went by different names in different eras: Scythians for ancient writers, Turks for early Arabic writers, and Tartars, or rather Tatars as Arabs, Persians and Turks pronounce it, for later writers. It is a short, clear account of how 'Tartar' became a catch-all label.
p.q: Chez les écrivains de l'antiquité, les peuples du nord de l'Asie et de l'Europe étaient des Scythes; chez les anciens écrivains arabes, ce sont des Turks; chez les écrivains postérieurs, ce sont des Tartares ou plutôt, comme prononcent les Arabes, les Persans et les Turks, des Tatars.
p.s: J. T. Reinaud (introduction, 1848)
p.t: For ancient writers, the peoples of northern Asia and Europe were Scythians; for the early Arabic writers they are Turks; for later writers they are Tartars, or rather, as the Arabs, Persians and Turks pronounce it, Tatars.
p.c: A nineteenth-century scholar's summary, not a medieval statement.

p.h: Temujin named after a captured Tatar chief
p.g: The annals of Chinggis Khan say that his father Yesugei had just captured the Tatar chief Temujin when his wife gave birth to a son clutching a clot of blood like a red stone. Yesugei named the boy after the captive to mark his victory. Here Tatar is the name of one rival tribe, not of the Mongols.
p.q: 初烈祖征塔塔爾部獲其部長特穆津宣懿太后諤楞適生帝手握凝血如赤石烈祖異之因以所獲特穆津名之志武功也
p.s: Song Lian and the Ming history office, History of the Yuan (Siku quanshu Wenyuange copy, Kanseki Repository transcription)
p.t: At first Liezu (Yesugei) campaigned against the Tatar tribe and captured its chief Temujin. Just then the empress Xuanyi, Ogelen (Hoelun), gave birth to the emperor, who held in his hand clotted blood like a red stone. Liezu thought it a marvel and named him after the captured Temujin, to record his military success.
p.c: The same story is told in the Secret History; the Siku copy re-spells Temujin as 特穆津 and the Tatars as 塔塔爾.

p.h: Why the Mongols are still called Tatars
p.g: Ney Elias's introduction quotes the Persian historian Rashid al-Din (writing about 1300 to 1310). The Tatars were once so powerful that other Turkic peoples called themselves Tatars for the prestige, just as in Rashid's own day everyone wanted to be a 'Mongol'. That, he says, is why the Mongols are still called Tatars in China, India, the Kipchak steppe, Arabia, Syria and Egypt.
p.q: Previous to this period it was the same with the Tatars, on account of their power, and this is the reason why the Mongols are still called Tatars in China and in India, by the Kirghiz, the Bashgirds, in the Kapchak country, in the north of Asia, in Arabia, in Syria, in Egypt, and in Africa.
p.s: Rashid al-Din, quoted (via d'Ohsson's French) in Ney Elias's introduction (1895)
p.c: Editorial introduction quoting a fourteenth-century source at second hand.
p.tg: tatar mongol name rashid al-din prestige

p.h: Four races of Tartars in China
p.g: The Mongol official Kwang tells Ellis that Tartars can hold office at eighteen and that there are four races of Tartars in China. Ellis's footnote explains the Manchu, Mongol and 'Tartarized Chinese' eight-banner system, and notes that Mongols have long been Buddhists while Manchus adopted Buddhism only after entering China.
p.q: Tartars, Kwang informed us, were eligible to office at eighteen; this is said to arise from the wish of government to bring them early into employment: there are four different races of Tartars in China; he himself is a Mongul, or, as called in China, a Mun-koo.
p.s: Henry Ellis, reporting the Mongol official Kwang

p.h: Not grey wolves but the pagan Tatars: the 'Khinova' comes to Rus
p.g: The poet builds the Horde's approach from omens: creaking carts between the Don and the Dnieper, the 'Khinova' marching on the Russian land, grey wolves howling by the river Mecha. Then he turns the image: those were not grey wolves but the pagan Tatars, come to take the whole Russian land. Sreznevsky's commentary suggests 'Khinova', an old poetic name for steppe enemies also used in the Lay of Igor, may hide the name of the Huns.
p.q: Идетъ Хинова на Рускую землю. Сѣріе волци воютъ, на рѣкѣ хотятъ на Мечи поступити въ Рускую землю. То ти были не сѣріе волци, придоша поганые Татарове, хотятъ проити воюючи, взяти всю землю Рускую.
p.s: Zadonshchina (Kirillo-Belozersk text), ed. I. I. Sreznevsky, 1858
p.t: The Khinova is marching on the Russian land. Grey wolves are howling; by the river Mecha they mean to cross into the Russian land. Those were not grey wolves: the pagan Tatars have come, they mean to pass through making war and take the whole Russian land.
p.c: Poetic imagery. The manuscript reads 'хинела'; 'Хинова' is Sreznevsky's correction (footnote on the same page), and the Huns etymology is his guess (commentary, n54 p.49).

p.h: 'The name of Tartary is unknown in those regions'
p.g: Setting out the geography north of the Hindu Kush, Elphinstone divides the lands into Turkestan (west of the Pamirs) and 'Chinese Turkestan' (east of them), using the local name for Turk-speaking country. Then he adds a blunt note: the people who live there do not call it Tartary. The word was a European map label, not a local one.
p.q: All the country west of Beloot Taugh, and north of the Oxus, is called Toorkistaun, a term which may be extended to the east of Beloot Taugh, as far as there is reason to think the Turkish language is spoken … The name of Tartary is unknown in those regions.
p.s: Mountstuart Elphinstone (1815)
p.pe: Uzbeks and other Turkic peoples of Central Asia
p.c: Based on what his Central Asian informants told him, not on a visit.

p.h: How the peninsula got the name Krim
p.g: In a history letter written before entering Crimea, Craven summarises its past: the Mongols or Tartars conquered it in 1237, and because they traded heavily at the town of Krim, the whole peninsula took that name, the only one Eastern peoples used. When she later reached the site (n198) she found 'not a vestige' of the ancient town left.
p.q: and, as the Tartars carried on a great trade in the town of Krim, the peninsula took the name of Krim, by which only it is known to the Orientals at this hour
p.s: Elizabeth Craven (letters published London, 1789)
p.pe: Mongols or Tartars of the Golden Horde
p.c: A second-hand summary of history from books she does not name.

p.h: Villages emptied by 'the Tartars'
p.g: Near Mashhad the caravan passed villages wrecked by Turkmen raiders. At Tibris, which Mohan Lal says was 'harassed by the Tartars', most of the people had been carried off as slaves, and the survivors ran up weeping to ask the travellers for news of their captive families. Here 'Tartars' simply means the Turkmen slave-raiders.
p.q: Tibris, a fine walled village, contains very few inhabitants, who are harassed by the Tartars. Some time ago it was destroyed by the Alamans, and most of the residents made slaves. On our approach, the villagers ran up to us, shedding a flood of tears
p.s: Mohan Lal (1846 edition)
p.tg: turkmens alaman slave raids tartar label

p.h: 'Of the Tatar race': a poem about Turkish slave soldiers
p.g: Listing places in the East, Mustawfi quotes a mocking poem about the Turkish pages of the Seljuk Sultan Sanjar, who fled before the Qara Khitay cavalry. The poet calls them swordsmen 'of the Tatar race'. Le Strange adds that Tatar is not a place-name but the name of a people. It is a glimpse of the word in Persian a century before the Mongol conquests.
p.q: Other places are Kasan, Tatar and Fay which a poet has mentioned in his verses on the Ghulams (Pages) of Sultan Sanjar, who had showed lack of bravery in their attack on the cavalry of the infidel Qara Khitay. He says: Bravo! O ye strong hearted Turkish swordsmen Of the Tatar race from Fay and Kasan
p.s: Hamdallah Mustawfi (translated by G. Le Strange, 1919), quoting a twelfth-century poem
p.pe: Turkish ghulams (slave soldiers) of Sultan Sanjar, called Tatars
p.w: 1141 (battle with the Qara Khitay), quoted c.1340
p.c: The poem is satire; Le Strange identifies the poet as Sharaf al-Din Kushkaki in his footnote.
p.tg: tatar ethnonym seljuks qara khitay poem

p.h: Yakut words are 'pure Turkish'
p.g: In Yakutsk Erman compared the Yakuts with the Tatars of western Siberia in looks and language. Their words for God, iron and other metals and fishing gear were 'all pure Turkish', and they named their milk spirits as the Turkish Tatars did. So he rejects the idea that the Yakuts owed their culture to Mongol neighbours.
p.q: It cannot by any means be maintained, that the Yakuts have received the better part of their civilisation, at some time or other, from Mongolian neighbours; their names for the Deity, for iron, and the other metals, (excepting the tin of the Buraets), for their fishing gear, &c. are all pure Turkish.
p.s: Adolph Erman (translated by W. D. Cooley, 1848)

p.h: Babur: a Turk by his father, a Mongol by his mother
p.g: Erskine explains that Babur belonged to 'both races of Tartars'. Through his father he descended from Timur, and so counted himself a Turk; through his mother he descended from Genghis Khan. Erskine adds that Babur's sympathies were entirely with the Turks and that he often speaks of the Mongols with hatred and contempt.
p.q: Baber had a close connexion with both races of Tartars, He traced up his descent on the father's side in a direct line to the great Taimur Beg, whence he always speaks of himself as being a Turk ; while by the mother's side he was sprung from Chengiz Khan, being the grandson of Yunis Khan, a celebrated prince of the Moghuls.
p.s: William Erskine, editor's introduction (1826)

p.h: Kulikovo: 'Ishmaelites' ruled by Mamai behind a puppet khan
p.g: The younger Novgorod text on the battle of Kulikovo explains the politics of the Horde: a weak khan reigned while Mamai did everything. It calls Mamai's army the pagan 'Ishmaelite race' and 'sons of Hagar', and when Dmitry arrays his troops it is 'against the pagan Polovtsy'. Old names for steppe enemies were simply reused for the Tatars.
p.q: въздвизается на крестьяны Измаилтескии родъ поганыи: нѣкоему убо у нихъ худу царствующу, а все дѣющу у нихъ князю Мамаю … великии же князь Дмитрии, съ братомъ своимъ съ Володимеромъ, изрядивъ полкы противу поганыхъ Половець
p.s: Novgorod First Chronicle, younger redaction (PSRL vol. 3, 1841)
p.pe: Tatars of the Golden Horde under the emir Mamai
p.t: the pagan Ishmaelite race rises against the Christians: for a certain feeble man reigns among them, and Prince Mamai does everything among them … and Grand Prince Dmitry, with his brother Vladimir, arrayed his regiments against the pagan Polovtsy
p.c: Written in Novgorod, far from the battle, in a religious register.

p.h: 'Turk' means a man from the highlands of Tartary
p.g: Chardin insists that the true 'Turkey' is the vast highland of Tartary, homeland of both the Turkmen herders and the Ottomans' ancestors. In the East, he says, 'Turk' simply means someone from those highlands, and Ottoman subjects find the name barbarous. He also scolds European travellers who write about countries without knowing the language.
p.q: For that among them Turk signifies one that comes from those High-lands of Tartary, let it be from what part it will.
p.s: Jean Chardin, 'The Coronation of Solyman III' (appended to the 1691 English edition)
p.pe: Turkmens and Turks, as seen from Persia

p.h: Turks, Tartars, Moguls and Tajiks
p.g: Two footnotes explain the troops sent to scout the mountains of Kafiristan. 'Turks' are the descendants of Moguls and Tartars; 'Tadgics' (Tajiks) are the Persian-speaking townspeople of Transoxiana and Iran, who are neither. It is a neat 1720s key to how Tartar, Mogul and Turk overlapped.
p.q: The Turks are those who descend from the Moguls and Tartars… The Tadgics are the inhabitants of the towns of Transoxiana, and all the country of Iran, who are neither Tartars, Moguls, nor Turks.
p.s: Translator's footnote (François Pétis de la Croix, carried into the 1723 English)
p.pe: Timur's Turkic soldiers and the Tajik townspeople
p.c: An editorial gloss, not Yazdi's own words.

p.h: 'Timurians', not 'Moguls'
p.g: Attending the marriage of a Delhi prince, Vigne insists on calling the Indian imperial house 'Timurians', after their ancestor Timur (Tamerlane), rather than the usual 'Mogul'. It is a small but telling point: the word Mogul (Mongol) had become a name for an Indian Muslim dynasty that itself descended from Central Asian conquerors.
p.q: I was fortunate in being present at the marriage of his grandaughter with Unjim Shikoh, one of the Princes of Delhi, or Timurians, as they are generally called … a much more correct name for the Indian Emperors than that of Mogul.
p.s: Godfrey Thomas Vigne (1842)

p.h: Ninety years of Tartar rule, 1206 to 1368
p.g: In his outline of Chinese dynasties Semedo says that after two thousand years of regional lords, the Tartars began conquering China piece by piece in 1206 and ruled it for ninety years until 1368, when Hongwu ('Hum Vu') found them grown careless and hated, drove them out and even subjected their borderlands. The Tartars here are the Mongols of the Yuan dynasty.
p.q: Permanecieron en la China los señores de Estados particulares mas de dos mil años, hasta que el de 1206. de nuestra Redencion, los Tartaros (entonces con otro poder i govierno) empeçando a conquistarla por partes, la vinieron a dominar por espacio de noventa años, que fenecieron el de 1368. en que el Hum Vu cogiendolos ya floxos de cuidado, i de tirania encendidos
p.s: Álvaro Semedo, S.J. (Spanish edition by Manuel de Faria e Sousa, Madrid 1642)
p.t: The lords of particular states remained in China more than two thousand years, until in the year 1206 of our Redemption the Tartars (then with another power and government), beginning to conquer it piece by piece, came to rule it for the space of ninety years, which ended in 1368, when Hum Vu, catching them now slack in their care and inflamed with tyranny
p.c: 1206 is the year Chinggis Khan was proclaimed, not the start of Mongol rule over all China (completed in 1279).
p.n: OCR normalized against the page image; long s normalized, abbreviation marks (q̃, õ, ẽ) kept as printed.

p.h: The peoples of the Dzungar realm, none of them called Tatars
p.g: Unkovsky lists the peoples under the Kontaisha: the Dzungars proper ('of the left hand'), Kyrgyz, Uriankhai, Telengits and others, the town-dwelling Bukharans of Yarkand, the Buruts (Kyrgyz) of lake Issyk-Kul and the Barabinians, who paid tribute to both Russia and the Dzungars. No one here is called a Tatar; the same land appears on Western maps of the time as part of 'Great Tartary'.
p.q: Подъ его контайшинымъ владѣніемъ обрѣтаются разные народы, а именно: его настоящей народъ, имянуемой Зюнгоры (или лѣвой руки), Киргизы, Урянхайцы, Теленгуты, Мингаты, Каюты, Кошеуты, Эркенскіе Бухарцы (въ городахъ живущіе, а лучше при немъ кочуютъ), Буруты, которые около озера Тускелъ кочуютъ, Барабинцы, которые ясакъ платятъ въ сторону Императорского Величества и Контайшѣ.
p.s: Ivan Unkovsky (ed. N. I. Veselovsky, 1887)
p.t: Under the Kontaisha's rule are various peoples, namely: his own people, called the Dzungars (or 'of the left hand'), the Kyrgyz, Uriankhai, Telengits, Mingats, Khoits, Khoshuts, the Bukharans of Erken (Yarkand), who live in towns, though the better sort roam with him, the Buruts, who roam around lake Tuskel (Issyk-Kul), and the Barabinians, who pay tribute to His Imperial Majesty and to the Kontaisha.
p.c: The identifications of Kayuty as Khoits and Tuskel as Issyk-Kul are editorial glosses by this reader, not Unkovsky's.

p.h: 'Yurt' Tatars: named for being born there
p.g: De Bruyn records the Russian name for the Tatars around Astrakhan, 'Jurtsge' (the Yurt Tatars), explaining it as 'because they were born there'. They paid no tribute to the Tsar but had to send a few hundred men to his wars, though they could field 20,000. On the same page he notes that Nogais tented near Terki and that Crimean Tatars came only to sell horses and cattle.
p.q: Les Russiens nomment les Tartares, qui habitent en ces quartiers-là, Jurtsge, parce qu'ils y sont nez. Aussi ne payent-ils aucun tribut au Czar; ils sont seulement obligés d'envoyer quelques centaines de leurs gens à la guerre, lors que ce Prince le souhaite.
p.s: Cornelis de Bruyn (French translation, Voyages de Corneille Le Brun, 1718)
p.t: The Russians call the Tartars who live in those parts Jurtsge, because they were born there. Nor do they pay any tribute to the Tsar; they are only obliged to send some hundreds of their people to war when that prince wishes it.

p.h: 'Nine Tatars' join the Oghuz against the khan
p.g: In the Bilge Qaghan inscription the khan says he campaigned against the Oghuz and 'devastated their houses and their buildings', and that the Oghuz then allied with the Nine Tatars and came against him. He fought two great battles at Agu, destroyed their army and enslaved their people. The Tatars appear here as a real political ally of the Oghuz, and the Oghuz are said to have houses and buildings.
p.q: j'entrai en campagne et dévastai leurs maisons et leurs bâtiments. Le peuple [ogouz] s'allia avec les Neuf-Tatars, et ils vinrent. Près d'Agou, je livrai deux grandes batailles; je dévastai leur armée et j'asservis là leur peuple.
p.s: Bilge Qaghan inscription, 735, in Vilhelm Thomsen's French translation (1896)
p.t: I went on campaign and devastated their houses and their buildings. The [Oghuz] people allied with the Nine Tatars, and they came. Near Agu I fought two great battles; I destroyed their army and there I enslaved their people.
p.c: A victor's account; the word Thomsen renders 'bâtiments' (barq) is discussed by Radloff as 'buildings', while 'houses' (eb) may mean yurts.
p.n: Checked against the page image.
