p.h: Tartars and Chinese: one government, one language, two characters
p.g: In a section headed 'Character of the Tartars', Hüttner says mixed marriages, a single government and a common language had made Tartars and Chinese hard to tell apart in their customs. Yet he found the Tartar, as travellers described him, rough, hard and blunt: sturdier in build, clumsier in manners and less clean in his dwellings than the Chinese, but without the deceitful double-dealing he attributes to his Chinese neighbour. On the next page the two mandarins conducting the embassy blamed the stubbornness and pride of the Tartars for trouble getting supplies in Tartary.
p.q: Vermischte Ehen der Tartarn und Chinesen, einerlei Regierung, einerlei Sprache bringen natürlicher Weise dieselben Sitten hervor. Da aber ein Volk seinen eigenthümlichen Charakter nie gänzlich verläugnen kann, so leuchten auch hier einige Züge hervor, die den Tartarn merklich von dem Chinesen unterscheiden. Reisende beschreiben den erstern als roh, hart und gerade; und so fanden wir ihn wirklich.
p.s: Johann Christian Hüttner (1797)
p.t: Mixed marriages of Tartars and Chinese, one and the same government, one and the same language naturally produce the same customs. But since a people can never wholly deny its own character, here too some traits shine through that clearly distinguish the Tartar from the Chinese. Travellers describe the former as rough, hard and blunt; and so we really found him.
p.c: National-character stereotypes, partly borrowed from earlier travellers, as Hüttner admits.
p.tg: manchus chinese intermarriage character tartar identity

p.h: The three great 'Tartar invaders'
p.g: Wood groups Genghis Khan, Tamerlane (Timur) and the Uzbek conqueror Shaybani Khan together as 'Tartar invaders', and says none of them seems to have reached the high valleys of Badakhshan. It shows how loosely 'Tartar' was used for Mongol and Turkic conquerors alike.
p.q: None of the three great Tartar invaders, Jangez Khan, Tamerlane, or Shebani Khan, seem to have penetrated so high up the valley of the Oxus, though some of the followers of Baber, when expelled from the rich plains of Soghdiana by the Uzbeks, sought shelter here
p.s: John Wood
p.pe: Genghis Khan, Timur and Shaybani Khan
p.tg: genghis khan timur shaybani conquest names

p.h: Kazan means 'kettle'
p.g: Georgi opens his description of Kazan with its name in several languages and a gloss: in Russian and Tatar a kazan is the cauldron from which a family eats. He then calls it the capital of the Tatar kingdom of Kazan conquered by Ivan IV in 1552. The previous pages tell the Tatar legend that the city was named after a servant's kettle that fell into the Kazanka.
p.q: Kasan (Rußisch und Tatarisch ein Kessel, aus welchem eine Familie speiset), Kosan Wotjakisch und Tschuwaschisch, Oson Tscheremissisch die Hauptstadt des 1552 von dem grossen Zaar Iwan Waßiljewitsch eroberten Tatarisch-Kasanischen Reichs
p.s: Johann Gottlieb Georgi
p.t: Kazan (in Russian and Tatar a kettle from which a family eats), Kosan in Votyak and Chuvash, Oson in Cheremis, the capital of the Tatar kingdom of Kazan conquered in 1552 by the great Tsar Ivan Vasilyevich

p.h: Forty outlaw horsemen: a Kazakh origin legend
p.g: Among several Kazakh origin stories Levshin gives one from the journal of Captain Rychkov (1771): seven sons of a Crimean khan, cheated of their inheritance, went into the steppe, joined other exiles to make a band of forty, lived by raiding, stole wives and multiplied. Forty is kyrk in Turkic, so they were called Kyrk-Kazak, 'forty Cossacks' or riders. Levshin himself calls most such traditions absurd but prints them as he found them.
p.q: Шайка сія, въ числѣ 40 человѣкъ, долго занимаясь грабежами сосѣдственныхъ съ ними земель; наконецъ, похитила себѣ женъ и размножилась. Сорокъ означается по-Турецки словомъ Кыркъ, а потому и толпа сія названа Кыркъ-Казакъ, то есть, сорокъ Казаковъ, или наѣздниковъ. Потомки ихъ сохранили названіе предковъ.
p.s: Aleksei Levshin, from the journal of Captain N. Rychkov (1832)
p.pe: Kazakhs (in legend, descendants of Crimean exiles)
p.t: This band, forty men strong, for a long time lived by plundering the lands around them; at last it stole wives for itself and multiplied. Forty is expressed in Turkic by the word kyrk, and so this crowd was called Kyrk-Kazak, that is, forty Kazakhs, or riders. Their descendants kept the name of their ancestors.
p.c: A folk etymology linking 'Kirghiz' to kyrk (forty); Levshin presents it as one tradition among several.
p.tg: origin legend crimea forty etymology kazakhs

p.h: How the Mongols split into Mongol and Manchu 'Tartars'
p.g: Grosier explains 'Chinese Tartary' with an origin story: all its tribes were once called Mongol Tartars, and when the Mongols were driven out of China in 1368, some fled east toward the Amur and kept Chinese customs, becoming the Manchus or 'Eastern Tartars', while the rest went back west and stayed Mongols. The Manchus did not in fact descend from the Yuan refugees; the story shows how Europeans tried to make one 'Tartar' family out of different peoples.
p.q: Those of the east retain their ancient name of Moungal or Mogul Tartars: the rest are known by the name of Mantchew or Eastern Tartars. Chinese Tartary is therefore divided into two parts, the eastern and western.
p.s: Jean-Baptiste Grosier (English translation, 1788)
p.c: The text as printed has 'east' and 'the rest' the wrong way round (it means the western group kept the Mongol name), and the origin story itself is mistaken. The quote swaps the printed long dash for a comma.

p.h: 'Never so happy as in the wilds of Tartary'
p.g: In his preface Cochrane calls all of northern Asia 'Tartary' and invites scientists to explore 'the vast fields of Tartary' after him. He closes by saying he was never so happy as in the wilds of Tartary. For him, as for many readers in the 1820s, 'Tartary' simply meant Siberia and the lands beyond it, not a country or a state.
p.q: I may be allowed to add, that after such a journey, I might be supposed cured of the spirit of travelling, at least in so eccentric a way; yet the supposition is far from the fact, for as I am conscious that I was never so happy as in the wilds of Tartary, so have I never been so anxious to enter on a similar field as at this moment.
p.s: John Dundas Cochrane (1824), preface
p.pe: All Siberian peoples ('Tartary' as a region)

p.h: Kurds who claim Mongol and Uzbek ancestors
p.g: Jaubert reports that the Kurds, settled or nomadic, claim descent from the Mongols and Uzbeks whose sudden raids so often shook Asia. He rejects the claim on the evidence of their large eyes, aquiline noses, fair skin and height, which he thinks 'belie this Tartar origin'.
p.q: Ces peuples, soit qu'ils mènent une vie sédentaire ou qu'ils errent dans les campagnes, se prétendent issus des Mongols et des Uzbeks, dont les irruptions soudaines ont si souvent troublé l'Asie. Mais la grandeur et la beauté de leurs yeux, leur nez aquilin, la blancheur de leur teint et l'élévation de leur taille, démentent cette origine tartare.
p.s: Pierre-Amedee Jaubert
p.t: These peoples, whether they lead a settled life or wander the countryside, claim descent from the Mongols and the Uzbeks, whose sudden incursions have so often disturbed Asia. But the size and beauty of their eyes, their aquiline noses, the fairness of their complexion and their tall stature belie this Tartar origin.
p.c: Jaubert argues from looks alone, a method of his time; the claimed ancestry reflects the prestige of Mongol and Uzbek descent.

p.h: A map of a land that 'lay in the dark'
p.g: The Royal Society's president greets Witsen's map as a Columbus-like discovery of a new world, and wonders aloud how anyone could chart deserts, bogs and mountains that seemed made for 'everlasting Solitude'. It is a vivid picture of how unknown 'Tartary' was to western Europe in the 1680s.
p.q: I Have lately had a great Effect of your Bounty in the Maps of Tartary. this is Columbus like, the Discovery of a New World; at least Tydings of those Parts, which from the beginning have layn in the Dark.
p.s: Sir Robert Southwell, President of the Royal Society, writing to Witsen

p.h: The Tatars called it Isker, not Sibir
p.g: In a footnote Coxe rejects the popular idea that Siberia was named after the captured fortress of Sibir, pointing out that the Tatars themselves called the fort Isker. He suggests the regional name came to the Russians earlier, through the Permian and Zyrian peoples.
p.q: Several authors have supposed the name of Siberia to derive its origin from this fortress, soon after it was first taken by the Russians under Yermac. But this opinion is advanced without sufficient foundation; for the name of Sibir was unknown to the Tartars, that fort being by them called Isker.
p.s: William Coxe (footnote, following Müller)

p.h: Three khans, one people
p.g: Bell names the three great 'Tartar princes' between the Volga and China: Ayuka Khan of the Volga Kalmyks, the Kontaysha of the Dzungars and the Tushetu Khan of the Khalkha Mongols. He treats all their subjects as one Kalmyk nation with the same looks, religion and language, and marvels at how far a traveller could go with that one language.
p.q: From the river Volga, to the wall of China, there are three great Tartar princes; the Ayuka-Chan, the Kontaysha, and the Tush-du-Chan. These three mighty nations have almost the same features, religion, and language; and live in the same manner. … whose subjects go by the general name of Kalmuks.
p.s: John Bell (Travels, 1763)

p.h: 'Kir Kasak': the Kazakhs of the steppe
p.g: The chapter on the 'Kirghiz' (the Kazakhs) says they are divided into three hordes, and that two of them call themselves Kir Kasak, which the author derives from kir, 'steppe or wilderness', and kasak, 'daredevil'. He describes 'my Kirghiz' as wholly Tatar in looks and temperament, with little courage but a strong taste for raiding, though they spare their captives. It shows how the Russian name 'Kirghiz' was then used for the people now called Kazakhs.
p.q: … die beiden andern nennen sich selbst Kir Kasak, von Kir Wüste und Kasak Wagehals. … Meine Kirgisen sind ganz von tatarischen Ansehen und Gemüthscharacter, wohl gewachsen … Sie haben wenig Muth, aber große Neigung zum Rauben, doch sind sie dabey nicht mörderisch, sondern schonen die Gefangenen.
p.s: J. P. Falck, arranged and supplemented by J. G. Georgi (1786)
p.pe: Kirghiz-Kaisaks (Kazakhs) of the Middle and Little Hordes
p.t: … the two others call themselves Kir Kasak, from kir, wilderness, and kasak, daredevil. … My Kirghiz are entirely Tatar in appearance and temperament, well grown … They have little courage but a great inclination to robbery, yet they are not murderous, but spare their prisoners.
p.c: The etymology is the author's; the character sketch is a frontier stereotype.
p.n: OCR normalized (checked against the page image; the OCR text is badly garbled).

p.h: Why the emperors were called 'Cheguthai'
p.g: In a footnote Vigne explains the name Zagatai (Chagatai) that Kashmiris still used for the old imperial rule: it comes from a son of Genghis Khan who founded the Chagatai branch in Transoxiana. This links the Indian Mughals directly to the Mongol conquests of the 1200s.
p.q: Or Cheguthai, the Mogul Emperors ; so called from Zagatai Khan, a son of Jenghiz Khan, who founded the Zagatai branch in Transoxiana.
p.s: Godfrey Thomas Vigne (footnote, 1842)

p.h: The Tartars of the West and their kings
p.g: Polo calls the Golden Horde the 'Tartars of the Ponent' (of the West). Their first king, 'Sain', conquered Russia, the Cumans, Alans, Circassians, Goths of Crimea and Khazaria. He lists the later khans down to Toqta, who reigned in Polo's time. Yule's note points out that 'Sain' (the Good) was really Batu's own surname, so Polo turned one khan into two.
p.q: The first lord of the Tartars of the Ponent was Sain, a very great and puissant king, who conquered Rosia and Comania, Alania, Lac, Menjar, Zic, Gothia, and Gazaria ; all these provinces were conquered by King Sain.
p.s: Marco Polo (translated by Henry Yule, 1871)
p.tg: golden horde batu russia cumans khans

p.h: Manchu soldiers who no longer speak Manchu
p.g: At the garrison town of Koukou-Khoton (Hohhot), Huc found that the 10,000 'Mantchou Tartars' stationed there hardly spoke their own language. Two centuries after conquering China, he says, the Manchus had become Chinese in manners, language and even homeland.
p.q: The soldiers of the New Town of Koukou Khoton are Mantchou Tartars; but if you did not previously know the fact, you would scarcely suspect it from hearing them speak. Amongst them there is perhaps not a single man who understands the language of his own country.
p.s: Évariste Huc (translated by William Hazlitt, 1852)

p.h: The 'water Mongols' who called themselves Tartars
p.g: In his commentary d'Avezac summarises Carpini's account of the four peoples who once lived in Mongolia: the Yeka Mongal ('great Mongols'), the Su-Mongal ('water Mongols') who called themselves Tartars after a river named Tatar in their land, the Merkit and the Mecrit. He confirms that Yeka and Su do mean 'great' and 'water'.
p.q: En ce pays étaient autrefois quatre peuples, savoir: les Yeka Mongal ou grands Mongals; les Su-Mongals ou Mongals aquatiques, lesquels se donnaient à eux-mêmes le nom Tartares, d'après un fleuve appelé Tatar qui coulait en leur pays; les Merkit; et enfin les Mécrit.
p.s: Armand d'Avezac (editor's commentary), paraphrasing John of Plano Carpini
p.t: In that country there were formerly four peoples, namely: the Yeka Mongal or great Mongols; the Su-Mongal or water Mongols, who gave themselves the name Tartars after a river called Tatar that flowed through their country; the Merkit; and lastly the Mecrit.
p.c: The 'river Tatar' is Carpini's explanation, repeated by d'Avezac; such a river is not otherwise attested and the name's origin remains uncertain.

p.h: Chinese Muslims as 'remnants of the Tartars'
p.g: Telling of a clash near Macao, the account notes that one of the Chinese magistrates was a 'Saracen' (Muslim) by origin and religion. Ricci explains that many remnants of the Tartars stayed on in China after the Mongols fell; after four generations they count as natives and may even sit the examinations and hold office. It shows Europeans linking China's Muslim communities with the Mongol period.
p.q: Ex iis Magistratibus erat unus origine ac professione Saracenus: nam ex Tartarorum reliquiis multi in eo regno remanserunt, qui post quartam generationem pro indigenis habiti, ne a litterariis quidem gradibus publicisque muneribus prohibentur.
p.s: Matteo Ricci, edited and translated into Latin by Nicolas Trigault (1615)
p.pe: Chinese Muslims, described as descendants of the Tartars
p.t: Among these magistrates was one who was a Saracen by origin and religion: for many of the remnants of the Tartars remained in that kingdom, who after the fourth generation are held to be natives and are not barred even from the literary degrees and public offices.
p.c: Ricci's own explanation; many Chinese Muslims descend from Central Asian and Persian Muslims settled under the Mongols rather than from Mongols themselves.
p.n: The scan's machine-read text is too damaged to confirm this quote automatically. Check it against the page.

p.h: A story that the Manchu emperors came from Kublai Khan
p.g: The Tartar princes at court, Staunton says, revered the emperor as a descendant of Kublai Khan: Kublai's heirs, driven out of China in the fourteenth century, fled to the Manchus, intermarried, and produced the 'Bog-doi Khans' who conquered China. It shows how the Qing dynasty was presented to, or understood by, its Mongol allies.
p.q: They hold the Emperor in the greater veneration, as considering him descended from Kublai-Khan, the conqueror of China in the thirteenth century. His descendants being in the fourteenth century expelled from the throne of that empire, fled into the country of the Man-choos in Eastern Tartary; and from their intermarriages with the natives, sprung the Bog-doi Khans
p.s: George Leonard Staunton
p.c: A genealogical belief reported at second hand; the Qing ruling clan is usually traced to Jurchen (Manchu) chiefs, not to Kublai.
p.tg: kublai khan manchu genealogy bogdo khan

p.h: The Bogdoi, 'Eastern Tartars' who took China
p.g: Avril's first 'nation' beyond China's frontier is the Bogdoi, whom the Chinese call Eastern Tartars and the Mongols 'Niouchi' (Jurchen). The next page gives his version of their history: an early invasion of China, the Yuan family ruling to 1368, the Ming to 1644, and then the Bogdoi returning to conquer China under Shunzhi, first emperor of the reigning Qing.
p.q: The first Nation is that of the Bogdoi, by the Chineses call'd the Eastern Tartars, and whom the Monguls call Niouchi
p.s: Philippe Avril (English translation, 1693)
p.c: His history is muddled; he credits the 'Tousbecks' (Uzbeks) with putting the Yuan family on the throne, where the Mongols are meant.

p.h: The Cheremis: 'Tartars' who speak Russian
p.g: Struys files the Cheremis under 'Tartars' (his chapter title calls them 'Tartares nommés Czérémisses'), yet on this page he says their everyday language is Russian and that they only understand, and in places speak, Tatar. They were in fact the Mari, a Finno-Ugric people. He also calls them rough and stupid, a sample of the book's contempt.
p.q: Ces peuples sont rudes, grossiers & stupides … Leur Langue ordinaire est la Moscovite, mais ils entendent le Tartare, & le parlent même en quelques endroits. Ils n'ont ni Prêtres ni Eglises, ni ne célèbrent aucun des mistéres de l'Evangile.
p.s: Jan Struys (French translation by Glanius, Amsterdam 1681)
p.pl: Middle Volga, between Nizhny Novgorod and Kazan
p.t: These peoples are rough, coarse and stupid … Their ordinary language is Muscovite [Russian], but they understand Tartar and even speak it in some places. They have neither priests nor churches, nor do they celebrate any of the mysteries of the Gospel.
p.c: Much of the Cheremis chapter follows Olearius, so this may be borrowed rather than observed.

p.h: 'Water Tatars' in Manchuria
p.g: Bretschneider summarises the Ming imperial geography of 1461 on the Jurchen homeland: after the Mongols overthrew the Jin, the Yuan set up military posts there, and the country was inhabited by Jurchens and 'Water Tatars', who gave their name to an administrative circuit. His footnote compares Carpini's 'Su-Mongal' or Water Mongols, who Carpini said called themselves Tartars after a river.
p.q: The country was inhabited by the Nü-chi and the Shui Ta-ta (Water Tatars), and formed the circuits of Ho-lan-fu and Shui Ta-ta.
p.s: E. Bretschneider, Mediaeval Researches vol. 2 (1888, reissued 1910), summarising the Ming Geography of 1461
p.c: A 19th-century summary in English of a Ming source, not the Yutang jiahua itself.
p.tg: water tatars shui dada jurchen manchuria ethnonym

p.h: The Tartar invasions, from Attila to the Uzbeks
p.g: Burnes opens a chapter 'On the Inroads of the Tartars' by lumping together Attila, Alaric, Genghis, Timur and the Uzbeks as expressions of 'the ever-wandering spirit of the Tartar people'. He places their homeland beyond the Jaxartes (Syr Darya) rather than in northern China. It shows the romantic, racial idea of 'the Tartar' that educated Britons held in the 1830s.
p.q: Attila and Alaric spread devastation in the empire of the Caesars. Jengis and Timour have succeeded them in more modern but equally destructive inroads. Through these great revolutions we trace the ever-wandering spirit of the Tartar people
p.s: Alexander Burnes (1834)
p.pe: Tartars as a catch-all for steppe conquerors
p.c: Burnes's own generalisation; Alaric was a Goth, not a steppe nomad.
p.tg: invasions attila genghis khan timur stereotype

p.h: 'Since our shan yu': the Mongols and the Xiongnu past
p.g: In the same letter Chinggis lists the peoples who have acknowledged him (the Song, the Hui-ho, the Tangut Xia and 'the barbarians in the west') and says no empire so vast has been seen 'since the remote time of our shan yu'. Bretschneider explains that shan yu was the title of the khans of the ancient Xiongnu of Mongolia from the second century BC, so the letter sets the Mongols in a line of steppe rulers reaching back to Han times. The diarist makes the same comparison at the Empress's ordo, whose carts and tents outshone anything the ancient shan yu had (p.58).
p.q: The Sung to the south, the Hui-ho to the north, the Hia … to the east, and the barbarians in the west, all together have acknowledged my supremacy. It seems to me that since the remote time of our shan yü such a vast empire has not been seen.
p.s: Letter issued in Chinggis Khan's name (1219), written in classical Chinese by a secretary and preserved in the Cho keng lu (translated by E. Bretschneider, 1888)
p.c: A boast: the Song never submitted to Chinggis, and Bretschneider notes the directions are muddled. 'Our shan yu' may be the Chinese secretary's classical vocabulary rather than Mongol tradition.

p.h: Thirty 'Tartarian' languages from the Black Sea to Japan
p.g: Strahlenberg announces the first part of his planned work: a comparative table of thirty languages spoken between the Black Sea and the Sea of Japan, which he calls the 'Tartarian' languages. He explains that the many peoples of Siberia and Tartary each have their own language besides the main languages used among them, and a footnote adds that they therefore cannot all properly go under the name of Tartars.
p.q: Das erste nun, ist ein Specimen Harmoniae linguarum Tartaricarum, bestehend in 30 Sprachen, die sich anheben von dem Schwartzen und sich endigen bey dem Japanischen Meer. … (indem unterschiedliche Völckerschaften in Siberien und der Tartarey vorhanden sind, welche nebst denen Haupt-Sprachen, so unter ihnen gebräuchlich sind, ihre eigene oder particuliere daneben haben)
p.s: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (Vorbericht, Stockholm 1726)
p.pe: Peoples of Siberia and 'Tartary' (Turkic, Mongolic, Uralic and others)
p.t: The first, then, is a Specimen of the Harmony of the Tartarian Languages, consisting of 30 languages, which begin at the Black Sea and end at the Sea of Japan. … (since various peoples live in Siberia and Tartary who, besides the main languages in use among them, have their own particular ones as well)
p.c: The OCR of this copy is badly garbled Fraktur; the quote has been restored letter by letter from the damaged text, so check the scan.
p.n: The scan's machine-read text is too damaged to confirm this quote automatically. Check it against the page.

p.h: The emperor of China is the 'Grand Cham of Tartary'
p.g: In his opening words Nieuhof explains that the Company sent its envoys to Peking 'to the Grand Cham of Tartary, the now Emperour of China'. The old European title for the Mongol Great Khan is simply transferred to the new Manchu ruler of China, the Shunzhi emperor. This is the vocabulary later writers like Witsen and Dapper inherited.
p.q: with Credentials, and a considerable train of Attendants, to Peking in China, to the Grand Cham of Tartary, the now Emperour of China, impowering to negotiate concerning a Free and Mutual Commerce with them in his Kingdoms and Territories.
p.s: Johan Nieuhof (English translation by John Ogilby, 1669)

p.h: Four Mongol peoples, one of them called Tartars after a river
p.g: After the Astrakhan Tatars, the text turns to the history of the Mongols, retelling medieval reports: the khan's seal read 'One God in heaven and one Khan on earth', and Batu's army counted 160,000 Tartars and 440,000 Christians and others. It then lists four Mongol peoples, including the 'Saniongals' or water Mongols (the Su-Mongals of Carpini), who were also called Tartars after the river Tartar.
p.q: Dieses Mongalen Land lieget nach Osten und ist … vier unterschiedene Völcker bewohnet; nemlich die … die Saniongals oder See-Mongalen, welche auch nach den … Tartar, Tartern genennet werden; die Merkates … Diese vier Völcker waren in der Sprache und Lebens-Art … ziemlich ähnlich, hatten aber jede ihr eigen Ober-Haupt.
p.s: Compiled historical note in the de Bruyn extract printed in Weber (after Plano Carpini)
p.t: This Mongol land lies to the east and is inhabited by four different peoples, namely the … the Saniongals or water Mongols, who are also called Tartars after the [river] Tartar; the Merkits … These four peoples were fairly similar in language and way of life, but each had its own chief.
p.c: Book learning from medieval sources, not observation; the OCR has gaps.

p.h: The Nogais: a splinter of the Golden Horde
p.g: Crossing the Nogai steppe she explains the horde's name: the Nogais split from the Golden Horde under a leader called Nogai, which, she suggests, let them escape Timur's destruction of the Horde in the 1380s and 1390s. She adds that Russian rule has greatly changed them since earlier travellers' accounts.
p.q: The Nogay Tartars, who have wandered for some ages in this desert (a part of the primitive or little Scythia of the ancients), were originally a subdivision of the famous golden horde placed in the Kaptchak by the conqueror Zingis Chan, (properly Tschinghis), who, on some quarrel among themselves, separated from the main body of their nation, under a chief or general named Nogay
p.s: Maria Guthrie (letter, translated by Matthew Guthrie, 1802)
p.tg: nogai golden horde origins genghis khan

p.h: A Manchu and a Budjak Tartar: one name, 1,500 leagues apart
p.g: In his opening essay de Tott argues that government shapes peoples more than climate. His example shows how widely 'Tartar' stretched in his day: a Manchu from beyond China and a Tatar from Bessarabia share the name and, he claims, the same kind of government.
p.q: Bring together a Manchou and a Bass-Arabian Tartar, you will search in vain the interval of fifteen hundred leagues that separates their countries: the climate differs but little; the government is the same.
p.s: Baron de Tott (Preliminary Discourse, English translation, 1785)
p.c: A rhetorical generalisation, not an observation.

p.h: Descended from the Mongols, not the Tartars
p.g: Asking where the Kamchadals came from, Krasheninnikov separates the 'Mungals' from the 'Tartars who live upon the river Amur'. His reasoning: if they had come from the Tartars they would have settled on the empty, fertile Lena rather than cold Kamchatka. He also claims the Mungals had used iron for two thousand years while 'the other Tartars' made knives and daggers of copper, yet the Kamchadals knew no iron at all.
p.q: The following reasons incline us to think that they take their origin from the Mungals, not from the Tartars who live upon the river Amur, nor from the Kuriles or Japanese; for if they had sprung from the Tartars it is probable they would have settled about the river Lena
p.s: Stepan Krasheninnikov (translated by James Grieve, 1764)
p.c: Scholarly speculation. The Kamchadals' own tradition, as he reports on the previous page, was that they were created on the spot.

p.h: 'Manchu Tartars' who conquered China
p.g: At Irkutsk, explaining the history of Russia's trade with China, Lesseps dates its beginnings to the invasion of the 'Manchu Tartars', who ravaged northern China for a long time and finally conquered the whole empire. Here 'Tartar' plainly means the Manchus.
p.q: Les relations primitives datent du milieu du dernier siècle, vers l'époque de l'invasion des Tartares Mantchoux, qui, après avoir ravagé pendant long-temps les provinces septentrionales de l'empire Chinois, finirent par le subjuguer entièrement.
p.s: Jean-Baptiste Barthelemy de Lesseps
p.t: The first relations date from the middle of the last century, around the time of the invasion of the Manchu Tartars, who, after ravaging the northern provinces of the Chinese empire for a long time, ended by subjugating it entirely.

p.h: The Tomsk Tatars call themselves Chat
p.g: Stopping in the Muslim Tatar village of Kaltai near Tomsk, Pallas notes that the six or seven hundred Tatar families of the Tomsk area call themselves Tschaty and differ little from the Kazan Tatars in dress, customs and religion. Their women wear a closed cap over the veil, and girls wear up to thirty braids at their wedding.
p.q: Die hier wohnenden Tataren, deren in und um Tomsk in allem etwan sechs bis sieben hundert Familien wohnen, nennen sich Tschaty und sind in ihrer Tracht und Sitten, so wie in der Religion, von den Casanischen wenig unterschieden.
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas (Reise, first edition, St Petersburg 1771-1776)
p.t: The Tatars living here, of whom about six to seven hundred families in all live in and around Tomsk, call themselves Tschaty and differ little from those of Kazan in their dress and customs, as in their religion.

p.h: Jochi's share: 'as far as the hoof of the Tatar horse has reached'
p.g: Describing how Chinggis Khan divided his realm among his sons, Juvaini says the eldest, Jochi, received everything from Qayaligh and Khwarazm to the far edge of Saqsin and Bulghar on the Volga, and westward 'as far as the hoof of the Tatar horse has reached'. This is the land that became the Golden Horde. Here 'Tatar' is simply another word for the Mongol cavalry.
p.q: و پسر بزرگتر توشی‌را از حدود قیالیغ و خوارزم تا اقصای سقسین و بلغار و از ان جانب تا انجا که سم اسب تاتار رسیدست بدو داد
p.s: Ata-Malik Juvaini (Persian text, ed. Mirza Muhammad Qazvini, 1912)
p.pe: Jochi (Tushi) and the Mongols, called Tatars
p.t: And to his elder son Tushi he gave the lands from the region of Qayaligh and Khwarazm to the farthest parts of Saqsin and Bulghar, and in that direction as far as the hoof of the Tatar horse has reached.
p.tg: jochi golden horde bulghar saqsin tatar as mongol

p.h: Where the Dobruja Tatars came from
p.g: Schlözer tells how the Tatars, after wasting Russia, had settled on the steppe on both sides of the Dnieper and ruled Podolia through their baskaks (governors), until Grand Duke Olgerd of Lithuania beat three Tatar khans at Siniawoda (the Blue Waters) and cleared them from the land as far as Ochakiv. The survivors, he says, settled on the Dobruja plains by the Danube, where their descendants still remembered that the Lithuanians had driven their ancestors out of Podolia. Olgerd's nephews then built castles in the freed land.
p.q: Die dem Schwerdt entflohen, ließen sich hierauf in den Dobruczer Ebenen an der Donau nieder, wo ihre Nachkommen … auch noch wissen, daß ihre Vorfahren durch die Littauer aus Podolien vertrieben worden.
p.s: August Ludwig Schlözer (1785), following Kojałowicz
p.pe: Golden Horde Tatars of Podolia; the Dobruja Tatars
p.t: Those who escaped the sword then settled on the Dobruja plains on the Danube, where their descendants … still know that their forefathers were driven out of Podolia by the Lithuanians.
p.c: Schlözer keeps his chronicle source's date of 1331; the battle of the Blue Waters is now usually dated 1362. The Dobruja tradition is reported, not checked.
p.tg: podolia dobruja blue waters olgerd exile

p.h: 'Kalmyk' means the ones who stayed behind
p.g: Strahlenberg rejects the view, in the French edition of Abulghazi, that 'Kalmyk' was an insult aimed at their religion. He says the name was given to them in the Tatar language and means a people that remained behind, from 'kal' (I stay) and 'umak' (tribe). A similar 'those who remained' explanation is still often repeated today.
p.q: den Nahmen von Kallmack erhalten, welches kein Scheltwort ihrer Religion halber ist, wie der Autor … remarquiret … sondern es bedeutet und heisset ein Volck oder Geschlecht, so nach- oder dableibet, denn Kall oder Call, heisset ich bleibe da oder nach, und Amack oder Umack ein Geschlecht, daher per syncop: Kallmack oder Kallmuck.
p.s: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (Vorbericht, Stockholm 1726)
p.t: received the name Kallmack, which is not a term of abuse on account of their religion, as the author remarks … but it means and signifies a people or tribe that stays behind or remains there, for Kall or Call means 'I stay there or behind', and Amack or Umack a tribe; hence by syncope Kallmack or Kallmuck.
p.c: The OCR of this copy is badly garbled Fraktur; the quote has been restored letter by letter from the damaged text, so check the scan.
p.n: The scan's machine-read text is too damaged to confirm this quote automatically. Check it against the page.

p.h: 'Hu': the Chinese word the translator turns into Uighurs or Tartars
p.g: The royal family of Tashkurgan in the Pamirs looked Chinese but dressed like the 'Hu'. Hu was a broad Chinese word for foreigners of the west and north. Beal adds '(Uighurs)' here, and in his index he lists 'Tartar (Hu) pilgrims', so the English 'Tartar' in this book is often the translator's choice for a Chinese catch-all word, not Xuanzang's.
p.q: The members of the royal family in appearance resemble the people of the Middle Country (China). They wear on their heads a square cap, and their clothes are like those of the Hu people (Uighurs).
p.s: Xuanzang and Bianji (translated by Samuel Beal, 1884; '(Uighurs)' is Beal's gloss)
p.pe: Hu (western and northern foreigners), glossed by Beal as Uighurs
p.c: The bracketed identification is the translator's, not the pilgrim's.

p.h: Kalmyk chiefs who fled Russia for China
p.g: At the emperor's birthday theatricals most of the guests who came to meet the British envoy were Tartars, since few Chinese were invited to Zhe-hol. Among them were two chiefs of 'Calmoucks' whose people had recently left Russian rule on the Caspian and migrated to Chinese Tartary, an event of 1771.
p.q: Most of them were Tartars ; few original Chinese being invited to Zhe-hol. There were likewise two Mussulmen, chiefs of some hordes of Calmoucks, who, not long since, on occasion of discontent or misunderstanding with the government of Russia, migrated in great numbers from the northern coast of the Caspian sea into Chinese Tartary, and put themselves under the Emperor's protection.
p.s: George Leonard Staunton
p.pe: Manchus and Mongols at court; Kalmyks from the Volga
p.c: The Kalmyks (Torghuts) who made the 1771 migration were Tibetan Buddhists, so calling their chiefs 'Mussulmen' looks like a confusion.

p.h: Five 'kingdoms of the Tartars' on the road to Bukhara
p.g: In a late summary of his travels, Jenkinson says he went forty days beyond the Caspian through five kingdoms 'of the Tartars' and the lands of the Turkmen and 'Zayatay' (Chagatai) to the great city of Bukhara. The editors' note names the five as Mangishlak, Vazir, Urgench, Kath and Bukhara. Here 'Tartar' covers the Muslim Turkic states of Central Asia.
p.q: of the Tartars, and all the land of Turkenian and Zayatay, and so to the great citie of Boghar, in Bactria, not without great perils and dangers sundry times.
p.s: Anthony Jenkinson, summary of his travels (ed. Morgan and Coote, 1886)
p.pe: Turkmen and Uzbek khanates of Central Asia
p.c: The sentence begins on the previous page ('passed through 5. kingdomes').
p.tg: bukhara chagatai turkmen central asia khanates

p.h: Lord of half the eastern world
p.g: Marignolli opens his travel memories by describing the ruler he was sent to: the Great Khan at Khanbaliq, 'supreme emperor of all the Tartars'. For this Florentine friar the Tartar ruler was not a tent chief but the master of countless cities, languages and peoples. The Khan was Toghon Temur, last Yuan emperor of China.
p.q: missus fui cum Apostolicis literis & donis nuncius & legatus ad Kaam, summum omnium Thartarorum Imperatorem, qui tenet quasi dominium medietatis orbis orientalis, cujus potestas & copia civitatum, terrarum, linguarum, diviciarum, & regiminis infinitorum quodammodo populorum excedit omnem narracionem.
p.s: Giovanni de' Marignolli (Latin text ed. Gelasius Dobner, 1768)
p.pe: Tartars (the Mongol Yuan emperor and his empire)
p.t: I was sent with apostolic letters and gifts as envoy and legate to the Khan, supreme emperor of all the Tartars, who holds lordship over almost half of the eastern world, whose power and wealth in cities, lands, languages, riches and rule over countless peoples is beyond all telling.
p.c: The printed text dates the departure 1334; the mission is otherwise dated to 1338, when Benedict XII answered the Khan's embassy.
p.tg: great khan yuan papal mission empire

p.h: 'Moccoli, that is, Tartar brigands'
p.g: Listing the tolls on the road from Ayas in Lesser Armenia to Tabriz, the capital of the 'lord of the Tartars' in Persia, Pegolotti adds a last charge for the extortion of the 'Moccoli, that is, Tartar brigands' along the way. 'Moccoli' is the Italian merchants' form of 'Mongols', and he treats it as a plain synonym for Tartars. In the Cathay chapter he likewise warns that the road beyond Tana is full of Moccoli, 'that is, armed men'.
p.q: E per forza che fanno i Moccoli, cioè Tartari Scherani per cammino
p.s: Francesco Balducci Pegolotti (ed. G. F. Pagnini, 1766)
p.pe: Moccoli (Mongols) in the Ilkhanate of Persia
p.t: And for the extortion that the Moccoli, that is, Tartar brigands, practise along the road
p.c: The amount of the charge is illegible in this OCR.

p.h: Marco Polo's northern Tartars read as Siberia
p.g: The compiler admits that older books say almost nothing about Siberia, and turns to Marco Polo, who 'entered Tartar service' but never crossed the land himself. He is sure Polo's northern country is what is now called Siberia, and quotes him on its Tartars: ruled by a king of the great khan's line, keeping the old Tartar customs, worshipping an earth god called Natigai, living in no towns but in the open country, and eating only milk and meat.
p.q: In den inwendigen mitternächtlichen Ländern wohnen viele Tartarn, deren König von dem Geschlecht des grossen Kaisers derer Tartaren abstammet; und selbige behalten noch die Sitten und Gewonheiten der alten Tartarn. Sie sind alle abgöttisch, beten einen Gott an, den sie Natigai nennen … Sie wohnen weder in Städten noch Flecken, sondern auf dem Felde zwischen Bergen und Felsen.
p.s: Marco Polo, quoted in German by the anonymous compiler
p.pe: Tartars of the far north (Marco Polo's 'northern Tartars')
p.t: In the inner northern lands live many Tartars, whose king descends from the family of the great emperor of the Tartars; and they still keep the manners and customs of the old Tartars. They are all idolaters and worship a god whom they call Natigai … They live neither in towns nor in villages, but in the open country between mountains and rocks.
p.c: A thirteenth-century report of the Mongol north, applied by the compiler to Siberia in 1720.
p.tg: marco polo natigai no towns siberia

p.h: Bashkirs, 'the shaven heads'
p.g: Erman argues that the Bashkirs are the 'bald-headed' Argippaei described by Herodotus, and that Herodotus's travellers mistook their shaved heads for natural baldness. He rejects the usual explanation of the name Bashkir as 'bee-head' and offers his own: bash (head) plus a word for shaven, so 'shaven heads'.
p.q: Thus, we shall render the gentile name, Bashkir, as written by the Russians Bashkuirtsi, by its natural synonym, shaven heads
p.s: Adolph Erman (translated by W. D. Cooley, 1848)
p.c: Learned speculation. The origin of the name Bashkir is still debated, and 'shaven heads' is not generally accepted.

p.h: Yakuts are Tartars: the Kazan test
p.g: Arriving in Yakutsk in October 1822, Cochrane states that the Yakuts are 'evidently of Tartar origin, as their language is understood by the Tartars of Kazan'. He praises them as ingenious smiths who make their own knives, guns and kettles, living mostly on horse-flesh, but also describes them with the harsh prejudice of his day.
p.q: They are evidently of Tartar origin, as their language is understood by the Tartars of Kazan. Their complexion is a light copper colour; they are generally of low stature, with more regular and pleasing features, than the Tongousi
p.s: John Dundas Cochrane (1824)
p.c: He repeats a common claim rather than testing it himself (compare Sarychev, W009). The rest of his character sketch is prejudiced.

p.h: A Moghul khan with a full beard and a Tajik face
p.g: A Muslim scholar expected Yunus Khan, as a 'Moghul', to be a beardless desert Turk, and was surprised to find an elegant man with a full beard and a Persian-looking (Tajik) face. The editor uses the story to show how far the ruling Moghul families had mixed with their Turkic and Persian neighbours.
p.q: I had heard that Yunus Khan was a Moghul, and I concluded that he was a beardless man, with the ways and manners of any other Turk of the desert. But when I saw him, I found he was a person of elegant deportment, with a full beard and a Tajik face
p.s: Maulana Muhammad Kazi, as reported by Mirza Haidar Dughlat (translated by E. Denison Ross, 1895)
p.c: The editor's racial reading ('Aryan') belongs to his time, not to the source.
p.tg: identity appearance yunus khan moghul turk

p.h: Eluth Tartars out, Manchu Tartar emperor in
p.g: Stewart dates Tibet's dependence on China from the 'expulsion' of a Tartar people the OCR prints as 'Ehatli', almost certainly the Eluths (the Dzungar Oirats who seized Lhasa in 1717 and were driven out in 1720). On the same page he calls the Chinese emperor 'a Mantchou Tartar'. Two very different peoples share one label.
p.q: ever since the expulsion of the Ehatli Tartars, the kingdom of Thibet is regarded as depending on the empire of China, which they call Cathay; and there actually reside two mandarines, with a garrison of a thousand Chinese, at Lahassa the capital,
p.s: John Stewart (Philosophical Transactions, 1777)
p.pe: Eluth (Dzungar Oirat) Tartars; Manchu Tartars of the Qing
p.c: 'Ehatli' is left as the OCR reads it; the identification with the Eluths is ours, not Stewart's.

p.h: Tokhtamysh, 'a certain tsar from the east, from the Blue Horde'
p.g: After his defeat at Kulikovo, Mamai heard that 'a certain tsar from the east named Tokhtamysh, from the Blue Horde' was coming against him. They met on the Kalka and Mamai lost. The passage shows the Rus knew the Horde as several 'hordes' with colours, and treated a new khan from the east as a stranger.
p.q: и се пріиде ему вѣсть, что идеть на него нѣкый царь съ востока, именемъ Тахтамышь, изъ Синіе Орды. Мамай же, еже уготова на великого князя Дмитреа Ивановича рать, съ тою ратью поиде противу его, и срѣтошася на Калкахъ
p.s: Nikon Chronicle, PSRL vol. 11 (1897)
p.pe: Tokhtamysh, khan from the eastern (Blue) Horde; Mamai
p.t: and news came to him that a certain tsar from the east, named Tokhtamysh, from the Blue Horde, was coming against him. And Mamai, with the army he had prepared against Grand Prince Dmitrii Ivanovich, went against him with that army, and they met on the Kalka
p.c: Historians still argue whether 'Blue Horde' meant the eastern or western wing of the Jochid ulus.

p.h: Why Siberia's rivers have Tatar names
p.g: Spafarii notices that the Irtysh, Tobol, Tura and other Siberian rivers have no Russian names: Russians still use the names the Tatars or Ostyaks gave them before the conquest. The Irtysh, he says, took its name from the Tatars because Kuchum, 'the Tatar tsar', ruled widely along it over Tatars, Ostyaks and other peoples. Even under Russian rule, he adds, a great multitude of Tatars and their faith lived along the river.
p.q: Рѣка Иртышъ имя руское не имѣетъ, для того что Иртышъ именуется по татарски, а не по руски … Такъ же рѣка Иртышъ приняла имя свое отъ Татаръ, потому что Кучюмъ, царь Татарской, владѣлъ по Иртышу пространно и не токмо надъ Татары, но и надъ Остяками и надъ иными иноземцы
p.s: Nikolai Spafarii (ed. Yu. V. Arsenyev, 1882)
p.pe: Siberian Tatars of Kuchum's former khanate
p.t: The river Irtysh has no Russian name, because Irtysh is named in Tatar and not in Russian … So too the river Irtysh took its name from the Tatars, because Kuchum, the Tatar tsar, ruled widely along the Irtysh, and not only over the Tatars but over the Ostyaks and other foreign peoples too

p.h: The emperor of China is an 'East Tartar'
p.g: Ides calls the Kangxi Emperor 'King of China and Tartary' and 'an East Tartar, or Mongalian', and says he favours his own people over the Chinese. On the next page he adds that a Chinese man seeking high office had to 'naturalize himself a Mansur or Tartar', and that most people inside Peking's walls were Tartars. Here 'Tartar' means the Manchus.
p.q: The present … or King of China and Tartary, is an East Tartar, or Mongalian, born in Nieucheu, near the River Sagahen Oula, or Amoer: He governs his Subjects very well, tho' he doth not heartily love the Chinese, but on all occasions prefers his own Nation before them
p.s: Evert Ysbrants Ides (English translation, 1706)
p.c: Two errors: the Manchus were not Mongols, and Kangxi was born in Beijing in 1654, not in Manchuria near the Amur.

p.h: The Manchu 'Tartars' take China and change nothing
p.g: After the rebel Li Zicheng's defeat, a Manchu prince led an army 'of Tartars and many Chinese' through the provinces. The annals, as rendered here, claim the conquerors followed their emperor's line, kept the old tribunals in Peking and simply doubled the posts so that Tartars could hold half; 'China, in changing masters, changed neither its form nor its government'. The passage shows 'Tartar' used plainly for the Manchus.
p.q: Un des princes Man-tchéous se mit à la tête d'une armée formidable, composée de Tartares & d'un grand nombre de Chinois … La Chine, en changeant de maîtres, ne changea ni de forme ni de gouvernement.
p.s: Joseph de Mailla (compiled from Chinese works, edited by Grosier)
p.t: One of the Manchu princes put himself at the head of a formidable army made up of Tartars and a great number of Chinese … China, in changing masters, changed neither its form nor its government.
p.c: An official, pro-Qing view of the conquest, written from Peking under the Manchu dynasty.

p.h: One great khan in Cathay and three Tartar kings
p.g: Hayton closes his history with the Tartar world as it stood when he wrote: a great emperor, Temur Khan, sixth of the line, ruling from the city of Jong in Cathay, and three other Tartar kings, Chapar in Turkestan, Toqta in Comania and Kharbanda (Oljeitu) in Tabriz, who all owe him reverence and take their quarrels to his court. It is a clear picture of 'Tartary' as a family of Mongol states, not a single city or civilisation.
p.q: Le grant empereor des Tartars, celui qui ores tient la seignorie, est només Tamor Can, e est le VI empereor. Au roiaume de Cathaï tient le siege de son empire, en une molt grant cité que est nomée Jong … Encores i a autres trois rois des Tartars, qui ont molt grant puissance, e tous portent reverence e obedience au grant empereor.
p.s: Hayton of Corycus, La Flor des estoires de la terre d'Orient (French text, 1307), ed. Ch. Kohler (1906)
p.t: The great emperor of the Tartars, the one who now holds the lordship, is named Temur Khan, and he is the sixth emperor. He holds the seat of his empire in the kingdom of Cathay, in a very great city called Jong … There are also three other kings of the Tartars, who have very great power, and all pay reverence and obedience to the great emperor.
p.tg: khanates great khan yuan golden horde ilkhanate

p.h: Manchu 'Tartars' on the emperor's pay
p.g: Arriving at the harbour of Kin-chow (Jinzhou), about fifteen leagues from Mukden (Shenyang), Gützlaff was told the Manchus of the area were numerous but lived idly, mostly in the direct or indirect employ of the emperor, a description of the hereditary banner garrisons. He adds that there seemed little jealousy between them and the Chinese labourers, and that the Manchus looked little different from the Chinese.
p.q: The Mantchou Tartars who live hereabouts are numerous, and lead an idle life, being principally in the employ of the Emperor, either directly or indirectly. There seems to be but little jealousy between them and the labouring class of Chinese.
p.s: Karl Gützlaff (1832)
p.c: This comes from 'the persons with whom I conversed', not from his own observation inland.

p.h: Ta-ta: the name in Chinese records
p.g: Klaproth says the Chinese first met the Tatars at the start of the ninth century and called them Ta-ta, later Ta-t'a-öl, a garbled form of 'Tatar' because Chinese has no R. He quotes the Chinese encyclopedia San-tsai t'u-hui of 1604, which places the Ta-ta in the Gobi as descendants of the 'barbarian Yuan' (the Mongols) and counts the Wa-la (Oirats) among them, and concludes that the Tatars were the present Mongols and Oirats (the Kalmyks of Central Asia).
p.q: Die Chinesen, welche die Tatar zu Anfange des neunten Jahrhunderts kennen lernten, nannten sie damals … Ta-ta, und in späteren Zeiten … Ta-t'a-öl, welches die verdorbene Aussprache des Wortes Tatar ist, indem die Chinesen kein R haben … Man sieht aus dieser Stelle deutlich, dass die … jetzigen Mongolen und Ölöten (d. i. Mittelasiatische Kalmücken) waren.
p.s: Julius von Klaproth
p.pe: The Ta-ta (Tatars) of Chinese sources, whom Klaproth identifies with the Mongols and Oirats
p.t: The Chinese, who came to know the Tatars at the beginning of the ninth century, then called them Ta-ta, and in later times Ta-t'a-öl, which is the corrupted pronunciation of the word Tatar, since the Chinese have no R … One sees clearly from this passage that the [Tatars] were the present Mongols and Oelöts (that is, the Kalmyks of Central Asia).
p.c: The Chinese characters are lost in the OCR; Klaproth's translations of Chinese texts were his own.
p.tg: ta-ta chinese sources mongols oirats etymology

p.h: Why 'Tungus' may be a Tatar word for pig-keepers
p.g: In a footnote Bichurin says the word Tungus does not exist in Manchu and no ancient Tungusic ruling house used it. He guesses the Russians took it from the Tatars of the Yenisei, since the Chinese histories say the Tungus peoples bred pigs, still used in shamanic sacrifice, and the Tatar word for pig is 'donguz'. It shows how names for Siberian peoples passed through Tatar speech into Russian.
p.q: Слова: Тунгусъ, нѣтъ въ маньчжурскомъ языкѣ: да и ни одинъ изъ древнихъ тунгузскихъ владѣтельныхъ Домовъ не былъ извѣстенъ подъ симъ названіемъ. Вѣроятно, что Русскіе, первоначально достигнувъ Енисея, заимствовали сіе названіе отъ енисейскихъ Татаръ. … а свинья на татарскомъ языкѣ называется Донгусъ.
p.s: Iakinf (N. Ya. Bichurin), footnote, 1851
p.t: The word Tungus does not exist in the Manchu language, and none of the ancient Tungusic ruling houses was known by this name. Probably the Russians, when they first reached the Yenisei, borrowed this name from the Yenisei Tatars. … and in the Tatar language a pig is called donguz.
p.c: Bichurin's etymology is a guess; linguists still debate the origin of 'Tungus'.
p.n: The scan's machine-read text is too damaged to confirm this quote automatically. Check it against the page.

p.h: Muscovites 'descended from Scythians and Tartars'
p.g: In a hostile character sketch of the Muscovites, Possevino claims that most of them descend from or are mixed with Scythians and Tartars, which in his view explains their cunning and suspicion. He adds that the grand princes' pride grew from the time they freed themselves from the Tartars, 'whose tributaries they had been'. This is Counter-Reformation polemic, not ethnography.
p.q: Ea in Schytis, & Tartaris perspicuè cernuntur, ex quibus cùm pleriq; Moscorum originem ducant, aut constent, mirum non est, quòd hactenus naturam illam non exuerint, quam pietas in alijs nationibus excoluit, ac vicit. … Quæ tria cùm in Magnis Moscouiæ Ducibus ab eo potissimùm tempore fuerint, quo se à Tartaris, quorum erant tributarij, in libertatem asseruerunt
p.s: Antonio Possevino, S.J. (Moscovia, Vilnius 1586)
p.pe: Muscovites; Tartars as their supposed ancestors and former overlords
p.t: These things are plainly seen in the Scythians and Tartars, from whom most of the Muscovites take their origin or of whom they are made up, so it is no wonder they have not yet put off that nature which piety has refined and overcome in other nations. ... Since these three things have been in the Grand Dukes of Muscovy above all from the time when they freed themselves from the Tartars, whose tributaries they had been
p.c: A prejudiced generalisation; 'Scythians and Tartars' is a stock label for steppe peoples, not a genealogy he could check.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR garbled); long s normalized.

p.h: Where China ends and 'Tartary' begins: the Wall at Gubeikou
p.g: On the road north the embassy slept every night in the emperor's own travel palaces, so Hüttner skips the small places, but not the little town on the famous Great Wall 'which forms the border between China and Tartary', called Chu-pa-ku, 'between or at the wall' (Gubeikou). For him the Wall is the line where Tartary starts. He adds that the old Wall had fallen in many places and its towers had no garrisons, and the embassy took away pieces of its stone and mortar as curiosities.
p.q: da wir alle Nächte in den Kaiserlichen Pallästen schliefen, in welchen der Kaiser selbst zu übernachten pflegt … Eine kleine Stadt ist indess zu merkwürdig, als dass ich sie nicht erwähnen sollte. Sie liegt an der berühmten Chinesischen Mauer, welche die Gränze zwischen China und der Tartarei macht, und heisst: Chu-pa-ku, d. i. zwischen oder an der Mauer.
p.s: Johann Christian Hüttner (1797)
p.pl: Gubeikou, Great Wall, Beijing municipality, China
p.t: since we slept every night in the imperial palaces in which the emperor himself is accustomed to stay … One small town, however, is too remarkable for me not to mention it. It lies on the famous Chinese Wall, which forms the border between China and Tartary, and is called Chu-pa-ku, that is, between or at the wall.
p.c: The details on the Wall's decay come from the next, badly scanned pages (p. 48 to 49).
p.tg: great wall border tartary label gubeikou

p.h: One book, many names: 'the Turkish Shahnameh'
p.g: The prose preface of the Herat manuscript says the book was finished 'in the land of Kashgar' and presented to Bughra Khan, who made the author his chamberlain, hence his title Khass Hajib. It boasts that the Chinese called it 'The Manners of Kings', the Iranians 'the Turkish Shahnameh', and the 'Turanians' Kutadgu Bilig. The Turks here are a named people with their own literary language, 'the Turkish tongue' of the eastern lands.
p.q: Die Leute von Cin haben es Adab ul Muluk, Sitten der Fürsten genannt; die Gelehrten des Fürsten von Macin haben Ajn ul Memleket, das Auge des Reiches geheissen; die Morgenländer haben es Zinet un Umera, Zierde der Fürsten betitelt. Die Iranier hiessen es das türkische Schah Nameh
p.s: Anonymous prose preface to the Kutadgu Bilig, in Vambery's German translation (1870)
p.t: The people of Chin called it Adab al-Muluk, 'the manners of princes'; the scholars of the prince of Machin called it Ayn al-Mamlaka, 'the eye of the realm'; the easterners called it Zinat al-Umara, 'the ornament of princes'. The Iranians called it the Turkish Shahnameh.
p.c: The preface is a later addition praising the book, not the author's own words; its claims about foreign names are a boast.
p.n: Checked against the page image.

p.h: The Uzbeks sweep south and take Bukhara
p.g: Elphinstone explains who the Uzbeks were: a people who crossed the Jaxartes (Syr Darya) around 1500 and drove the heirs of Tamerlane out of Bukhara, Khwarazm and Ferghana. The next sentence is badly damaged in the scan, but it seems to say that the Uzbeks belong to the great division of mankind known in Asia as Turks, who together with the Moguls (and a third people whose name is illegible) 'compose what we call the Tartar nation'. So for him 'Tartar' is a European umbrella word for Turks and Mongols together.
p.q: The Uzbeks first crossed the Jaxartes about the beginning of the sixteenth century, and pouring on the possessions of the descendants of Tamerlane, soon drove them from Bokhaura, Khoarizm, and Ferghauna, and spread terror and dismay to the remotest parts of their extended empire.
p.s: Mountstuart Elphinstone (1815)
p.c: Page is heavily garbled; the words after this sentence can only be read in part.

p.h: 'The ferocity of Tartar blood' in a Persian prince
p.g: Describing the Shah's eldest son, Mohammad Ali Mirza, Jaubert notes that he was born of a Khwarazmian slave woman and says 'the ferocity of Tartar blood' had shown in him since childhood, though he was also precociously brave. Here 'Tartar' marks a mother from Khwarazm, south of the Aral Sea, and carries the old stereotype of Tartar savagery.
p.q: Mehemed-Aly-Mirza, que les partisans de son compétiteur appellent Myr-Aly-Khan, fils aîné de Feth-Aly-Chah, est né d'une esclave khouarezmienne; et la férocité du sang tartare, qui coule dans ses veines, s'est fait reconnaître en lui dès son enfance.
p.s: Pierre-Amedee Jaubert
p.t: Mohammad Ali Mirza, whom the partisans of his rival call Mir Ali Khan, eldest son of Fath Ali Shah, was born of a Khwarazmian slave woman; and the ferocity of the Tartar blood that flows in his veins showed itself in him from childhood.
p.c: Court gossip dressed in a racial stereotype; the Qajar dynasty was itself of Turkic origin.

p.h: Turkmens: 'true Tatars' by language and face
p.g: On his second Persian voyage, Gmelin landed among the Turkmens of the Mangyshlak coast. He calls them 'true Tatars' by their language and their faces, and notes that as nomads they had no mosques and prayed in their felt tents, which were like Kalmyk ones but rounder on top. A few pages earlier he records their own origin story, that their Abdal tribe descends from a son born to a woman visited by 'a man from the sun'.
p.q: Nur können sie bey ihrer wandernden Lebensart keine eigentliche Medscheten oder Tempel haben, sondern sie verrichten den Gottesdienst in ihren Filz-Zelten, daher beständig einige Mulla oder Priester unter ihnen herum ziehen … Nach der Sprache sind sie wahre Tataren, nach der Gesichts-Bildung auch.
p.s: Samuel Gottlieb Gmelin (part 4, compiled by P. S. Pallas, 1784)
p.pe: Turkmens of Mangyshlak, east Caspian coast
p.t: But with their wandering way of life they cannot have proper mosques or temples; instead they hold their services in their felt tents, so that some mullahs or priests are always travelling about among them … By their language they are true Tatars, and by their features too.
p.c: 'Tatar' here is a language label for a Turkic people, not a claim of shared history.

p.h: Tartary begins at Tana on the Don
p.g: In his closing table of distances Jordanus says it is a thousand miles by sea, always eastwards, from Constantinople to 'Tana or Tartary'. Tana was the Italian trading post at the mouth of the Don, in Golden Horde territory, so for a traveller of 1330 'Tartary' started at the Sea of Azov.
p.q: De Constantinopoli usque Tanan vel Tartariam sunt milliaria mille, semper eundo versùs orientem, per mare.
p.s: Jordanus Catalani of Séverac, O.P. (Latin text, ed. Coquebert de Montbret, Recueil de voyages IV, Paris 1839)
p.t: From Constantinople to Tana or Tartary is a thousand miles, going always towards the east, by sea.

p.h: Ruins the Tatars call the 'Shepherds' Fortress'
p.g: On a headland of the Crimean south coast, Hablizl saw the remains of old columns and fallen masonry. The Tatars called the ruins Choban-kale, 'the shepherds' fortress', not after whoever built them but because the herds grazing there used them as a shelter. It is a small example of how Tatar place names often describe present use rather than claim ancient origins.
p.q: Auf dem Gipfel des Vorgebirges sieht man jetzt noch die Trümmer von ehemaligen Säulen und verfallenes Mauerwerk, welche Ruinen von den Tataren Tschoban-kale oder die Hirten-Festung genannt werden, weil sie den dort weidenden Heerden zum Zufluchtsorte dienen.
p.s: Karl Ludwig Hablizl (German translation, 1789)
p.pl: South coast of Crimea, west of Sudak
p.t: On the summit of the headland one still sees the remains of former columns and ruined masonry, which ruins are called by the Tatars Choban-kale, or the Shepherds' Fortress, because they serve as a refuge for the herds grazing there.
