p.h: Water-Mongols who took their name from the river Tatar
p.g: In a footnote Rockhill quotes Carpini's account of the four nations of Mongolia before Genghis Khan. One, the Su-Mongal or 'Water-Mongols', called themselves Tartars after a river named Tatar. Rockhill's longer note on the next page traces the name Tatar back to a Turkic inscription of AD 732 and to Chinese annals.
p.q: That country had once four nations : one called Yeka Mongal, or the Great Mongals, the second called Su-Mongal, or Aquatic-Mongals, though they called themselves Tartars from a certain river which flows through their country and which is called Tatar (or Tartar)
p.s: John of Pian de Carpine, quoted in W. W. Rockhill's footnote (1900)
p.c: Editorial footnote quoting Carpini; the river etymology is one of several medieval guesses.

p.h: Bakhchysarai, 'seraglio of gardens'
p.g: Kohl explains the town's name from the Tatar word for garden and places the Crimean Khanate in history as the last surviving piece of the Mongol empire in Europe. It shows how a nineteenth century writer linked the Crimean Tatars back to the Mongols.
p.q: The word “Baktsha,” signifies in the Tartar language “garden” and the name of Baktshiserai would, therefore, signify “seraglio of gardens.” This city was for centuries the capital of the remarkable state which formed the last fragment of the great Mongolian empire in Europe
p.s: J. G. Kohl (English abridged translation, 1844)

p.h: Why the Tatar ruler is 'khan' and a sultan is a mere prince
p.g: In notes on coins of the last Crimean khan, Shahin Giray, the French orientalists Langlès and Millin explain that among Turks and Persians 'sultan' means sovereign and 'khan' a lesser officer, but among the Tartars it is the reverse, perhaps because 'khan' is a Tartar word found in Kalmyk, Mongol and Manchu. They add that Shahin was the 39th and last khan and descended from Genghis Khan.
p.q: Among the Tartars on the other side, a directly contrary usage prevails, and the sovereign only has a right to the distinction of khan, which he places before his proper names, either it is because the word is originally Tartar, and is to be found, indeed, in the Calmuc dialects, Monghol, Mantchou, &c.; while sultan is Arabian
p.s: Numismatic notes by L. Langlès and A. L. Millin, printed in Reuilly's Travels (English translation, 1807)
p.tg: khan sultan titles coins genghis khan

p.h: The Yakuts are 'of Tartar nation' by their language
p.g: Opening his chapter on the origin of the Itelmens, Steller says the Yakuts belong to the Tartar nation, as their language shows, being a dialect of Crimean Tatar and modern Turkish. It is a clear example of 'Tartar' used as a language family, not a single people, and he notes that the Yakuts knew nothing of Kamchatka or its people.
p.q: Die Jakuten, so von tartarischer Nation, nach Ausweisung ihrer Sprache, so ein Dialect von der krimmischen und heutigen türkischen Sprache ist, wissen nicht das geringste von denen Itälmenen, so wenig als sie von dem Lande Kamtschatka selbsten die geringste Nachricht hatten
p.s: Georg Wilhelm Steller (ed. J. B. Scherer, 1774)
p.t: The Yakuts, who are of Tartar nation as their language shows, which is a dialect of the Crimean and modern Turkish language, know nothing at all of the Itelmens, just as they had not the slightest news of the land of Kamchatka itself

p.h: Kirghiz and Uzbeks: cousins by blood
p.g: The Kirghiz horde Wood visited had come down to winter in Wakhan at the invitation of the Uzbeks of Kunduz, whom they claimed as blood relatives. Wood agrees they are one stock, and puts their differences in build down to climate.
p.q: They had been solicited to do so by the Uzbeks of Kunduz, with whom the Kirghiz profess to be connected by blood. The two people are evidently of the same stock, though the effects of location, or in other words, the difference between a temperate and a rigorous climate is observable in the well proportioned frame of the Uzbek and in the stunted growth of the Kirghiz.
p.s: John Wood
p.c: The climate explanation is Wood's own theory.

p.h: Every northern empire was a 'Tatar confederacy'
p.g: In his memorandum Hastings sketches Tibetan history from Chinese sources and calls every northern power a 'Tatar confederacy': the Typa (Tuoba) in the fourth century, the Turks in the eighth and ninth, and on the next page the Mongols under Möngke Khan. It shows 'Tatar' used as a catch-all for any steppe people in the 1770s.
p.q: In the fourth century, the Tatar confederacy of the Typa subdued the north and east of Tibet. In the eighth and ninth centuries, when the Tatar confederacy of the Turks became feeble, the power of those nations, which now acknowledge the supremacy of the Dalai Lama, was very great.
p.s: Warren Hastings (memorandum on Tibet, 1774)
p.pe: Tuoba, Turks and Mongols, all called Tatars

p.h: The Torghut flight to China, as told by the Panchen Lama
p.g: The Panchen Lama told Bogle he had been busy with Kalmuk business, and explained that some years before 'a tribe of Tatars' subject to Russia had gone over to China (the Torghut exodus from the Volga in 1771), that the Chinese emperor had imprisoned Russian envoys sent to reclaim them, and that war might follow. It shows news of the steppe travelling through Tibetan religious networks.
p.q: He told me that he had been so much engaged with some Kalmuks, and had so much to write on their account, that he had not been able to see me sooner; that several years ago a tribe of Tatars, who were subject to Russia, had gone over to the Chinese
p.s: The Panchen (Teshu) Lama, as reported by George Bogle (edited by Markham, 1876)
p.pe: Torghut Kalmyks (a tribe of Tatars subject to Russia)

p.h: A Manchu 'Tartar' at the Tibetan court
p.g: Turner's most important informant, Soopoon Choomboo, the Panchen Lama's cup-bearer and second officer of the court, was Manchu by birth. Turner calls him a 'Mantchieux Tartar', using the European habit of calling the Manchu rulers of China Tartars. Two pages on he describes his 'Tartar' features: small eyes, thin eyebrows, high cheek bones, no beard.
p.q: Soopoon Choomboo, who was styled also Sadeek, held the second rank in the court of Teshoo Loomboo. He was by birth a Mantchieux Tartar
p.s: Samuel Turner (1800)

p.h: The King of China is a Tartar
p.g: In China, Ibn Battuta says plainly who ruled: the king was a Tartar, a descendant of the Genghis Khan who had laid waste to Muslim lands. He adds that every Chinese province had a separate town for Muslims, with their own mosques, and that the kings honoured them.
p.q: The King of China is a Tartar, and one of the descendants of Jengiz Khan, who entered the Mohammedan countries, and desolated many of them. In all the Chinese provinces, there is a town for the Mohammedans, and in this they reside.
p.s: Ibn Battuta (translated by Samuel Lee, 1829)

p.h: Russian labels: the Tatars of Tobolsk, Tomsk, the Ob and Krasnoyarsk
p.g: Rémusat explains the Siberian 'Tatars': southern Siberia is full of Turkic nations, partly descended from armies the Mongols brought in the thirteenth century and partly older inhabitants. The Russians who conquered them in the late sixteenth century call most of them simply Tatars, adding the name of the town or district where they live: Tatars of Tobolsk, of Tom, of the Ob, of Krasnoyarsk.
p.q: Les Russes qui les ont soumis à la fin du xvi.e siècle, les désignent, pour la plupart, par le nom commun de Tatars, auquel ils ajoutent celui de la ville ou du canton où ils les trouvent fixés. C'est ainsi qu'ils distinguent les Tatars de Tobolsk, de Tom, de l'Obi, de Krasnoyar, ceux du Tchoulim
p.s: Jean-Pierre Abel-Rémusat
p.t: The Russians, who subdued them at the end of the sixteenth century, call most of them by the common name of Tatars, to which they add the name of the town or district where they find them settled. Thus they distinguish the Tatars of Tobolsk, of the Tom, of the Ob, of Krasnoyarsk, those of the Chulym

p.h: Dagestan Tartars versus Lezgi Tartars
p.g: Cook admits writers were confused about the peoples of the eastern Caucasus and sets his own rule: 'Dagestan Tartars' for the hill people between Derbent and Circassia, 'Lezgi Tartars' for those south and south-east of Derbent to the Kura. It shows 'Tartar' being used simply as a label for Muslim mountaineers who spoke many languages.
p.q: The difference between the Dagestan and Lesgee Tartars, I think is not clear in authors; I therefore desire my readers to remember, that I call the Dagestan Tartars, those who inhabit the hills between Derbent and Circassia; and I call those who inhabit the hills south, and south-east of Derbent, all the way to the north banks of Cura, Lesgee Tartars.
p.s: John Cook (published 1770)

p.h: Our Tartars: the missionaries' drivers
p.g: The 'Tartars' who appear on almost every page of the journey are the two hired drivers of the missionaries' carts, not the Kalmyks of the title. Both spoke Russian; the elder, Andre, also spoke Kalmyk and had been baptised in the Orthodox Church, while the younger was a Muslim. Later Zwick notes that Andre spoke the dialect of the Kazan Tatars.
p.q: To transport our copies of Scripture, which were packed in chests, we bought a couple of two-wheeled Tartarian carts, (called arba,) with the requisite horses and tackle, and hired two Tartars as drivers. They both understood Russian, and Andra, the elder of the two, was acquainted with the Calmuc tongue also. He had been baptized into the Greek Church, in his youth ; the other was a Mahometan.
p.s: Heinrich August Zwick (English edition, 1831)

p.h: A Khan descended from Genghis
p.g: Coxe describes Muscovy's early raids into western Siberia, when 'Tartar tribes' paid tribute, and one chief, Yediger, promised a thousand sables a year. Yediger was then overthrown by Kuchum Khan, whom Coxe identifies as a direct descendant of Genghis Khan who had only recently founded his realm there.
p.q: Some Tartar tribes were indeed laid under contribution; and a chief, whose name was Yediger, consented to pay an annual tribute of a thousand sables. But this expedition was not productive of any lasting effects; for soon afterwards Yediger was defeated, and taken prisoner by Kutchum Chan; the latter was a lineal descendant of the celebrated Zinghis Chan
p.s: William Coxe (compiling G. F. Müller)

p.h: Attila's court, seen as a Kalmyk khan's household
p.g: Bergmann argues that the Huns were a Mongol people. He compares Jordanes' description of Hunnic faces with the Kalmyks, and says that reading Priscus' account of his embassy to Attila feels like entering a Kalmyk khan's dwelling: the ruler on a raised seat facing the door, guests ranked on his right and left, and Attila eating from a wooden bowl while his guests used silver and gold. He goes on to explain Hunnic names from Mongol words.
p.q: Der Gesandte erblickt ihn dem Eingange gegenüber auf einem erhabenen Lager; ganz wie bey den Kalmüken und bey allen mongolischen Völkerschaften. Die Gesandten setzen sich, wie bey den Kalmüken, zu beiden Seiten des Fürsten, die vornehmsten rechts, die übrigen links. … aber Attila folgt der Sitte seines Volks, wenn er das dargebrachte Fleisch aus einer hölzernen Schaale speist, und sein Getränk aus einem hölzernen Becher trinkt.
p.s: Benjamin Bergmann, paraphrasing Priscus
p.pe: Huns, whom Bergmann identifies with the Mongols
p.t: The envoy sees him opposite the entrance on a raised couch, just as among the Kalmyks and all Mongol peoples. The envoys sit, as among the Kalmyks, on both sides of the prince, the most distinguished on the right, the others on the left. … but Attila follows the custom of his people when he eats the meat offered to him from a wooden bowl and drinks from a wooden cup.
p.c: Bergmann's own theory, built on comparing ancient texts with what he saw among the Kalmyks.

p.h: A hundred cities, none with a Chinese name
p.g: Heading west past the Tangut frontier, the envoy says he passed more than a hundred cities with no Chinese names and was told of many tribes living there. The list runs on over the page (Mo-li-hi, Mo-k'o-ti, Ho-li-ki-sz, Nai-man, Hang-li, Gui-gu, T'u-ma, Ho-lu), ending 'all are barbarian tribes'. Bretschneider identifies them as the Merkits, perhaps the Mekrins, the Kirghiz, Naimans, Kankali, Uighurs, Tumats and Karluks, peoples Chinggis had just brought under his rule. None of them is called Mongol or Tatar.
p.q: I passed through more than a hundred cities: not one of them had a Chinese name. Inquiring about the country, I was told that many tribes were living there, namely, the Mo-li-hi
p.s: Wu-ku-sun Chung-tuan (Wugusun Zhongduan), as written down by the recorder of the Pei shi ki (translated by E. Bretschneider, 1888)
p.pe: Steppe tribes: Merkits, Kirghiz, Naimans, Kankali, Uighurs, Tumats, Karluks
p.c: Bretschneider warns that the envoy's route and distances are too vague and exaggerated to trace, and that his line about rivers flowing east and west is copied from the Han history.

p.h: The 'Bogdoi Tartars' who rule China
p.g: Describing the borders of Siberia, Perry notes that the Great Wall was built against the 'bordering Tartars', who about seventy years before had conquered China anyway, and that the 'Chams of Great Tartary', called the Bogdoi Tartars, were still emperors of China. 'Bogdoi' comes from the Mongol title Bogd Khan used for the Qing emperor.
p.q: …to defend them from the Incursions of the bordering Tartars, who have notwithstanding, about 70 Years since, made themselves Masters of the Countrey; and the Chams of Great Tartary, who are called the Bogdi Tartars, continue Emperors of China to this Day.
p.s: Captain John Perry (The State of Russia, 1716)
p.tg: manchus qing bogdoi great wall china

p.h: Were the builders of Madzhari Tatars? Gmelin guesses 'Scythians'
p.g: Gmelin admits he knows too little medieval history to say who lived at Madzhari. He reports that in 1735, when Tatars still held the district, the Astrakhan governor Tatishchev sent an armed party to search the ruins and received a writing on blue, very strong paper and some coins, which Tatishchev took for 'Scythian'. Gmelin guesses a 'Scythian tribe called Madshar' lived there and mentions a claim that the Ingush of the Caucasus descend from them. On the previous page he says the Tatar grave mounds around the site probably did not belong to Madzhari, since the Madzharians 'were probably not Tatars'.
p.q: Der ehemalige Astrachanische Gouverneur von Tatistschew schickte im Jahr 1735, als die Tataren diese Gegend noch inne hatten, einige Leute … zur Untersuchung der Madsharischen Ruinen … Man brachte ihn eine Schrift auf blauen, sehr festen Papier, und verschiedene Münzen, welches dieser Geschichtsforscher für Scytische hielt. … Vermuthlich wohnte hier ein Scythischer Stamm der Madshar hieß
p.s: Samuel Gottlieb Gmelin (part 4, compiled by P. S. Pallas, 1784)
p.t: The former Astrakhan governor Tatishchev sent some people in 1735, when the Tatars still held this district, … to investigate the Madzhari ruins … They brought him a writing on blue, very strong paper and various coins, which this historian took for Scythian. … Presumably a Scythian tribe called Madshar lived here
p.c: An open guess by Gmelin. Modern archaeology treats Madzhari as a Golden Horde trading town, so 'Scythian' here reflects 18th-century uncertainty.

p.h: The 'raw-eaters' come with their wives
p.g: In 1257 'evil news' reached Novgorod that the Tatars wanted the tamga (a trade tax) and a tithe. In the winter of 1259 the Tatar officials Berkai and Kasachik arrived with their wives and many others. The chronicler calls them 'accursed Tatar raw-eaters' (syroyadtsy), a standard insult for steppe nomads.
p.q: Приде вѣсть изъ Руси зла, яко хотять Татарове тамгы и десятины на Новѣгородѣ, и смятошася люди черезъ все лѣто. … Тои же зимы приѣхаша оканьнии Татарове сыроядци, Беркаи и Касачикъ, съ женами своими, и инѣхъ много
p.s: Novgorod First Chronicle (PSRL vol. 3, 1841)
p.pe: Tatar officials of the Golden Horde (Berkai and Kasachik)
p.t: Evil news came from Rus that the Tatars wanted the tamga and the tithe from Novgorod, and the people were in turmoil all through the summer. … That same winter the accursed Tatar raw-eaters arrived, Berkai and Kasachik, with their wives, and many others
p.c: 'Raw-eaters' is an insult, not a description the chronicler checked.

p.h: Kalmyks and the hadith of the Turks
p.g: Evliya lists the many spellings of the Kalmyk name and says all historians call them the 'yellow folk' (Bani Asfar). He applies to them a hadith about God's soldiers in the east 'whose name is Turk'. He adds that twenty years earlier the Kalmyks were not on this steppe and 140 Nogay tribes grazed it, sending butter to Taman to be sold cheaply in Istanbul; when the Kalmyks arrived the Nogays were routed and butter became dear.
p.q: قالمق وقالماق وقلماق وقلماخ وقلماغ جمیع مورخان بونلره بنی عصفر قومی درلر ... حتی بوقالمق قومی یکرمی سنه مقدم بوهیهات صحراسنده وجودلری اولمیوب جمله نوغای قومنك یوز قرق عدد قبیله‌لری صحرای هیهاتده قنوب کوچوب
p.s: Evliya Celebi (Ottoman text, Istanbul 1928, vol. 7)
p.t: Kalmuk, Kalmak, Kalmaq, Kalmakh and Kalmagh: all the historians call them the people of Bani Asfar [the 'yellow folk'] … Indeed, twenty years ago this Kalmyk people were not present on this vast steppe, and all the hundred and forty tribes of the Nogay people camped and migrated on the open steppe.
p.c: The print reads 'Bani Asfar' with a misprint noted by the editor. The dating of the Kalmyk arrival is roughly right (1630s); the religious framing is Evliya's.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR is partly garbled); bracketed variant markers omitted.

p.h: Where the name 'Tartary' came from: a river, a province or a Syriac word
p.g: Before describing China, the enlarged 1734 edition inserts a compiled chapter on Tartary 'from the most approved historians'. It offers three origins for the name: a river called Tartar, a province of that name mentioned by Hayton, or a Syriac word 'Tartaroye' meaning a numerous nation. It then divides Tartary into old and new, little and great, stretching from Jesso (Hokkaido) to the Sea of Azov, Poland and Russia.
p.q: Die Tartarey, welche etwan von dem Fluß Tartar …, oder nach Haithony Bericht von einer also genannten Provintz, oder von dem syrischen Wort Tartaroye, welches eine zahlreiche Nation bedeutet, seinen Nahmen bekommen, wird von einigen in die alte und neue Tartarey, item in die kleine und grosse, oder in dieß- und jenseits des Bergs Imaus gelegene, eingetheilet
p.s: Compiled chapter in the 1734 enlarged edition of Brand's journey (from earlier historians)
p.t: Tartary, which got its name perhaps from the river Tartar …, or according to Hayton's account from a province so called, or from the Syriac word Tartaroye, which means a numerous nation, is divided by some into old and new Tartary, likewise into little and great, or into that lying on this side and beyond Mount Imaus
p.c: Book learning added to the 1734 edition, not something Brand learned on the road.

p.h: Yurt Tatars, village Tatars and wandering Tatars
p.g: Gmelin explains the Russian names for the Astrakhan Tatars. They were first called 'Yasak Tatars' because after the conquest of the Astrakhan kingdom the tsar took into service all who had deserted the khan and the murzas, and laid a tribute (yasak) on them. They were divided into settled 'Yurt' Tatars and wandering ones, with 'Aul' Tatars for those living in villages, since aul means village in Tatar. He adds that most of the wandering Tatars had joined the Kalmyks or gone off to the Crimea, the Kuban, the Kazakhs and the Bashkirs.
p.q: Jassaschnije Tataren wurden sie anfänglich, … weil der Zaar … nach der Einnahme des Astrachanischen Königreichs alle von dem Chan den Mursas und schwarzen Tataren … abgefallene zu Astrachan in Diensten genommen und mit einem Jassak oder mit einem Tribut belegt hat. Man theilt sie füglich in die Jurtowische und in die Kotschewnyesche ein. Jene sind seßhafte Tataren, diese ziehen Hordenweise … Aul bedeutet in der Tatarischen Sprache ein Dorf.
p.s: Samuel Gottlieb Gmelin
p.t: They were at first called Yasak Tatars, … because after taking the kingdom of Astrakhan the tsar took into service at Astrakhan all who had deserted the khan, the murzas and the black [common] Tatars, and laid on them a yasak, or tribute. They are conveniently divided into Yurt and Kochevye [nomadic] Tatars. The former are settled Tatars, the latter move about in hordes … Aul means a village in the Tatar language.
p.c: Marginal headings break into the OCR lines here and are left out with ellipses.
p.tg: yasak yurt tatars aul nomads tribute

p.h: No river called Tatar
p.g: Medieval writers such as Vincent of Beauvais said the Tartars took their name from a river Tata or Tatar. Strahlenberg asked the Tungus peoples in Siberia and reports that they had never heard of such a river. He himself thought the Tungus and the Manchus were the 'original Tartars' from whom the name spread to others.
p.q: But then his Conjecture as to the Derivation of the Name Tartar, is erroneous, when he supposes they have taken it from a River call'd Tata, which, according to him, runs thro' their Country; … For after all possible Enquiry made among these Nations, I have been able to procure no Intelligence of any such Thing; Their Answer being constantly; that they know of no River call'd either Tata or Tatar.
p.s: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (English translation, 1738)
p.c: His claim that the Tungus and Manchus were the first Tartars is his own theory.
p.tg: etymology tungus manchus vincent of beauvais

p.h: 'Tartar' as a look, not a nation
p.g: Abbott calls the Jamshidis Turkish by descent and 'decidedly Tartar' in their features, using 'Tartar' as a racial type. He adds an insult that recurs in the book: that all Tartars fear artillery.
p.q: The Jumsheedees are of Toorkish descent, as their habits and physiognomy imply. They are short, stout, very dark, with decidedly Tartar features. … They are arrant cowards, and like all Tartars, superstitiously fearful of artillery.
p.s: James Abbott
p.c: Prejudiced generalisation. The Jamshidis are usually counted today among the Persian-speaking Aimaq peoples, not as Turks.

p.h: Philosophers protected by the Great Kam
p.g: The book explains how its peaceful city survives among the Tartars: the Great Kam admires the citizens' honesty and lets them live in peace, and in return they send him a volunteer regiment of 300 young men. That service, the author says, is how they learn the 'Tartarian Language' needed for trade at their fair.
p.q: Now altho' they lye surrounded by the Tartarians, yet are they not at War with any body : For the Great Kam, who has always had a high esteem for them, by reason of their Integrity, permits them to live in Peace and Tranquillity one among another.
p.s: 'Heliogenes de L'Epy' (English translation, 1689)
p.c: Fiction; the 'Great Kam' is the stock European name for a Tartar emperor, used here without any real ruler in view.

p.h: A mountain chain that crosses 'the land of the Tatars'
p.g: Tracing the great mountain chain that ends in Syria, al-Umari starts it in China at the encircling ocean and says it cuts across 'the land of the Tatars' along its mines before reaching Fergana. Here 'land of the Tatars' is simply the Mamluk name for Mongol-ruled inner Asia, much as Europeans used 'Tartary'.
p.q: فإن أوله بالمشرق من الصين من البحر المحيط . فيقطع بلاد التتر على معادنها إلى أن يأتى فرغانة
p.s: al-Umari (Arabic text ed. Ahmad Zaki Pasha, Cairo 1924)
p.pl: Inner Asia, from China to Fergana
p.t: Its beginning is in the east, in China, at the Encircling Ocean. It cuts across the land of the Tatars, along its mines, until it reaches Farghana.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR is partly garbled); vowel marks omitted.
p.tg: bilad al-tatar tartary map label mountains

p.h: Yakut horse-breeders: 'very opulent Tartars'
p.g: Sauer and the Russians around him still called the Yakuts and their neighbours Tartars. Describing the Lena valley, he says the little Russian posts existed to collect fur tribute from 'the wandering tribes of Tartars' nearby. Here, crossing the Aldan on horseback with Yakut guides, he describes the plains as home to 'very opulent Tartars' with huge herds of horses and cattle: the cattle- and horse-breeding Yakuts.
p.q: The woods abound in wild beasts and game; and the plains are inhabited by very opulent Tartars, who possess immense numbers of horses
p.s: Martin Sauer (1802)
p.c: The sentence continues 'and herds of cattle' on the next page.

p.h: The envoy himself: a man 'from Ye-ho in Tartary'
p.g: Tulishen opens by introducing himself as coming originally from Ye-ho in Tartary, meaning the Yehe lands of the Manchu (Jurchen) confederation north-east of China. John Bell, who met him in 1720, called him 'a Mandshu Tartar by birth'. In this book the Chinese court's envoy to the 'Tartar' Kalmyks was himself a 'Tartar', a reminder of how loosely Europeans used the word.
p.q: am originally from the country of Ye-ho in Tartary. My ancestor, O-yen … was a man honorably distinguished in the country of Ye-ho by his fidelity and exertions.
p.s: Tulishen (translated from the Chinese by George Thomas Staunton, 1821)

p.h: Vambery: East Turkestan, 'also called Chinese Tartary'
p.g: In his introduction Vambery places the Uighur homeland in 'today's East Turkestan or Chinese Tartary, as it is also called'. For a nineteenth-century scholar, 'Tartary' is just an older map name for the region where the Kutadgu Bilig was written, next to the modern term. He also claims Samarkand and Karshi as Uighur foundations from the meaning of their names, an etymological guess.
p.q: Wenn wir daher als die Heimat der Uiguren das heutige Ostturkestan oder die Chinesische Tatarei, wie es auch genannt wird, bezeichnen, so muss jedoch bemerkt werden, dass einzelne Colonien sich auch ausserhalb der bezeichneten Grenzen befanden
p.s: Hermann Vambery, introduction to his edition Uigurische Sprachmonumente und das Kudatku Bilik (Innsbruck 1870)
p.t: If we therefore describe the homeland of the Uighurs as present-day East Turkestan, or Chinese Tartary as it is also called, it must be noted that some colonies lay outside these borders.
p.c: Vambery's statement that Samarkand means 'rich city' in Uighur and that it was an Uighur colony is his own speculation.
p.n: Checked against the page image.
p.tg: chinese tartary east turkestan uighurs map name

p.h: Turkish as 'a dialect of Tartar'
p.g: In a note drawn from his own Turkish grammar, Jaubert calls Turkish a dialect of 'Tartar' brought to Constantinople by the Ottomans in 1453, later enriched with Arabic and Persian words. For him 'Tartar' is the name of the whole Turkic language family.
p.q: Comme la langue turque est écrite et parlée dans plusieurs provinces de la Perse, nous croyons devoir insérer ici quelques réflexions extraites d'une grammaire que nous avons composée il y a quelque temps … Cette langue, disons-nous, est un dialecte du tartare, apporté par les Ottomans à Constantinople en 1453.
p.s: Pierre-Amedee Jaubert (footnote from his Turkish grammar)
p.t: Since the Turkish language is written and spoken in several provinces of Persia, we think we should insert here some reflections taken from a grammar we composed some time ago … This language, we say, is a dialect of Tartar, brought by the Ottomans to Constantinople in 1453.
p.c: Turkic speech reached Anatolia with the Seljuks in the 11th century; 1453 is only the Ottoman capture of Constantinople.

p.h: Tartars who look and dress like the Chinese
p.g: Barrow says the Manchu conquerors took over Chinese dress, manners and laws and, being in his view of the same stock, are hardly distinguishable from the Chinese except that they are shorter and stockier. On the following pages he contrasts their blunt, rough character with Chinese ceremoniousness.
p.q: The Tartars, by assuming the dress, the manners, and the habits of the Chinese, by being originally descended from the same stock, and by a great resemblance of features, are scarcely distinguishable from them in their external appearance. And if any physical difference exist, it seems to be in stature only
p.s: John Barrow
p.c: The 'same stock' idea is Barrow's racial theory, not an observation.

p.h: Batu, 'king of kings', and the princes who invaded
p.g: Roger lists the Tartar leaders who entered Hungary. Batu is the 'king of kings'; under him a commander Roger calls Bochetor held most power, and Kadan was the bravest. Several more names follow in garbled Latin forms, and Roger gives the army as 500,000 men. It shows how a Latin writer who had met the invaders understood their chain of command.
p.q: Rex regum et dominus Tartarorum qui Hungariam intrauerunt Bathus suo nomine vocabatur. Rector erat sub ipso in militia potentior Bochetor appellatus. Cadan in probitate melior dicebatur. Coacton Feycan Peta Hermeus Cheb Ocadar maiores reges inter Tartaros censebantur; quamquam essent inter eos alii reges quamplurimi, principes et potentes, qui cum quinquies centenis millibus armatorum regnum Hungariae inuaserunt.
p.s: Master Roger (Rogerius), Carmen miserabile, in the 1885 Budapest edition (Chronica minora)
p.t: The king of kings and lord of the Tartars who entered Hungary was called by name Bathus [Batu]. Under him the commander more powerful in the army was called Bochetor. Cadan [Kadan] was said to be the most valiant. Coacton, Feycan, Peta, Hermeus, Cheb and Ocadar were counted as the greater kings among the Tartars; though there were among them very many other kings, princes and mighty men, who invaded the kingdom of Hungary with five hundred thousand armed men.
p.c: The figure of 500,000 is a wild overestimate. Only Batu and Kadan are securely identified; the other names are Latin garblings of Mongol princes and generals.

p.h: Islam among the Cumans was called 'the Tartar rite'
p.g: Kuun notes that Islam had spread among the Cumans and that later Latin church writers called their religion 'the Tartar rite'. He quotes John, deacon of Kukullo, saying that King Louis I of Hungary had the Cuman people, 'wrapped in the Tartar rite', converted to Catholicism. So in church Latin 'Tartar' could simply mean 'Muslim steppe people'.
p.q: Religio Muhammedanica … etiam apud Cumanos propagata fuit, eam Cumanorum religionem scriptores ecclesiastici latini posteriores «ritum tartaricum» nominabant, ita e. g. Joannes diaconus Küküllőiensis: «Hic etiam gentem Chomanorum, ritui Tartarico involutam … ad fidem Catholicam converti procuravit (scilicet Ludovicus I. rex Hungariae)»
p.s: Geza Kuun, Latin introduction to his edition of the Codex Cumanicus (Budapest 1880), quoting John of Kukullo (14th century)
p.t: The Muhammadan religion … spread also among the Cumans, and later Latin church writers called this religion of the Cumans 'the Tartar rite', for example John, deacon of Kukullo: 'He (namely Louis I, king of Hungary) also had the Cuman people, wrapped in the Tartar rite, converted to the Catholic faith'.
p.c: Kuun's statement that the Cumans were Muslims is his interpretation; many Cumans were pagan.
p.n: Checked against the page image; a dash in the printed quotation is replaced by an omission mark.
p.tg: islam religion tartar rite cumans conversion

p.h: Where 'Tartary' begins on the ground
p.g: Crossing the Akrobat pass north of Bamiyan, Burnes notes that he was leaving the kingdom of Kabul and entering Turkestan, 'which is denominated Tartary (more properly Tatary) by Europeans'. At the next village the first ruler was an Uzbek who paid his overlords partly in slaves taken in raids.
p.q: Toorkistan, which is denominated Tartary (more properly Tatary) by Europeans.
p.s: Alexander Burnes (1834)

p.h: 'Cream of Tartar' and the cream of the Tartars
p.g: Explaining the title 'Kaima-Kan' (the khan's first minister), Craven confesses in a footnote that someone in her party called him 'cream of Tartar', after the chemist's powder. Afraid he would hear of it, she turned it into 'the cream of the Tartars'. A reminder of how English ears played with the word.
p.q: a person called him cream of Tartar … which I fearing he should be told of, turned into the cream of the Tartars
p.s: Elizabeth Craven, footnote (letters published London, 1789)
p.tg: pun cream of tartar kaymakam humour

p.h: Turkic peoples who are called Tartars
p.g: Strahlenberg lists the Turkic-speaking peoples who 'are call'd Tartars': the Budjak, Crimean, Kuban, Kazan and Kasimov Tatars, the Nogais, the Astrakhan and Bashkir Tatars, the Tatars of Tyumen, Tobolsk and Tomsk, the Uzbeks, Turkmens, Kazakhs and others. On the same page he adds that, according to learned Bukharans, they took the name from the original Tartars without being descended from them.
p.q: Secondly, we find, in Europe, the Budziack, and Crimm-Kubann … Casan- and Cassinowan Tartars, and, in little Nagai, Nagaian Tartars: And in Asia and Great Nagai, the Astracan, Ovinian and Baskirian Tartars. … All these are Mahometans: … However, they, like the former, have, as it were, one Dialect with the Turks. All the Nations mention'd in this Paragraph are call'd Tartars.
p.s: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (English translation, 1738)
p.pl: Crimea, Volga, Caucasus, Siberia, Central Asia
p.pe: Turkic-speaking 'Tartars' (Crimean, Kazan, Nogai, Siberian, Uzbek and others)
p.tg: crimean tatars kazan tatars nogais turkic classification

p.h: The Kuban Tartars, raiders subject to the Turks
p.g: Describing the Torghut country between the Volga and the Yaik, Tulishen places to the west the Ho-pang, which Staunton identifies as the Cuban Tartars, also called Mang-vu-te (Mangyt, a Nogai clan name). He says they were subjects of the Turkish sultan and constantly raided both Russians and Torghuts. It shows a Chinese writer mapping the Nogai Tatars by their own clan name.
p.q: lies the country of the Ho-pang (Cuban Tartars) otherwise called Mang-vu-te, a nation subject to Kung-ke-eur Khan, king of the Tu-li-ye-se-ko, (Turks). This people are constantly in the practice of coming across the boundary, in order to attack and plunder their Russian and Tourgouth neighbours.
p.s: Tulishen (translated from the Chinese by George Thomas Staunton, 1821)
p.c: The identification 'Cuban Tartars' is Staunton's gloss in brackets.
p.tg: nogai kuban tatars mangyt ottomans raids

p.h: Timur's four tribal vizirs and the Barlas
p.g: Ibn Arabshah opens his life of Timur by explaining that the Turks, like the Arabs, are divided into tribes. The four chief officers of the Chaghatayid sultan came from four tribes, the Arlat, Jalayir, Qauchin and Barlas, and Timur was the son of the Barlas chief. On the same page he reports a Persian genealogy linking Timur to Chinggis Khan through the female line, and explains Timur's title Gurkan as Mongol for 'son-in-law', since he married royal daughters.
p.q: والترك لهم قبائل وشعب تكاد توازي قبائل العرب وكل واحد من هؤلاء الوزراء كان من قبيلة … احدهم تسمى ارلات وقبيلة الثاني تدعى جلابر وقبيلة الثالث يقال لها قاوجين وقبيلة الرابع اسمها برلاس وكان تيمور ابن رابعهم
p.s: Ahmad ibn Arabshah (Arabic text, print catalogued 1842)
p.t: The Turks have tribes and clans that almost match the tribes of the Arabs, and each of these vizirs was from a tribe … the first of them called Arlat, the tribe of the second called Jalabir [Jalayir], the tribe of the third called Qauchin, and the tribe of the fourth named Barlas; and Timur was the son of the fourth of them.
p.c: Ibn Arabshah wrote as an enemy of Timur. The print misspells Jalayir as Jalabir; the tribal list matches other Timurid sources.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this print is garbled); vowel marks and the asterisk dividers of the rhymed prose omitted.

p.h: A Lhasa ruler 'of ancient Tartar stock'
p.g: The Austrian Jesuit John Grueber reached Lhasa in 1661. As Wessels summarises his report, Tibet then had two kings: a secular governor 'of ancient Tartar stock' who ran the government, and the Dalai Lama, worshipped as a god in his palace. Wessels adds that the Potala was begun in 1642 by the Fifth Dalai Lama, who had risen to power 'with the aid of the Tartar prince Gushi Khan'. The Tartars here are the Qoshot Mongols who held military power in Tibet.
p.q: There are two kings in this kingdom; one, the Deva (Deba), of ancient Tartar stock, carries on the government; the other, who is worshipped as a deity, lives in seclusion within the precincts of his palace. … the energetic Ngavang Lobsang, who from being the head of the Tashi Lhumpo monastery had, with the aid of the Tartar prince Gushi Khan, worked his way up
p.s: C. Wessels (1924), summarising John Grueber's 1661 report (via Kircher) and adding his own historical comment
p.pe: Qoshot Mongols (Gushi Khan and his heirs)
p.c: The first sentence is Wessels's paraphrase of Grueber as printed by Kircher; the Gushi Khan sentence is Wessels's own history, not Grueber's.
p.tg: qoshot gushi khan dalai lama potala grueber

p.h: Khan, sultan, murza: Tartar titles explained
p.g: Herberstein closes his Tartar chapter with a little glossary of ranks: khan (king), sultan (a king's son), murza (a duke's son) and said (chief priest), with other noble grades in between. The same titles run through later Russian records of Tatar nobles. He also names the four great councillors of the Tartar kings.
p.q: The titles of dignity amongst the Tartars are nearly as follows : khan, as I have said above, signifies a king ; sultan, the son of a king ; … mursa, the son of a duke ; … said, a chief priest.
p.s: Sigismund von Herberstein (translated by R. H. Major, 1851-52)
p.c: The OCR garbles several of the rarer titles on this page (bey, noble ranks); check the page image for them.

p.h: Uzbeks replace the 'Turks or Tatars'
p.g: Wolff says that after the 'Turks or Tatars' were driven out, the Uzbeks became the ruling people, brought to the Oxus by Shaybani Khan with their first centre at Urgench in Khiva. He treats 'Turk' and 'Tatar' as one name for the earlier rulers.
p.q: Since the expulsion of the Turks or Tatars, the Usbecks are the dominant people. Sheybek Khan brought them to the country of the river Amoo in the year 1498, when they had the centre of their empire at Organtsh, in Khiva.
p.s: Joseph Wolff
p.c: Wolff's date is approximate; Shaybani Khan's conquest of Transoxiana is usually dated to about 1500 to 1507.

p.h: Turkestan speech sounds like Kazan Tatar
p.g: While in Peking, Timkovsky talked through an interpreter with men from Little Bucharia (the Tarim basin towns) and noticed that their language was very like that of the Kazan Tatars, 'who are also of Turkish origin'. Here 'Tartar' means the Turkic-speaking Muslims of the Volga, a different people entirely from the Mongols he had just crossed.
p.q: In the conversations I had in China, through the medium of an interpreter, with natives of Little Bucharia who had come to Peking, I observed that their language much resembles that of the Tartars of Kasan, who are also of Turkish origin.
p.s: George Timkowski (English translation, 1827)
p.pe: Turkic peoples of Eastern Turkestan; Kazan Tatars

p.h: From Mongol refugees to the kingdom of Niuche
p.g: Martini tells how, after the Ming founder drove the Yuan out in 1368, he carried the war into Tartary itself, and the storm fell chiefly on the province of Niuche 'whither the Tartars of China being expelled were retired'. These Tartars then came to Liaodong every year to trade ginseng, furs and horsehair, multiplied into seven 'Hordes', and about 1550 formed the kingdom of Niuche. Like Grosier later, he blends the Yuan Mongols and the Jurchen into one Tartar story.
p.q: This Storm of War fell chiefly on the Tartars of the Province of Niuche, whither the Tartars of china being expelled were retired.
p.s: Martino Martini (English translation, London 1654)
p.pe: Tartars of Niuche (Jurchen, ancestors of the Manchus)
p.c: The idea that the Yuan refugees became the Jurchen of Niuche is Martini's mistake.

p.h: Manchu 'Tartars' in a Tibetan garrison
p.g: At Gyantse, a small town on the road to Lhasa, Campbell's informants reported a Chinese officer with three or four hundred soldiers, a few of them 'Mantchoo Tartars of the Chinese army' and the rest local Tibetans. Here 'Tartar' is simply the standard English word for the Manchus who ruled Qing China.
p.q: There is a Chinese officer stationed here with 3 or 400 soldiers, a few of whom are Mantchoo Tartars of the Chinese army. The rest are native Tibetans.
p.s: Archibald Campbell, reporting his informants
p.pe: Manchu soldiers of the Qing army ('Mantchoo Tartars')

p.h: 'Moghuls are a tribe of Tartars'
p.g: Correcting an earlier traveller who listed 'Moghuls' among the people of Herat, Fraser explains that Moghuls are properly one tribe of Tartars, and that in India the word was used loosely for Muslims in general because many descended from the Mughal conquerors.
p.q: Moghuls are, in truth, a certain tribe of Tartars, very few of whom could possibly be in Herat as part of its permanent population. Probably Captain Christie inserted this word in his journal somewhat loosely, annexing to it the same meaning which is given to it in Hindostan, where it is often applied to Mussoolmans in general
p.s: James Baillie Fraser (footnote)

p.h: Chinggis Khan hires the Alans to punish the world
p.g: In his world history after Noah, Marignolli derives the Alans from Elam, son of Shem, calls them the noblest nation on earth, and says the Tartars won the Empire of the East only with their help. Chinggis Khan, 'first king of the Tartars', hired 72 of their princes when he set out, by God's command, to chastise the world. The Tartars are fitted into Bible history as God's scourge.
p.q: a quo nobilis generacio Alanorum in oriente dicitur exorta, & est hodie maior & nobilior nacio mundi, & homines pulcriores, & forciores, quorum auxilio Tartari optinuerunt Imperium orientis, & sine quibus nunquam habuerunt victoriam gloriosam. Conduxit enim Cingwis Caam primus Thartarorum Rex de eis LXXII. principes, quando voluit precepto Dei castigare mundum.
p.s: Giovanni de' Marignolli (Latin text ed. Gelasius Dobner, 1768)
p.pe: Tartars (Mongols) under Chinggis Khan, and the Alans
p.t: from whom [Elam] the noble race of the Alans in the East is said to have sprung; and it is today the greatest and noblest nation in the world, the handsomest and strongest men, with whose help the Tartars won the Empire of the East, and without whom they never won a glorious victory. For Chinggis Khan, first king of the Tartars, hired seventy-two of their princes when he wished, at God's command, to chastise the world.
p.c: Biblical genealogy plus praise of the Alans, who were in fact conquered by the Mongols in the 1220s and 1230s rather than hired by Chinggis.

p.h: Scythians under a new name
p.g: Chevalier opens his Tartar chapter by saying the name 'Tartar' was only about four hundred years old and that the people were really the ancient Scythians under a new label. He reports the scholar Leunclavius's view that the name came from a 'River Tartar' in their homeland.
p.q: The Tartars have not been known by this name, but for about four hundred years, and are properly the Scythians; some Authors, as Leunclave and others, derive this name from the River Tartar, in the Countrey where they did inhabit
p.s: Pierre Chevalier (translated by Edward Brown, 1672)
p.pe: Tartars in general, including the Crimean Tatars
p.c: The river etymology is reported from earlier authors, not Chevalier's own finding.

p.h: The Kirghiz: 'their language and faith are Tatar'
p.g: In the Krasnoyarsk district, Spafarii says, the Russian villages and their thousand or so servicemen were always in danger from the Kirghiz: only about a thousand men, but very warlike, 'and their language and faith are Tatar'. Elsewhere he lists the Kirghiz among the 'Tatars' living at the head of the Ket. In Siberian Russian usage 'Tatar' reached well beyond Kuchum's old realm.
p.q: толко всегда опасно отъ Киргызъ: ихъ человѣкъ съ 1000, толко гораздо воисты, и языкъ и вѣра ихъ татарская.
p.s: Nikolai Spafarii (ed. Yu. V. Arsenyev, 1882)
p.t: only it is always dangerous from the Kirghiz: there are about 1000 of them, but they are very warlike, and their language and faith are Tatar.
p.c: He only sailed two days on the Yenisei, so Krasnoyarsk news is hearsay from Yeniseisk.

p.h: The Nogays, a wandering horde made to settle
p.g: Holderness explains who the Nogay Tatars were: the old nomads of 'Nogay Tatary', who had roamed the steppes north of Crimea with tents, flocks and herds for ages. By her time the Russian government had gathered them into villages and pushed them to farm, though they still preferred grazing and horses.
p.q: The Nogay Tatars, if not the original inhabitants of the country, at least wandered over the immense Stepps of New Russia, with their tents, flocks, and herds, at the time of the Russian Conquest, and for ages before: this remnant of the Nomades of Nogay Tatary, are now collected together in a number of villages
p.s: Mary Holderness
p.c: On the next page she describes the Nogays' moral character in very hostile terms, reflecting settler prejudice.

p.h: Crimeans, Nogais and 'the whole nation of the Tartarians'
p.g: An English visitor to Ivan IV's court lists the Tsar's usual enemies: Lithuania, Poland, Sweden, Denmark, Livonia, and three kinds of Tatars. He separates the Crimeans and the Nogais from 'the whole nation of the Tartarians' and praises them all as tough fighters.
p.q: His enemies, with whom he hath warres for the most, are these : Litto, Poland, Sweden, Denmarke, Liefland, the Crimmes, Nagaians, and the whole nation of the Tartarians, which are a stoute and a hardie people as any vnder the Sunne.
p.s: Narrative of the 1557 voyage with the Russian envoy Osep Napea, attributed to Robert Best (ed. Morgan and Coote, 1886)
p.pe: Crimean Tatars, Nogais and other Tatars
p.c: Authorship attribution to Robert Best is the editors' (following Hamel).

p.h: Manning's 'Tatar mandarin' at Lhasa
p.g: Thomas Manning, travelling to Lhasa in disguise, was dismayed to learn that the chief imperial official there was 'the identical Tatar chieftain' who had been disgraced at Canton over the British occupation of Macao in 1808. Throughout his diary 'the Tatar' means this Manchu amban, whom Manning also calls 'the Tatar dog'.
p.q: I had learnt now, to my great sorrow and discomfort, that the chief mandarin at Lhasa was the identical Tatar chieftain who had been disgraced at Canton for his management during the Bengal expedition to Macao. That he was a man of a particular suspicious temper, detested at Lhasa, and that he certainly would give us all the trouble in his power.
p.s: Thomas Manning (diary, edited by Markham, 1876)

p.h: The Himalaya as a 'Tartar bulwark'
p.g: Stewart describes the mountain wall north of Bengal as a continuation of the Caucasus and calls it a 'stupendous Tartar bulwark' that the Mughals and other Muslim conquerors had always thought impassable. On the same page he says the Jesuit account of Tibet in Du Halde was compiled 'from Tartar relations'. Here 'Tartar' simply means everything beyond the mountains.
p.q: This stupendous Tartar bulwark had ever been held impassable by the Mogols, and all other Mussulman conquerors of India:
p.s: John Stewart (Philosophical Transactions, 1777)
p.pe: none named; Tartary as the lands north of India

p.h: 'Tat': the Tatars' word for outsiders
p.g: In the southern Crimean valleys Pallas finds people descended from Greeks and other settlers, strangers to the Tatar and above all the Mongol race. The 'original natives' of the Crimea, he says, look on them as aliens and call them by the scornful name 'Tat'. A later footnote derives it from the Turkish 'Mur-Tat', renegade.
p.q: …and who were strangers to the Tartar race, but especially to that of the Mongoles: hence the original natives of Crim-Tartary consider them as aliens, and point them out by the contemptible name of Tat.
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas (English translation, 1812 edition)

p.h: 'Abakan Tatars': the Kirghiz' descendants in 1895
p.g: Radloff notes that the Yenisei inscriptions were left mostly by the Kirghiz, and that their descendants still form a large part of the Turkic population there, 'the Abakan Tatars and Soyots'. In the nineteenth century Russian usage called many Siberian Turkic groups 'Tatars'. The same people who carved runic stones in the early Middle Ages were called Tatars by the time Radloff wrote.
p.q: Als die Russen sie im XVI. Jahrhundert im südlichen Theile des Jenisseischen Gouvernements kennen lernten, waren die Kirgisen vollkommene Türken und noch jetzt bilden Nachkommen der Kirgisen einen grossen Theil der türkischen Bevölkerung desselben Gebietes, der Abakan-Tataren und Sojonen.
p.s: Wilhelm Radloff, Die alttuerkischen Inschriften der Mongolei (1895)
p.pe: Kirghiz (Khakas), called Abakan Tatars in Radloff's time
p.t: When the Russians came to know them in the sixteenth century in the southern part of the Yenisei province, the Kirghiz were complete Turks, and even now descendants of the Kirghiz form a large part of the Turkic population of that area, the Abakan Tatars and Soyots.
p.c: Radloff's own ethnographic judgement; his claim that the Kirghiz were first a non-Turkic people rests on a Chinese remark about red hair and blue eyes.
p.n: Checked against the page image.
p.tg: abakan tatars kirghiz khakas yenisei siberian tatars

p.h: Votyaks are not Tartars
p.g: Stopping at the Votyak hamlet of Sowialova, Chappe notes that some authors had counted the Votyaks among the Tartars, but that he could see no connection between the two peoples. It is a small example of a traveller correcting the catch-all use of the word.
p.q: Sowialova est un Hameau habité par des Wotiakes. La singularité de ce Peuple & de leur habillement me détermina à m'y arrêter une partie de la journée. Quelques Auteurs ont placé les Wotiakes au nombre des Tartares, mais je n'ai reconnu aucun rapport entre ces deux Nations.
p.s: Jean Chappe d'Auteroche
p.t: Sowialova is a hamlet inhabited by Votyaks. The peculiarity of this people and of their dress made me decide to stop there part of the day. Some authors have placed the Votyaks among the Tartars, but I recognised no relation between these two nations.

p.h: Kamchatka's people pushed out by the 'East Tartar kingdoms'
p.g: Steller argues that the Itelmens once lived outside China in the Mongol steppe along the Amur and gradually withdrew north and east along the Sea of Okhotsk as the 'East Tartar kingdoms' rose. In a footnote on the same page he links the ending -men in their own name, Itelmen, to the Turkic and Tatar word men ('I'). It is a scholar's hypothesis based on language, looks and customs, not a tradition of the people themselves.
p.q: Was die argumenta affirmativa anbelanget, daß diese Völker ehedem ausserhalb China in der mungalischen Steppe unter dem Amur gewohnet, und sich bey Aufrichtung derer ostlich-tartarischen Reiche nach und nach immer weiter an der penschinischen See retiriret
p.s: Georg Wilhelm Steller (ed. J. B. Scherer, 1774)
p.t: As for the positive arguments that these peoples formerly lived outside China in the Mongol steppe below the Amur, and, when the East Tartar kingdoms were set up, withdrew little by little ever further along the Penzhina Sea [Sea of Okhotsk]
p.c: Steller's own speculation; he says he wrote it from memory without any books.
p.tg: itelmen origins amur east tartary migration

p.h: 'The high plains of Tartary' are not the centre of Asia
p.g: Explaining why he calls his book 'Central Asia', Humboldt warns that terms like 'Central Asia' and 'High Asia' are used loosely. Travellers from India who cross the Himalaya to the sacred lakes of Tibet, on the plateau once called 'the high plains of Tartary', are in fact as far from the true centre of Asia as a Siberian at Tobolsk.
p.q: Lorsque les voyageurs de l'Inde franchissent la chaîne de l'Himalaya … et arrivent aux deux Lacs Sacrés, sur le plateau que l'on a cru devoir nommer jadis « les hautes plaines de la Tartarie, » ils marchent sans doute vers l'Asie centrale, mais ils se trouvent encore … aussi éloignés du centre de l'Asie que le sont des habitants de la Sibérie sous le parallèle de Tobolsk
p.s: Alexander von Humboldt
p.t: When travellers from India cross the Himalaya … and reach the two Sacred Lakes, on the plateau that people once saw fit to call 'the high plains of Tartary', they are no doubt heading towards Central Asia, but they are still … as far from the centre of Asia as are the inhabitants of Siberia on the parallel of Tobolsk
p.tg: tartary map label central asia tibet

p.h: Uzbek speech: a Persian-laced variety of 'Tatar'
p.g: Counting the peoples of Bukhara, Eversmann reckons Uzbeks at a quarter and Tajiks at three quarters of the townspeople. He calls the Uzbeks' language a variety of Tatar, known as Türki, which the Tatars can understand, though heavily mixed with Persian; Persian is the main language of the city. It shows how a Tatar-speaker from Siberia heard the Turkic languages of Central Asia as one family.
p.q: Die Sprache der Usbeken ist eine Abart der tatarischen Sprache, welche Türki genannt wird, so dass die Tataren sie verstehen können: sie ist aber sehr mit persischen Wörtern gemischt. Die Tadschiken sprechen persisch, und dieses ist hier die Hauptsprache, denn wenn ein Usbek mit einem Tadschik spricht, so wird persisch gesprochen.
p.s: Eduard Eversmann
p.pe: Uzbeks, Tajiks and Jews of Bukhara; Tatars of Russia
p.t: The language of the Uzbeks is a variety of the Tatar language which is called Türki, so that the Tatars can understand it: but it is much mixed with Persian words. The Tajiks speak Persian, and this is the main language here, for when an Uzbek speaks with a Tajik, Persian is spoken.
p.c: The same page carries a harsh tirade against the Bukharans' character: prejudice, not observation.

p.h: Tatars by the rivers, reindeer people to the north, camel herders on the steppe
p.g: What Yermak is said to have heard about Siberia before setting out: a map in words that sorts the peoples. The Tatars live along the Tura, Tobol and Irtysh and travel by boat and horse; the Ostyaks and Samoyeds of the Ob ride reindeer and dogs and live on fish; Kalmyks, Mongols and the Kazakh horde ride camels on the steppe. 'Tatar' here is one people among many, not a label for all Siberians.
p.q: по Турѣ же и по Тоболу живутъ Татара, ѣздятъ въ лодкахъ и на коняхъ. А Тоболъ палъ въ Иртышъ; и на Иртышѣ царство близь устья и многіе Татара, и Иртышъ палъ въ Обь, а Обь рѣка пала въ море двѣма устьи, а по ней живутъ Остяки и Самоѣдь, ѣздятъ на оленяхъ и псахъ и кормятся рыбами; а по степи Калмыки и Мунгалы и казачья орда, ѣздятъ на вельбудахъ
p.s: Kungur (Remezov) chronicle, article 9 (1880 printed text)
p.pe: Siberian Tatars, Voguls, Ostyaks, Samoyeds, Kalmyks, Mongols, Kazakhs
p.t: and along the Tura and the Tobol live Tatars, who travel in boats and on horses. The Tobol falls into the Irtysh; and on the Irtysh near its mouth is a tsardom and many Tatars; the Irtysh falls into the Ob, and the Ob falls into the sea by two mouths, and along it live Ostyaks and Samoyeds, who ride reindeer and dogs and feed on fish; and on the steppe the Kalmyks and Mongols and the Kazakh horde, who ride camels
p.c: Framed as hearsay Yermak gathered from people on the Chusovaya; written down long afterwards.

p.h: Two different 'Tartar' conquests of China
p.g: In Peking Bell retells the history as it was told to him: about five hundred years earlier 'western Tartars' (the Mongols) broke through the Great Wall and ruled China until driven out; then in the 1640s the Manchus conquered the whole empire. The passage shows that 'Tartar' covered both peoples, centuries apart.
p.q: However, about five hundred years ago, the western Tartars found means to get through the wall, and, with a powerful army of horse, entered the country, carrying terror along with them wherever they went. … From this time they enjoyed long peace, till the fatal year one thousand six hundred and forty, when the Mantzur Tartars conquered the whole empire of China; which conquest they retain to this day;
p.s: John Bell (Travels, 1763)
p.c: Bell's dates are approximate: the Manchu conquest of Beijing was in 1644.

p.h: Scythians 'called at the present day Tartars'
p.g: The humanist Poggio Bracciolini, writing up travellers' reports in Rome, describes an envoy from 'upper India' who crossed the lands of the northern Scythians on his way west. Poggio adds that these Scythians are now called Tartars, a typical Renaissance habit of mapping the new name onto the classical one.
p.q: Travelling through the country of the northern Scythians, who are called at the present day Tartars, and of the Parthians, for the space of several months, he arrived at length at the Euphrates ; then, having embarked at Tripoli, he proceeded to Venice, and afterwards to Florence.
p.s: Poggio Bracciolini (translated by J. Winter Jones, 1857)
p.c: Poggio relays an envoy's report through an interpreter; the Scythian identification is a learned label, not observation.

p.h: Altyn Obo, the Tatars' 'hill of gold'
p.g: At Kerch's museum Spencer saw finds from a mound opened in 1830 that the Tatars called Altyn Obo, 'hill of gold', and which was claimed to be the tomb of Mithridates. The gold vases and ornaments justified the name, he says, though the best had gone to St Petersburg. The Tatars named the mound; the treasures were Greek work.
p.q: we then extended our promenade to the Museum, the collection of which has been considerably augmented since the opening of a tumulus in 1830, called by the Tartars, Altyn Obo, or the hill of gold ; pretended to have been the tomb of Mithridates.
p.s: Edmund Spencer
p.c: The 1830 excavation was of the Kul-Oba kurgan; Spencer's 'Altyn Obo' may conflate names. He himself says the finds were 'unquestionably of Grecian workmanship'.
p.tg: kurgan gold kerch museum place names

p.h: 'Kurgan': the grave of a Tatar prince
p.g: Visiting saltpetre works in the black-earth country near Voronezh, Gmelin found the heaps of leached earth called 'saltpetre kurgans' by the Ukrainians. He explains that the word kurgan means the burial of a Tatar prince, over whom earth five or six fathoms high was heaped as a sign of his presence, and promises to open some real princely kurgans when he can. It shows how, in 1760s Russia, the great steppe mounds were all assumed to be Tatar graves.
p.q: in der That haben ihnen auch die Maloroßianer die Benennung, Salpeter-Kurganen gegeben, ein Wort, welches so viel als das Begräbniß eines Tatarischen Fürsten bedeutet, auf dem die Erde fünf oder sechs Faden hoch zum Zeichen seiner Gegenwart …
p.s: Samuel Gottlieb Gmelin
p.pe: Ukrainian saltpetre workers, about old Tatar burial mounds
p.t: and indeed the Little Russians [Ukrainians] have given them the name saltpetre kurgans, a word that means the burial of a Tatar prince, over which the earth [is heaped] five or six fathoms high as a sign of his presence …
p.c: The idea that every kurgan is a Tatar prince's grave is the folk explanation of the time; many steppe mounds are far older.

p.h: The Nogays: a fragment of the Golden Horde
p.g: Alexander describes the Nogays' faces and then explains who they are: a part of the Golden Horde scattered by Timur (Tamerlane), whose wars shattered the Horde in the 1390s. It is a short, fairly accurate piece of steppe history attached to a first-hand description.
p.q: Their noses are short, eyes elongated, and beards scanty : such are the Nogays, a party of the Golden Horde dispersed by Timoorlung (Tamarlane).
p.s: James Edward Alexander (1830)
p.c: The physical description reflects the racial typing common in travel books of his day.

p.h: 'The Tatars are exceedingly numerous'
p.g: When a large Mongol army under Chormaghun crossed the Oxus, Sultan Jalal al-Din of Khwarazm, though on bad terms with the caliph and the rulers of Anatolia and Syria, sent envoys to each of them. Rashid writes 'Mughul' (Mongol) in his own voice, but gives the substance of the warning as 'the Tatars are exceedingly numerous'. The same army is Mongol in the narrative and Tatar in the alarm.
p.q: پیش هریك رسول فرستاد و از حال وصول مغول خبر داد و مضمون پیغام آنك تاتار بغایت بسیارند و این نوبت زیادت از هر بار
p.s: Rashid al-Din (Persian text ed. E. Blochet, 1911)
p.t: He sent an envoy to each of them and gave news of the Mongols' coming; the substance of the message was that the Tatars are exceedingly numerous, and this time more than ever before.
p.c: Reported speech summarised by Rashid some seventy years later.

p.h: The Su-Mongols, 'also called Tartars after the river Tartar'
p.g: Back in Astrakhan in 1707, de Bruyn adds a note from older books: in 1246 the Tartars chose 'Kuine' (Güyük) as their ruler, calling themselves Moals or Mongals. Their land, Mongol, held four nations, among them the water Mongols, also called Tartars after a river Tartar that runs through their country. This is the explanation given by the friar John of Plano Carpini in the 1240s, repeated second-hand.
p.q: En l'an 1246, ils choisirent pour chef de la Tartarie un certain Kuine, qu'ils surnommérent Gog Cham, c'est-à-dire, Roi ou Empereur, se nommant eux-mêmes Moales ou Mongales … les Saniongals, ou Mongales marins, qu'on nomme aussi Tartares, d'après la riviere de Tartar, qui traverse leur pais
p.s: Cornelis de Bruyn (Le Brun), repeating medieval sources, ultimately John of Plano Carpini
p.t: In the year 1246 they chose as head of Tartary a certain Kuine, whom they surnamed Gog Cham, that is, King or Emperor, calling themselves Moals or Mongals … the Saniongals, or sea Mongols, who are also called Tartars, after the river Tartar, which crosses their country
p.c: Copied from older books; 'Gog Cham' is presumably a garbled form of Güyük's name, not a link to Gog and Magog.
p.tg: name origin mongols tartar river carpini

p.h: Before they ruled, the Turks were ironsmiths
p.g: In his addenda Schott explains a note from the Chinese encyclopedias Hoan-jü-ki and Ma Tuan-lin: the chief Tu-lun of the S'en-sen took the title K'o-han (khagan, 'khan') in the time of T'ai-wu-ti (reigned 424 to 451), emperor of the Wei dynasty under which the 'Tatar people Topa' ruled northern China, and the Tu-kiu later followed his example. He adds that the S'en-sen were overthrown by the Tu-kiu, who had first served them as ironsmiths. Schott's point is that the title and these peoples are documented in Chinese records centuries before Chinggis Khan.
p.q: Heu-Uei (oder Juan-Uei) war der chinesische Name, unter welchem das tatarische Volk Topa (Tö-pö) über das von ihm eroberte nördliche China herrschte. … Die S'en-sen, von denen die chinesische Geschichte sagt, dass sie ein Stamm der Hiung-nu gewesen, waren eine Zeitlang im östlichen Turkistan mächtig, und unterlagen den Tu-kiu, die ihnen anfänglich Frohndienste (als Eisenschmiede) geleistet hatten.
p.s: Wilhelm Schott (explaining Chinese sources, the Hoan-jü-ki and Ma Tuan-lin)
p.pe: Topa (Tuoba) of northern China, the S'en-sen (Rouran) and the Tu-kiu (early Turks)
p.t: Heu-Uei (or Juan-Uei) was the Chinese name under which the Tatar people Topa (Tö-pö) ruled the northern China it had conquered. … The S'en-sen, who according to Chinese history were a tribe of the Hiung-nu, were for a time powerful in eastern Turkistan, and fell to the Tu-kiu, who had at first done forced labour for them (as ironsmiths).
p.c: Schott's romanisations are his own (Heu-Uei is the Later or Northern Wei; S'en-sen is usually written Rouran or Juan-juan).
p.tg: khagan title turks ironsmiths chinese sources

p.h: A Tatar gift that made Bogle look Russian
p.g: An eccentric official decided that English dress was exactly like Russian dress, because Bogle wore a tunic and square cap that the Lama had been given by 'some Turki Tatars'. Markham adds a footnote calling this 'an instance of the confusion caused by the indiscriminate use of the word Tatar or Tartar'.
p.q: the tunic which I wore, and also my cap, the cut of which was four-square instead of being round, had been made a present of to the Lama by some Turki Tatars.
p.s: George Bogle (edited by Clements R. Markham, 1876)

p.h: Yakuts who look and talk like Tartars
p.g: Lesseps notes that the Yakuts are strong and tall, that their features resemble those of the Tartars, and that people say the two languages are closely related. He only vouches for the fact that Yakuts speak very briefly and do not run their words together.
p.q: Les Yakoutes sont robustes & généralement grands; l'ensemble de leurs traits a quelque analogie avec la figure des Tartares; on dit même que les deux idiomes se rapportent beaucoup. Tout ce que je puis affirmer, c'est que les Yakoutes ont la parole extrêmement brève, & qu'ils ne lient point leurs mots.
p.s: Jean-Baptiste Barthelemy de Lesseps
p.t: The Yakuts are robust and generally tall; their features as a whole bear some likeness to those of the Tartars; it is even said that the two languages are closely related. All I can affirm is that the Yakuts speak extremely briefly and do not run their words together.
p.c: The language link was hearsay to Lesseps; Yakut (Sakha) is indeed a Turkic language, related to Tatar.

p.h: Tatar, Tartar, Mongol: the editor explains
p.g: In a footnote to a Russian chronicle's account of the siege of Kiev in 1240, printed in the same volume, Bretschneider explains the names. Russian annals always call the Mongols Tatars, Western chronicles call them Tartars, and so do Carpini, Rubruck and Marco Polo; but the name comes from a real Mongol-era tribe, the Tatar, which is how Muslim and Chinese writers spell it.
p.q: The Mongols are invariably termed Tatars in the Russian annals. The Hungarian and other Western chronicles of the thirteenth century call them Tartars. Piano Carpini, Rubruck, M. Polo, also write Tartar. But the original Mongol name of the tribe, from which this appellation is derived, was Tatar. Thus the Mohammedan and the Chinese authors spell the name.
p.s: E. Bretschneider, editor's footnote (Mediaeval Researches, 1888)
p.pe: Mongols, called Tatars in Russian annals
p.c: An editor's note from another part of the volume, not Yelü Chucai's text.

p.h: Could anyone know the name 'Tatar' in the 6th century?
p.g: In a note, Frähn discusses a 16th-century Ottoman writer who claimed the Persian king Anushirvan (6th century) built the Caspian Gates for fear of 'Turks and Tatars'. Frähn replies that although Arab writers mention the Tatars earlier than some scholars thought, the name can hardly have been known that early in western Asia. It is a scholarly warning against reading 'Tatar' back into ancient history.
p.q: denn erwähnen gleich Arabische Schriftsteller der Tataren früher, als in den trefflichen Mémoires sur l'Arménie T. II. p. 263 angemerkt ist; so früh kann man wohl kaum Bekanntschaft mit ihrem Namen im westl. Asien annehmen.
p.s: C. M. Frähn, editor's note (1823)
p.t: for although Arab writers mention the Tatars earlier than is noted in the excellent Mémoires sur l'Arménie (vol. II, p. 263), one can hardly assume that their name was known so early in western Asia.
p.c: Editorial, not Ibn Fadlan.
p.tg: tatar name anachronism caspian gates derbent

p.h: Proud heirs of Chinggis Khan
p.g: Bergmann reports that the Kalmyks counted themselves one people with the Mongols, remembered with pleasure the deeds of their forefathers under Chinggis and his successors, and that most of their princes traced their blood to him. No Kalmyk doubted that the heirs of that heroic stock could match those deeds again if there were more of them. He then records a Kalmyk asking him whether the Prussians had not been defeated by the Kalmyks, since some 4,000 had served in the Russian army against Prussia.
p.q: Die Kalmüken rechnen sich zu einem … Volke. Sie denken mit Wohlgefallen an die Thaten ihrer Vorältern unter Tschingis und dessen Nachfolgern. Der größte Theil der jetzigen Kalmükenfürsten ehrt in sich selbst das Blut jenes großen Helden, von welchem sie ihre Abkunft herleiten. Kein Kalmük zweifelt daran daß die Nachkommen des mongolischen Heldenstamms, die ehemaligen Thaten erreichen könnten, wenn eine größere Anzahl ihren Muth unterstützte.
p.s: Benjamin Bergmann
p.pl: Kalmyk steppe west of the lower Volga (Kalmykia)
p.t: The Kalmyks count themselves as one [Mongol] people. They think with pleasure of the deeds of their ancestors under Chinggis and his successors. Most of the present Kalmyk princes honour in themselves the blood of that great hero from whom they derive their descent. No Kalmyk doubts that the descendants of the Mongol heroic line could equal the deeds of old, if greater numbers backed up their courage.
p.c: One word is lost in the scan after 'zu einem'.

p.h: What 'Orda' meant
p.g: Nikitin passes 'the Orda' on the Volga. The editor explains that 'orda' (horde) was the name for the seats of the Tartar kings who ruled Russia, and later for the successor kingdoms such as the Golden Horde and the Crimean Horde. It shows that 'horde' named a royal seat or state, not just a mob of riders.
p.q: This is the name formerly given to the seats of the Tartar kings that ruled over Russia ; subsequently it was also applied to the different kingdoms that sprung up from the immense empire of Baty in the beginning of the fifteenth century ; as the Zolotaia Orda (golden or great orda), Krimskaia Orda, the Ordea of Crimea, etc, etc.
p.s: Editorial footnote in the 1857 Hakluyt Society edition
p.pe: Tartar khans who ruled Russia; the Golden Horde and Crimean Horde
p.tg: orda horde golden horde crimea etymology

p.h: Torghuts, Eleuths and the four branches of the Dzungar nation
p.g: The emperor's monument explains who the Torghuts were: one of the branches of the Eleuths. Four branches once made up the whole Dzungar ('Tchong-kar') nation; they split, the Eleuths dominated the rest, and in Kangxi's time the Torghut chief Ayuki fled with his people into Russian territory and settled on the 'Etchil', which Amiot's note identifies as the Volga.
p.q: Les Tourgouths sont une des branches des Eleuths. Quatre branches differentes formoient autrefois toute la nation de Tchong-kar. Il seroit difficile d'expliquer leur commune origine, sur laquelle d'ailleurs on ne sait rien de bien certain. Ces quatre branches se séparerent, & firent chacune une nation à part.
p.s: The Qianlong emperor (monument on the Torghut migration), translated by Joseph-Marie Amiot
p.t: The Torghuts are one of the branches of the Eleuths. Four different branches once formed the whole nation of Dzungar. It would be hard to explain their common origin, about which nothing very certain is known. These four branches separated and each became a nation of its own.

p.h: 'Sokpo, also called Giongar, that is to say, independent Tartary'
p.g: Describing Ladakh, Desideri lists its neighbours and names the land to the north as 'Sokpo, also called Giongar, that is to say, independent Tartary'. Sokpo is the Tibetan word for the Mongols, and Giongar is the Dzungar state. The same page describes Leh, the Ladakhi capital, as a town climbing a mountain to the palace and fort, with 'no large towns' elsewhere, only villages, farmsteads and castles.
p.q: On the former side it borders on Baltistan, towards the north on Caxkar and some parts of the kingdom of Sokpo, also called Giongar, that is to say, independent Tartary.
p.s: Ippolito Desideri, in C. Wessels's English translation of the Italian manuscript (1924)
p.c: Translation by Wessels from the manuscript; Desideri knew Ladakh first hand but the Dzungar lands only by report.

p.h: The 'Water Mongols', named Tartars after the river Tartar
p.g: In Ramusio's Italian 'Two journeys to Tartary', drawn from the papal envoys of 1245 to 1247, the land called 'Mongal, or Tartaria' once held four peoples: the Yeka Mongol ('great Mongols'), the Su Mongol ('water Mongols'), who were the Tartars proper, named after a river Tartar that watered their land, and the Merkit and the Mecrit. Chinggis came from the first and conquered the rest.
p.q: Hebbe anticamente quattro Popoli (come si dice) il primo Popolo in lingua loro diceuasi Iekamongal, cioè, grandi Mongali. Il secondo, Summongal, cioè, Aquatici Mongali, che erano essi Tartari da un fiume Tartar cosi nominati, ilquale bagna il suo paese. Il terzo Merkath. Il quarto, Metrith.
p.s: John of Plano Carpini (and Simon of Saint-Quentin), via Vincent of Beauvais, in Ramusio's Italian 'Due viaggi in Tartaria'
p.pe: Mongols and Tatars (Carpini's four peoples of 'Mongal')
p.t: It anciently had four peoples (as is said): the first people in their language was called Yekamongal, that is, great Mongols. The second, Summongal, that is, water Mongols, who were the Tartars themselves, so named from a river Tartar which waters their country. The third, Merkath. The fourth, Metrith.
p.c: A medieval Latin report reached Ramusio through Vincent of Beauvais's encyclopedia; the river Tartar is a folk explanation of the name.

p.h: Tungus who looked like the 'Pekin Tartars'
p.g: Dobell says the Tungus he met on the Okhotsk to Yakutsk road looked strikingly like 'the Tartars, who have conquered China', meaning the Manchus. His two Cantonese servants, who had seen Manchu bannermen in Beijing, agreed, and the servants and the Tungus greeted each other as 'brats', Russian for brothers. It is a vivid glimpse of 'Tartar' meaning Manchu in an English book of 1830.
p.q: means of my two Chinese servants, who were born in Canton, and had seen many of the Pekin Tartars, and were themselves struck with the likeness between them and the Tongusees. They always called each other brats (which means, in Russian, brothers) when they met
p.s: Peter Dobell
p.pe: Tungus (Evenki), compared with the Manchus of Beijing
p.c: A comparison of faces made by the author and his servants; it proves nothing about ancestry.

p.h: Sog-po and Hor: the Tibetan words for 'Tartar'
p.g: Das's index to the Tibetan history glosses the Tibetan word Sog po as 'Tartary or a Tartar', and Sog yul (Sog land) as 'Mongolia, Hor, Tartary'. The English word Tartar in this edition is therefore a translation of Tibetan words for the Mongols, not a name the Tibetan author used.
p.q: Sog-po, the Tibetan for Tartary or a Tartar … Sog-yul Mongolia, Hor, Tartary
p.s: Sarat Chandra Das, index to his edition of Sumpa Khenpo (Calcutta, 1908)

p.h: Mogores, named after Magog
p.g: Cruz says these peoples trade as far as Hormuz, border the Caspian and have the Tartars at their side. The Greeks called them Scythians, but across Asia they are called Mogores, a name he believes they kept from their ancestor Magog. It is a learned folk etymology linking the Mughals (from 'Mongol') to the biblical Magog.
p.q: Vem muitos delles cõ fazendas a Ormuz, confinẽ cõ ho mar Caspio, e ao lado com os Tartaros: e inda q̃ os gregos a estes chamẽ Scythas: por toda Asia mayor e menor sam chamados Mogores perseuerãdo nelles ha primeira denominaçam q̃ tomaram do pay Magog dõde decẽdem e se denominarã.
p.s: Gaspar da Cruz, O.P. (Tractado, Évora 1569)
p.pe: Mogores (Mughals and related Central Asian peoples) living beside the Tartars
p.t: Many of them come with goods to Hormuz; they border on the Caspian Sea, and at their side are the Tartars. And although the Greeks call these people Scythians, throughout Asia the greater and the lesser they are called Mogores, keeping the first name they took from their father Magog, from whom they descend and take their name.
p.c: The Magog derivation is Cruz's own guess; 'Mogor' actually comes from 'Mongol'.
