p.h: 'The Cossacks are a species of Tartars'
p.g: Passing through Cossack villages on the Khoper, Hanway describes clean, well-dressed people and women with crescent-shaped caps. He then files the Cossacks under 'Tartars', explaining that their name means freebooters. It shows how loosely an eighteenth-century Englishman used 'Tartar' for any steppe people on Russia's frontier, even Orthodox Russians.
p.q: The Cossacks are a species of tartars: their name signifies free-booters; but in these parts they are civilized, and faithful to the Russian government,
p.s: Jonas Hanway (Historical Account, 1753)

p.h: A Beijing emperor 'of Mongol race'
p.g: Baikov calls Beijing by its old Mongol name Kanbalyk (Khanbaliq) and reports that the reigning emperor, the 'Bogda', was of Mongol race, and that the last Chinese emperor hanged himself when the 'Mongols' took over China. He means the Manchus, who had taken Beijing in 1644. It is the Russian counterpart of the Western habit of calling the Manchus 'Tartars'.
p.q: А въ Китайскомъ Царствѣ въ Канбалыкѣ Царь Богда Мунгальскаго рода; а прежде того былъ Царь Китайскаго рода Даба; а какъ одолѣли Мунгальцы Китайскимъ Царствомъ, и тогда тотъ Даба Царь обѣсился
p.s: Fyodor Baikov (1788 Novikov printing)
p.pe: Manchus (Qing dynasty), called Mongols by Baikov
p.t: And in the Chinese Tsardom, in Kanbalyk, the tsar is the Bogda, of Mongol race; and before him there was a tsar of Chinese race, Daba; and when the Mongols overcame the Chinese Tsardom, that Tsar Daba hanged himself
p.c: Hearsay gathered while confined in Beijing. 'Daba' is Baikov's rendering of the Ming ruler (the Chongzhen emperor hanged himself in 1644).
p.tg: manchus qing khanbaliq beijing mongol race

p.h: Crimean and Nogai refugees in the Caucasus
p.g: Explaining why his book includes a Tatar vocabulary, Spencer says many Circassians knew the language and that Crimean and Nogai Tatars who had fled Russian rule were settled throughout the Circassian provinces. He adds that the word lists should disprove the common idea that Circassians and Tatars shared an origin.
p.q: many of the Circassians are not only acquainted with it, but we every where find, throughout the whole of these provinces, Krim and Nogay Tartars domiciliated, who, on the subjection of their country to the rule of Russia, fled into the Caucasus.
p.s: Edmund Spencer

p.h: The 'first Siberian Tartars' are Voguls
p.g: As soon as he crosses from Europe into Asia, Ides meets his first 'Siberian Tartars' on the Chusovaya river and names them Wogulski. These are the Voguls, today's Mansi, who speak an Ugric language and are not Turkic Tatars at all. The passage shows how 'Tartar' worked for travellers: it meant almost any native, non-Russian people east of the Urals.
p.q: we came too, and touched at a pleasant Shoar on the 25th of May, amongst the first Siberian Tartars, called Wogulski. … But the Wogulskian Tartars to which this River led us, are stupid Heathens
p.s: Evert Ysbrants Ides (English translation, 1706)
p.c: Ides's scorn ('stupid Heathens') is his own; he spent one night among them.

p.h: Moscow as a 'Tartar Rome'
p.g: Kohl opens his chapter on Moscow's churches with Madame de Staël's famous exclamation on first seeing the city: 'Voilà Rome Tatare'. It shows how Western Europeans used 'Tartar' as shorthand for Moscow's un-European look.
p.q: Madame de Staël, when she beheld Moscow … turned to her companions and exclaimed, “Voilà Rome Tatare.” The Russians themselves like to compare their city to that world subduer
p.s: J. G. Kohl (English abridged translation, 1844), quoting Madame de Staël
p.pe: Tartars as a byword for the Asiatic side of Russia
p.t: 'Voilà Rome Tatare' means 'There is a Tartar Rome'.
p.c: An anecdote repeated from De Staël's memoir, not Kohl's observation.

p.h: Kipchak: the boy born in a hollow tree
p.g: The legendary conqueror Oghuz Khan's officer died in battle, and his pregnant widow gave birth inside a hollow tree. The khan raised the boy and named him Kipchak, said to mean 'hollow tree' in old Turkish. The Kipchaks gave their name to the Dasht-i Kipchak, the steppe that later became Batu's Golden Horde.
p.q: she could find no other Place to retire to when her Time was come but an old Hollow-Tree; into which having crept when her Labour came on, she there brought forth a Son. … and gave him the Name of Kipzak, which signifies in the antient Turkish, an Hollow-Tree.
p.s: Abu'l Ghazi Bahadur Khan (English translation, 1730)
p.pe: Kipchaks (ancestors of the Golden Horde's Turkic subjects)
p.c: A folk etymology from the Oghuz legend.

p.h: The Turkmen: 'these Tartars' under Uzbek rule
p.g: In his essay on a possible Russian invasion of India, Conolly weighs whether Russia could win over the Turkmen, who then gave unwilling allegiance to 'their Oosbeg conquerors' at Khiva. He concludes the Turkmen would follow their interests, and that Russia, as in the Caucasus, might in time 'subdue these Tartars'. It shows 'Tartar' as a British strategic label for the Turkic peoples of the desert.
p.q: I am sure that the Toorkmuns would be chiefly influenced by what they thought their interests; and when I look to what we have done in Hindoostan, or, to speak nearer to the point, what the Russians have done in Persia, I cannot decide that they may not subdue these Tartars
p.s: Arthur Conolly (1834)
p.c: A political argument, not an observation.

p.h: The 'wild Tartars' with waist-long hair
p.g: Contarini separates the Tatars of the 'Lordo' between the Don and Volga, whom he calls brutes who live on milk and meat, from another numerous people beyond the Volga, called 'wild Tartars', with hair to their waists. He admits he did not visit the Lordo himself and relies on what he was told.
p.q: But there is said to be another tribe of Tartars living beyond the Volga, in an east-north-easterly direction, who are supposed to be very numerous. They wear long hair reaching to their waists, and are called wild Tartars. They wander in search of pasturage and water like the others; and, in the winter, when there is much cold and ice, they are said to come as far as Citracan
p.s: Ambrogio Contarini (translated by S. A. Roy, 1873)
p.pe: Tatars between the Don and Volga; 'wild Tartars' east of the Volga
p.c: Hearsay; Contarini's dislike of the Tatars shows throughout.

p.h: Samoyed and Tungus country, 'situated in Tartary'
p.g: The Latin title page of Gerritsz's 1612 collection announces Isaac Massa's description of the Samoyed and Tungus regions 'lying in Tartary', recently acquired by the Muscovite empire, with a Russian map translated into Latin. Here 'Tartary' is simply the name of the far north-east of Asia, not a kingdom.
p.q: Isaaci Massae Harlemensis Samoiediae atque Tingoessae, regionum ad Orientem ultra Fretum Weygats in Tartaria sitarum, nuperque Imperio Moscovitico adquisitarum descriptio
p.s: Hessel Gerritsz, title page (Latin version by R. Vitellius)
p.pl: Northern Siberia (east of the Vaygach Strait)
p.pe: Samoyeds and Tungus, in a land called Tartary
p.t: Isaac Massa of Haarlem's description of Samoyedia and Tingoesia, regions lying in Tartary to the east beyond the Vaygach Strait, and recently acquired by the Muscovite Empire

p.h: Uzbek means 'own master'
p.g: Muraviev explains the Uzbek name as 'own master' (uz = self, beg = master) and adds, with some irony, that since Muhammad Rahim Khan made himself absolute ruler, the Uzbeks of Khiva now called themselves 'khidmatgar', servants.
p.q: "Us" in Turkish signifies "self" and "Beg" master, so Usbeg may be translated as "Own Master." The name was appropriate enough up to the time of the reigning Khan, Mahomed Ragim, who, by ability, craft, and force, established himself as uncontrolled Ruler, since when his countrymen in Khiva style themselves "Khidmatgar" (servant) instead of "Usbeg."
p.s: Nikolai Muraviev (translated by W. S. A. Lockhart, 1871)
p.c: A popular folk etymology; the name probably comes from the 14th-century Golden Horde khan Özbeg.

p.h: 'Yusbek': a hundred lords, or 'he is the lord'?
p.g: Chardin gives two etymologies for the Uzbeks. Persians derived it from 'yuz' (a hundred) and 'bek' (lord), mocking a land split among a hundred petty princes; the Uzbeks rejected that and said it meant 'he is the lord'. He adds that Tartar and Turkish are one language, Turkish being a dialect of it.
p.q: They are called Yusbecks, at least if the Persian Etymology be true, by reason of the great number of Sovereign Princes by which the Tartars are Govern'd; for Yus, as well in the Language of the Tartars as Turks, which is but a Dialect of it, signifies a hundred, and Bek, Lords
p.s: Jean Chardin, 'The Coronation of Solyman III' (appended to the 1691 English edition)
p.pe: Uzbeks, whom Chardin calls the Tartars of Lesser Tartary

p.h: The Karakhitai: steppe exiles who swapped carts for camels
p.g: The envoy tells how Ta-shi (Yelu Dashi), a Khitan of the fallen Liao house, fled north-west with the frontier tribes, moving from pasture to pasture for years. Blocked by rocks and snow, they abandoned their carts, loaded their goods on camels, conquered the Muslim lands and founded an empire. After a regent princess was executed for killing her husband and a weak ruler took over, the realm decayed, and the few Khitan left had adopted Muslim customs and dress. It is a compact picture of a nomad people turning into a settled empire and then dissolving into its subjects.
p.q: They were obliged to leave their carts behind, and to carry their baggage on camels. Thus they arrived in the country of the Hui-ho (Mohammedans), took possession of the land and founded an empire. … the empire fell into decay, and was finally destroyed by the Hui-ho. At the present day there are few of these people left, and they have adopted the customs and the dress of the Hui-ho.
p.s: Wu-ku-sun Chung-tuan (Wugusun Zhongduan), as written down by the recorder of the Pei shi ki (translated by E. Bretschneider, 1888)
p.c: Told from the Jin side; Bretschneider points to the fuller Liao history account in his Part II. The Changchun diary (W113, p.73) blames the fall on the Naiman prince Guchluk and the Sultan of Khwarazm rather than simply 'the Hui-ho'.

p.h: How the Nogais came to the Crimea
p.g: In his history chapter Reuilly says that when Mengli Giray became khan under Ottoman protection (1478), few Tatars actually lived in the Crimea; the khan settled thousands of Nogais captured in wars on the Volga, and his successors peopled the Kuban and the lands between the Don and Dniester the same way.
p.q: When the sovereignty of the peninsula passed to Menguely Guerai, there were not many Tartars amongst its inhabitants; but the wars which he carried on with them on the banks of the Volga, afforded him an opportunity to bring with him into the Crimea, several thousand Nogays, who were obliged to establish themselves in that country.
p.s: Jean Reuilly (English translation, 1807)
p.c: Compiled history from earlier authors; the claim of few Tatars before 1478 is his source's view.

p.h: 'Godless Moabites, called Tatars'
p.g: The Galician chronicler opens the Kalka story with an 'unheard-of army': godless Moabites 'called Tatars' who fell on the Polovtsian land. Even the greatest Cuman chief could not stand against them. After the rout the Tatars 'went back to their vezhi', the steppe word for nomad tent camps. The biblical name Moabites shows how the chronicler fitted a new enemy into scripture.
p.q: Приде неслыханая рать: безбожніи Моавитяне, рекомыи Татарове, придоша на землю Половецькую. Половцемь же ставшимъ, Юрьгій Кончаковичь бѣ болійше всихъ Половець, не може стати противу лицо ихъ; бѣгающи же ему, и мнози избьени быша, до рѣкы Днѣпра, Татарове же возвратишася, идоша въ вѣжа своя.
p.s: Hypatian Chronicle (Galician-Volhynian part), PSRL vol. 2 (1843)
p.t: There came an unheard-of army: the godless Moabites, called Tatars, came onto the Polovtsian land. The Polovtsy made a stand, but Iurii Konchakovich, who was greatest of all the Polovtsy, could not stand against their face; he fled, and many were killed, as far as the river Dnieper, and the Tatars turned back and went to their tent camps.
p.c: Written decades after 1223; the date 6732 was added by a later copyist.
p.tg: moabites tatar name kalka vezhi polovtsy

p.h: Kalmyks and Mongols as heirs of Chinggis Khan's Tartars
p.g: After recounting how China destroyed the Zunghar Kalmyk state in 1757, Chappe says the other Kalmyk branches kept the courage they had under Chinggis Khan, whose conquests were made with these peoples, and that the Mongols between China and Siberia descend from the same Tartars. Here 'Tartar' means the Mongol-speaking peoples as a whole.
p.q: Plusieurs autres branches des Calmouks habitent encore dans cette partie de l'Asie. Ils ont conservé le courage & la bravoure qu'ils avoient du temps de Gengis-kan & de ses Successeurs. C'est avec ces Peuples que ces Princes firent tant de conquêtes & donnerent la loi à l'Asie. Les Mongales situés entre la Chine & la Sibérie descendent des mêmes Tartares, & ils ne sont pas moins courageux.
p.s: Jean Chappe d'Auteroche
p.t: Several other branches of the Kalmyks still live in that part of Asia. They have kept the courage and bravery they had in the time of Chinggis Khan and his successors. It was with these peoples that those princes made so many conquests and laid down the law to Asia. The Mongols situated between China and Siberia descend from the same Tartars and are no less courageous.
p.c: Chappe learned of the Zunghar collapse from Kalmyk refugees and Russians in Siberia; his view of the Kalmyks as Chinggis Khan's own army is a loose generalisation.

p.h: 'Tartar nations': Kalmyks, Mongols and Buryats
p.g: In a note Coxe praises Pallas's new work on the 'Tartars' living between Siberia and the Great Wall, whom Pallas divides into Kalmyks, Mongols and Buryats, split in religion between shamanism and the Dalai Lama's Buddhism. It shows 'Tartar' used in 1780 as an umbrella term for Mongolic peoples.
p.q: No writer has placed the religion and history of the Tartar nations in a more explicit point of view than Mr. Pallas … concerning the Tartars, who inhabit parts of Siberia, and the territory which lies between that country and the Chinese wall … as they are divided into Calmucs, Mongols, and Burats.
p.s: William Coxe (note on P. S. Pallas)

p.h: Murad Beg of Kunduz, 'a Tartar' and a robber
p.g: In his preface Wilson blames the failure of the expedition on Murad Beg, the Uzbek chief of Kunduz, whom he calls 'a Tartar of activity and ambition, but a barbarian and a robber'. Moorcroft's own journal (T0023, n459, p.446) quotes Murad Beg answering a plea to keep his word: 'What have I, what has an Uzbek to do with character?' Here 'Tartar' means an Uzbek.
p.q: His death, and the dissensions which ensued amongst his sons, transferred the ascendancy to Murad Beg, a Tartar of activity and ambition, but a barbarian and a robber.
p.s: Horace Hayman Wilson (editor's preface, 1841)
p.c: The editor's judgment, written from Moorcroft's papers and hostile to Murad Beg.

p.h: Turkmens with 'Tartar' faces
p.g: Fraser sorts the Turkmen tribes by how 'Tartar' they looked: the Teke most, the Goklen less, the Yomut least, with big differences even within one family. It shows 'Tartar' being used as a physical type rather than a nation.
p.q: The Tuckehs have a great deal of the Tartar physiognomy; many of the men were tall, stout and well made, with scanty beards, eyes small, and drawn up at the corners ; high cheek bones, and small flat noses: some on the contrary had handsome features, more resembling those of Europeans than Asiatics.
p.s: James Baillie Fraser
p.c: Racial typing typical of the period.

p.h: 'Mongul Tartary' beyond Lake Baikal
p.g: Holman calls the whole country between Lake Baikal and the trading towns of Kiakhta (Russian) and Maimachin (Chinese) 'Mongul Tartary', wild and rugged and full of wild animals. Here the old map name Tartary survives as a regional label. A page earlier he describes the Buryats as 'of Mongul origin'.
p.q: The whole country between these points and the Baikal, which has the name of Mongul Tartary, is wild and rugged in the extreme, and often dangerous to the traveller in consequence of the great number of wild animals that inhabit it.
p.s: James Holman (1825)
p.c: Holman did not travel to Kiakhta himself; this is a general description.

p.h: The people of Spiti are 'completely of Tartar appearance'
p.g: On his side trip to Spiti (Piti), Trebeck described the people as 'completely of Tartar appearance in form and face', then went on to their dress, drinking, and the braided hair of the women decorated with amber and coral. It shows 'Tartar' used by British travellers for any Tibetan or Central Asian looking highlander.
p.q: The people of Piti are completely of Tartar appearance in form and face; the men are less robust and better grown than those more to the north, and the women are far from good looking.
p.s: George Trebeck (journal, edited by H. H. Wilson, 1841)
p.c: A physical stereotype, not an ethnic identification.

p.h: The Natukhai, 'originally Tartars'
p.g: Vorontsov told Spencer he had been visited at Anapa by a prince of the Natukhai, a tribe 'originally Tartars' who had fled into the Caucasus after Russia conquered the lands of the Kuban and Azov. Spencer calls them Russia's most uncompromising enemies there. The Natukhai are usually counted as a Circassian (Adyghe) tribe.
p.q: he had been honoured with a visit from a Circassian prince, chief of the Natouhay tribe, originally Tartars, who had fled into the mountains of the Caucasus upon the conquest of the provinces on the banks of the Kouban and the sea of Azov.
p.s: Edmund Spencer, reporting Count Vorontsov
p.pe: Natukhai (Circassian tribe said to be of Tatar origin)
p.c: The Tatar origin is a claim reported at second hand.

p.h: Chatyr-Dag, the 'Tent Mountain'
p.g: Hablizl notes that one of the two great mountains closing the valley near Alushta, thought to be the highest in all Taurida, is called by the Tatars Chatyr-Dag, 'Tent Mountain', because from a distance its summit looks like a tent.
p.q: Sein Gipfel hat von weitem die Gestalt eines Zeltes, und eben … deswegen wird er von den Tataren Tschatür-dag … oder Tschatür-dagi genannt, welches auf deutsch so viel als Zeltberg heißt.
p.s: Karl Ludwig Hablizl (German translation, 1789)
p.t: From a distance its summit has the shape of a tent, and for that very reason the Tatars call it Chatyr-Dag or Chatyr-Dagi, which in German means as much as 'Tent Mountain'.

p.h: Tibetan robbers 'erroneously styled Kalmaks'
p.g: On a stage called 'the place of thieves', where robbers hid in underground burrows, Hodgson adds a footnote: the Catholic missionary Huc wrote much about Tibetan robbers, who were black-tent Tibetan nomads, 'erroneously styled Kalmaks'. It shows 'Kalmak' being stretched to cover any nomad raiders of Inner Asia.
p.q: M. Huc in his narrative speaks much of the robbers of Tibet, who, he says, are Kalos or black-tent nomadic Tibetans, erroneously styled Kalmaks. They are mounted gang robbers.
p.s: Footnote by B. H. Hodgson, summarising Évariste Huc
p.c: An editorial note, not Campbell's informants.

p.h: Milton's 'roving Tartar' on the Himalaya
p.g: Standing on the Pir Panjal pass, Vigne quotes in a footnote Milton's famous simile of a vulture bred on Imaus (the Himalaya), 'whose snowy ridge the roving Tartar bounds'. It shows the English literary picture of the Tartar that travellers carried with them: a wandering herdsman on the far side of the great mountains.
p.q: On Imaus bred, Whose snowy ridge the roving Tartar bounds, Dislodging from a region scarce of prey. To gorge the flesh of lambs or yeanling kids, On hills where flocks are fed, flies towards the springs Of Ganges or Hydaspes, Indian streams
p.s: John Milton, Paradise Lost iii.431, quoted in a footnote by Vigne
p.c: A poem, not a report; included for the image of the Tartar it carries.

p.h: Rhubarb from Tartary
p.g: After seeing a wild rhubarb near the snowline in Bhutan, Saunders notes that the true medicinal rhubarb grows in cold country: the north of China, Tartary and parts of Russia. He then describes his own experiment drying a root, which lost far less weight than the traders claimed. Rhubarb was one of the great goods Europeans associated with Tartary.
p.q: The true rhubarb (Rheum palmatum) is likewise the native of a cold climate ; and though China supplies us with much of this drug, it is known to be the growth of its more northern provinces, Tartary, and part of the Russian dominions.
p.s: Robert Saunders (Philosophical Transactions, 1789)
p.pe: none named; Tartary as a region north of China
p.c: A general statement of where rhubarb grows, not an observation of Tartary itself.
p.tg: rhubarb trade botany tartary as region

p.h: A great khan at Samarkand, heir of Tamerlane
p.g: Perry reports that the lands between Siberia and the Caspian hold many hordes of Tartars, each with its own chief, but many recognise one principal khan at Samarkand said to descend from Tamerlane. He adds that their religion is close to Islam, except that they eat horse meat, which the Turks and Crimean Tartars refuse. By 1700 Samarkand had no such overlord; this is hearsay.
p.q: Many of them acknowledge one principal Cham as their Chief, who has his Residence at Samarcand, … and derives his Pedigree, as 'tis said, from the Great Tamerlane.
p.s: Captain John Perry (The State of Russia, 1716)
p.pl: Samarkand and the steppe east of the Volga
p.pe: Bukharans, Mongols, Kalmyks and other 'Hordes of Tartars'
p.c: Hearsay; Perry never went east of the Volga steppe.

p.h: Ancient Greek place names 'corrupted by the Tartars'
p.g: In a note on Strabo's temple of Achilles at the mouth of the Sea of Azov, the translators quote the French scholars Du Theil and Peyssonel, who wondered whether the Tatar fort of 'Achou' was the ancient Achilleum, its Greek name worn down in Tatar mouths. It is a small example of how Tatar place names were layered over Greek ones on the Black Sea coast.
p.q: Is not the fort of Achou, which is 8 leagues more to the east on the Palus Maeotis, the true Achilleum, the name being corrupted and abridged by the Tartars?
p.s: Footnote by the 1854 translators (H. C. Hamilton and W. Falconer), quoting Peyssonel via Du Theil
p.pe: Tatars of the Azov coast (Crimean or Nogai), as seen by eighteenth century French scholars
p.c: Editorial conjecture, not Strabo's text.
p.tg: place names sea of azov footnote greek colonies

p.h: Reindeer Koryaks with 'Tartar' features
p.g: Meeting a Chukchi man and the Reindeer Koryaks in northern Kamchatka, Dobell sorts them by looks: the Chukchi resemble North American Indians, while the Koryaks have the high cheekbones and small eyes 'by which the Tartars are distinguished'. Here 'Tartar' is simply a label for an East Asian face type, not a nation he met.
p.q: The Reindeer Karaikees, on the contrary, have those very high cheek bones and small eyes, as well as those features generally by which the Tartars are distinguished; and they certainly resemble much the Northern Chinese.
p.s: Peter Dobell
p.pe: Reindeer Koryaks, compared with Tartars and northern Chinese
p.c: A racial generalisation typical of the period.

p.h: The sultan who 'vanquished the Tatars'
p.g: In the dedication al-Umari praises the Mamluk sultan al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun as king of Arabs, Persians and Turks and 'vanquisher of the Rum, the Franks, the Georgians, the Armenians and the Tatars'. For a Mamluk official the Tatars are one of the great enemy peoples, set beside the Crusaders.
p.q: هازم الروم والفرنج والكرج والأرمن والتتار ، سلطان البسيطه
p.s: al-Umari (Arabic text ed. Ahmad Zaki Pasha, Cairo 1924)
p.pe: Tatars (Ilkhanid Mongols), enemies of the Mamluks
p.t: vanquisher of the Rum, the Franks, the Georgians, the Armenians and the Tatars, sultan of the wide earth
p.c: Court flattery; the Mamluks defeated Ilkhanid armies, notably in 1303, and made peace with them in 1323.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR is partly garbled); vowel marks omitted.

p.h: Kuban means wild hog
p.g: Woodroofe says the Chuvash were descended from the Kuban Tartars and explains that 'Kooban' means a wild hog in Russian, a name given for their fierce nature, because Ivan the Terrible found them harder to subdue than the Crimean or Nogai Tartars. It is a folk etymology (the Kuban is a river), but a vivid example of how names for Tartar groups were explained.
p.q: Kooban, in the Russian language signifies a wild hog; which name was given to these Tartars on account of their fierce and savage nature, having cost Ivan Wassilowitz more trouble to subdue them,
p.s: Captain Thomas Woodroofe, his 1740 journal as printed by Jonas Hanway (1753)
p.c: A folk etymology: the Kuban Tatars were named after the Kuban river, and the Chuvash are not descended from them.

p.h: Proof by word endings and faces
p.g: He concludes that the Kamchadals once lived in 'Mungalia beyond the river Amur' and were one people with the Mongols, pushed out to the edge of the world by 'Eastern conquerors', much as the Lapps and Samoyeds were pushed north in Europe. His evidence is a list of word endings he thought sounded 'Mungal Chinese', and a list of shared bodily features and supposed character traits.
p.q: Thus it appears likely, that the Kamtschadales lived formerly in Mungalia beyond the river Amur, and made one people with the Mungals, which is farther confirmed by the following observations, such as the Kamtschadales having several words common to the Mungal Chinese language, as their terminations in ong, ing, oang, chin, cha, ching
p.s: Stepan Krasheninnikov (translated by James Grieve, 1764)
p.c: Resemblance in word endings is weak evidence, and the character traits he lists are prejudice, not observation.
